concepts.persona: Chess coach: master-strength player, twenty years coaching club players from their first games to 2000+
concepts.perspective_summary: Under 1000 a rating moves for one reason only: the player stops leaving pieces where they can be taken, and that is a habit built in the half-second before the piece lands, not an understanding gained from an evaluation afterwards. What a live coach does that no app has done is sit beside the student, stop their hand, ask one question ("what defends that square?"), let them play the bad move when they insist and feel the recapture, come back to the same mistake next week in a fresh position, and say nothing at all about the ninety percent of moves that do not matter at their level.

concepts.name: Hold on
concepts.one_liner: A game against a beginner-strength engine where the coach stops your hand before a hanging move lands, asks one question, and lets you take it back or play it anyway and feel the punishment.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The interrupt before the move. Every product in the world points out the blunder after it was played: Game Review, the eval bar turning red, this repo's own coach.py printing "Your knight on e5 is undefended!" after the move is committed. Here, when you release a piece on a square that hands over material, the piece does not land. It hovers, ghosted on the target square, the board dims one shade, and the coach says: "Hold on. Before you let go of the knight: what defends e5?" You answer with your fingers, by tapping squares on the board, never by typing. The coach responds to the squares you tapped ("The c6 knight does guard e5. Is that the only defender? Look at the pawns."). Then you choose: "Take it back" (the piece floats home and you pick again) or "Play it anyway", in which case the engine takes immediately and the coach says one sentence: "That's the one. Knight for pawn. Now you've felt it." On the other ninety percent of moves nothing happens at all: no eval bar, no labels, no "inaccuracy", no move list. The interrupt fires only on what decides games under 1000: a piece left where it can be taken for a net loss of two points or more, a free capture ignored, a mate in one allowed or missed. A coach who is silent except when it matters, with a hand on your wrist, is not in the world.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh and everyone under 1000: knows how the pieces move, opens 1.e4, loses to hung pieces and one-move threats, has studied nothing, will not read a manual, has a phone. Not for anyone who already runs the blunder check by habit; they would find the silence boring, which is the point.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a board, white pieces at the bottom, starting position, and one line above it in the coach's voice: "Your move. I'll stay quiet unless it matters." Nothing else on screen except a small badge on the far side reading "Black: Beginner" and a three-dot menu. 0 to 5 s: he taps the e2 pawn, the legal squares glow softly, he taps e4; the pawn lands; Black replies 1...e5 within half a second. 5 to 20 s: 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3. Nothing is said. The board stays quiet and he realises the coach meant it. 20 to 30 s: Black plays 4...Nxe4?! (in game one, Black follows a small scripted beginner tree out of 1.e4, built from the verified lesson positions, so that something hangs by move five whichever natural moves he plays; after move six Stockfish at Skill Level 1 takes over). He reaches for 5.Nc3, a developing move. The knight hovers over c3, the board dims, and the coach says: "Hold on. Their knight just took on e4. What can you take?" He looks, taps d3 or e4. "The d3 pawn takes it. A knight for a pawn. Take it back?" He taps "Take it back", plays 5.dxe4, and the coach says "That's it." and goes quiet again. Thirty seconds in he is a piece up, he found it himself, and he understands exactly what this page does and does not do. (Lesson 0001 verified this position: 5.dxe4 +3.9 at depth 20; 5.Nc3 loses 556 centipawns.)
concepts.core_loop: 1. You move (tap-tap or drag). 2. The engine gate runs silently: the current position was already searched to depth 12 while you were thinking, so only the position after your pending move needs a depth-10 search for the opponent's best reply, about 0.3 s. 3a. Clean: the piece lands, the opponent replies in under a second, silence. 3b. Gate fires: the piece hovers, the board dims, "Hold on." appears at once from the rule, and the coach's question streams in within a second. 4. You answer by tapping squares, or tap "Show me" and the refutation plays on the board as a ghost line (7.Nxe5 dxe5) and rewinds. 5. The coach replies to the squares you tapped. 6. "Take it back" or "Play it anyway". 7. If played anyway, the engine takes immediately, the coach says one sentence, the moment is recorded; after the second "play anyway" in a game the coach stops interrupting and saves the rest for the close. 8. The game ends (mate, or the Beginner bot resigns a queen down, so games actually finish) and the coach closes with two sentences and the hold-on moments as small boards: "Two hold-ons today, both pieces put on a square a pawn attacks. Here they are." One button: "Again". 9. The next game opens with one line that names the thing: "Watch the pawns today."
concepts.llm_role: Claude is called only when the gate fires (zero calls in a clean game, two to six in a typical beginner game) and once at the close. Every call is modelTier "quick" (about a second) because the chess is already settled by the engine before Claude is asked anything; thinking would only add a stall to a moment that must feel like a beat. The page uses sample.json with a schema {question, highlight: [squares], expected_squares: [squares], follow_up_if_right, follow_up_if_partial, follow_up_if_wrong}. The page sends: the FEN, the pending move in SAN, the engine's verdict (eval before and after from the mover's side, the depth-10 refutation, e.g. "7.Nxe5 dxe5, -3.97"), the chess.js facts (attackers and defenders of the landing square and of every piece of yours left attacked, with piece values), which of the three looks this is (what did their last move attack / what can I take / what can they take after my move), the moves so far, and the player's record (hold-ons this game, which questions he got right before, whether he already pressed "play anyway"). Instructions: exactly one question of at most twenty words that names squares and pieces; never give the move; never give a number unless asked; mention nothing but the one issue; respond to the squares he tapped. Example in the verified Italian position after 6...d6, when he reaches for 7.Nxe5: "Hold on. The knight is about to land on e5. What defends that square?" He taps d6: "Yes, the d6 pawn. A knight for a pawn. Take it back?" He taps c6 only: "The c6 knight does guard e5. Is that the only defender? Look at the pawns." Page tools given to Claude in the MVP: none. Every fact it needs is in the prompt, and a tool round would double the latency of the beat; highlights come back in the JSON and the page draws them, the ghost line is the engine's own refutation and needs no language. In iteration two, when the player can also type a reply ("but the c6 knight is pinned"), Claude gets evaluate(fen) and legal_moves(fen) backed by the in-page Stockfish, on the default tier, because then checking the claim before answering is worth a wait. The close is one more quick call with the list of hold-on moments (category, FEN, taken back or played) returning two sentences in the coach's voice; it is triggered by his final move, which is an explicit action. Without sample (not granted, rate limited, or stubbed in tests through window.__stubSample) the gate still fires and the page shows the templated question built by chess.js, "Hold on. What defends e5?", with the same tap-to-answer and ghost line; the product works, it is only less adaptive.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish 18 lite in a Web Worker does four jobs, none of which needs language. (1) The opponent: Skill Level 1 to 3 at depth 4 to 6, replies in under half a second, loses to a careful beginner, and punishes a hung piece every single time, which a human beginner opponent often fails to do and so teaches nothing. (2) The silent gate: while the player thinks, the engine searches the current position (depth 12, multipv 3) so the best move and its eval are known; when a move is pending, go depth 10 on the resulting position gives the opponent's best reply; cp loss = eval before minus eval after from the mover's side. The gate fires on cp loss of 200 or more when the refutation is a capture or a check (what a one-move look would have caught; a quiet positional loss of 200 is not this band's business and is ignored on purpose), on a free capture ignored (the engine's best move is a capture winning two points or more and he played something else), and on a mate in one missed or allowed. The gate is suppressed when he is already five points down ("we'll look at this one afterwards"). (3) The demonstration: the refutation line played on the board as a ghost, the "feel why". (4) After the game, a depth-14 trace of every move builds the close and the memory. The threshold rules are the coach's judgment encoded; Claude never decides whether to interrupt, only how to ask.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus the vendored files: a tap-and-drag board in the look of the existing FEN renderer, chess.js for legality, the Stockfish worker as Black at Skill Level 1, and the gate for ONE category: your move leaves a piece capturable for a net loss of two points or more with a one-move refutation (cp loss of 200 or more at depth 10 and the engine's reply is a capture). The hover state, "Hold on." plus Claude's question (quick tier, sample.json, stubbed in tests), answer by tapping squares, "Show me" ghost line, "Take it back" and "Play it anyway". A plain end screen listing the hold-on positions as small boards, saved in localStorage (db plus user in iteration two). Nothing else: no eval bar, no move list, no settings, no chat box. The day's acceptance test, all from verified lesson positions: in the Italian after 6...d6 (FEN r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2NP1N2/PPP2PPP/R1BQ1RK1 w - - 0 7) reaching for 7.Nxe5 triggers "Hold on", tapping d6 gets the right follow-up, "Show me" plays 7.Nxe5 dxe5 and rewinds, 7.Bxf7+ also triggers, and the quiet 7.h3 passes in silence; in the Ruy after 3...a6, 4.O-O triggers and 4.Ba4 passes.
concepts.delight: The piece hangs in the air and the coach says "Hold on." That half-second is the feeling of a hand on your wrist, which no app has ever given a beginner. Then he taps the d6 pawn himself and the coach says "That's the one." He was not told; he found it; and he gets to take it back.
risks: Fires too often and becomes nagging: the thresholds must stay strict (200 cp AND a capture or check refutation AND not already losing badly), and after the second "play anyway" in a game the coach must go quiet until the close.

The beat: if the quick call takes two or three seconds the hover feels like a stall; "Hold on." must come from the rule instantly, the question must stream in, and a not_granted or rate_limited error must fall back to the templated question without the player noticing.

The opponent: Stockfish at Skill Level 0 or 1 plays strange moves, not human-beginner moves; it needs a thin persona (prefer developing moves, occasionally hang a piece) or the free-capture gate rarely fires and games feel alien.
A single-threaded engine cannot search the opponent's move and the pre-search at the same time; the worker's command sequence must be designed, not improvised, or the gate's verdict arrives late.
He will sometimes want Black: board flip and the gate from Black's side are iteration two, not optional.
Games must end: beginners do not resign and the bot must, or a won game drags on for forty moves and the close never comes.
Privacy of the memory: localStorage is per browser; the moment he opens the page on a second device the coach has forgotten him, so db plus user must follow quickly.

concepts.name: Their chair
concepts.one_liner: Two-sided puzzles from real beginner games: first sit in the opponent's chair and punish the move, then come back to your own chair, one move earlier, and find the move that would never have allowed it.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Every puzzle product asks "find the best move". A coach does something else with a beginner: shows them a move a player exactly like them just made, turns the board around, and says "You're Black now. Punish it." The player takes the hanging piece with their own hand; it disappears from the board; they have done the punishing. Then the board turns back: "Now you're White, one move earlier. What would you have played instead?" and the coach accepts any move that hangs nothing. Punish, then prevent. The second half is what makes it transfer to his own games: he learns to see his own move from the other side, which is the third look of the blunder check ("after my move, what can they take?") and the one beginners never do on their own. The positions are from 1.e4 e5 beginner games, verified with the engine before shipping, and later from his own games. Lichess puzzles and Chess.com puzzles never flip the chair, never ask you to prevent, and at the 800 band are still mostly two-move motifs he is not ready for.
concepts.who_for: The same under-1000 band, in the five-minute gaps when he will not start a full game: a bus, a queue, a phone. Also a club coach who wants to hand a student a drill by link.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a board already flipped, Black at the bottom, with one line: "White just played 4.O-O. You're Black. Punish it." (Ruy Lopez after 3...a6 4.O-O??, verified in lesson 0001: 4...axb5 wins the bishop, a 455-centipawn swing.) 0 to 10 s: he looks, sees the bishop on b5 standing where the a6 pawn attacks it, taps a6, taps b5. The pawn takes, the bishop fades out, one line: "A bishop for nothing." 10 to 20 s: the board turns around with a short animation (none under prefers-reduced-motion): "Now you're White, a move earlier. Your bishop is attacked. What do you play?" 20 to 30 s: he plays Ba4 (or Bxc6, Bc4, Be2, any move that saves it): "Saved. Next." The second puzzle loads. Thirty seconds, two decisions, both his, nothing read.
concepts.core_loop: 1. A position appears, flipped to the punishing side, with the setup line ("White just played 4.O-O. Punish it."). 2. He plays a move. 3. The engine checks it instantly: a punishing move passes if it is within 50 cp of the engine's best at depth 12 (4...axb5 passes, 4...Nf6 fails). 4. Pass: the capture plays out on the board, one line of confirmation. Fail: one question from the coach ("Develop later. Which white piece is standing on a square your pawn attacks?"), a second try, and if that fails too, "Show me" plays the ghost line. 5. The board flips to the other chair, one move earlier: "Prevent it. What would you have played?" 6. Any move passes whose cp loss is under 100 at depth 12 and that leaves nothing of his attacked-and-undefended by chess.js; otherwise one question and a second try; afterwards the engine's top three are shown so the judgment never feels arbitrary. 7. "Next." Sets of ten. 8. After ten, the count and the coach's two-line observation, then "Ten more" or "Make ten from my game".
concepts.llm_role: Claude is not called on a correct answer; there is nothing to say and the engine confirmed it. On a wrong punishing or preventing move, one modelTier "quick" call through sample.json with the position, his move, the engine's refutation and eval, the chess.js attacker and defender facts, and the category, returning {question, highlight: [squares]}: one Socratic question, never the move. Example, if in the Ruy position he plays 4...Nf6 instead of 4...axb5: "Develop later. Which white piece is standing on a square your pawn attacks?" After a set of ten, one quick call with the ten results (category, right or wrong, tries) returns two sentences in the coach's voice: "Eight of ten punished. The two you missed were both bishops attacked by pawns; you look at pieces and forget that pawns attack too. The next ten are all pawns." The third thing is bigger and worth a wait: when he pastes a PGN of his own game, or finishes a game in the Hold-on page, Claude on the "default" tier with the page tools evaluate(fen, depth) and line(fen, sanMoves), both backed by the in-page Stockfish, and legal_moves(fen) from chess.js, builds the next ten from his game: it picks the moves that lost 200 cp or more to a one-move capture, confirms each refutation with line, confirms with evaluate that a preventing move exists, and writes the one-line setup for each ("You played 9.Nd5 here. Sit in Black's chair."). That call takes 30 to 60 s, runs once per game behind a visible "Making your ten from this game, checking each with the engine...", and the page refuses to include any puzzle whose refutation the tool log does not show as confirmed. Without sample, the drill runs on the built-in verified sets with templated prompts ("Punish it." / "What defends b5?") and the set summary is a plain count.
concepts.engine_role: Instant judge of every answer: punishing moves against the depth-12 best (within 50 cp), preventing moves against cp loss under 100 plus the chess.js hanging-piece check, so Ba4, Bxc6 and Bc4 all pass and O-O fails. Multipv 3 supplies the "other good answers" shown after each puzzle ("Bxc6 also keeps the material"). Built-in sets were verified at depth 20 before shipping, the way the lesson comments record it. For sets made from his own games the engine is the gatekeeper of every claim Claude makes: line confirms the refutation, evaluate confirms the escape, chess.js confirms legality; the page gates on the engine's confirmation, never on Claude's text. The engine also plays the ghost lines for "Show me".
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: a flipped board with tap-to-move, ten built-in positions from the two verified lessons stored in a JSON file with their refutation and acceptable preventing moves pre-verified: the Ruy 3...a6 4.O-O??; the Italian 4...Nxe4?, 5...Ng4?, 7.Nxe5?? and 7.Bxf7+?? (each playable from the punishing chair and then the preventing chair); the Scholar's 3...Nf6?? allowing 4.Qxf7#; the placement's 7...O-O? leaving the g4 bishop. Punish, flip, prevent; the worker checks his move at depth 12; the templated question on a wrong try; "Show me" ghost line; the ten-count at the end. Claude's question-on-wrong-try on the quick tier is the one LLM feature in the slice, stubbed in tests. Generating a set from his own game is iteration two.
concepts.delight: The flip. He punishes the bishop with his own thumb, watches it vanish, and then the board spins to put him in the seat he just beat: the same position looks completely different from the other side, and he sees in one glance what the other player should have seen. Nobody has ever shown him his own kind of mistake from the opponent's chair.
risks: Puzzle supply: ten built-in positions last two sessions; making sets from his games needs games, and without a Lichess or Chess.com account the only sources are the Hold-on page and pasted PGNs.

"Prevent" acceptance is fuzzy because many moves save the bishop; the rule (cp loss under 100, nothing left hanging) must be the only judge, and the engine's top three must be shown afterwards or it feels arbitrary.
A drill decays into "find the capture" pattern matching; one in six positions must have nothing to punish, where the right answer is a quiet move, to keep the look honest.
Claude's generated sets could contain an unverified puzzle if the tool discipline slips; the page must gate on the engine's confirmation in the tool log, never on the text.
Flipping confuses some beginners; the "You're Black" line and the side badge must be unmissable, and the flip animation must respect prefers-reduced-motion.
Default-tier set generation at 30 to 60 s needs honest progress copy; a blank spinner will be read as broken.

concepts.name: Your three
concepts.one_liner: After every game the coach pulls the three moments that decided it, verifies each with the engine, and asks you about them next time, in the same position and then in a new one, until that mistake stops happening.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Game Review shows all your mistakes once, in a list, with an evaluation; you nod and forget. A human coach does the opposite: picks the ONE thing (at this level, the hung piece), says "you did this three times this week", and brings it back next lesson in a fresh position, without hints, until it is gone. Here, after a game (played in the Hold-on page, or a PGN pasted from Chess.com or Lichess, the only text input in the product and one tap away from the board), the page shows "Your three": three small boards from his own game, each a moment where a one-move look would have saved material, each a question in the coach's voice, each confirmed by the engine before it is shown. Next time the page opens on the same three, harder: no highlighted squares. The time after that, the same mistake in a position he has never seen, which Claude builds and the engine confirms (if the confirmation fails, the original position comes back; a hallucinated puzzle never reaches him). Across games the coach keeps a memory by category and says the one line no app says: "Four of your last six hung pieces were to a pawn. Pawns are the ones you don't see."
concepts.who_for: Sambudh after his first three games, and anyone under 1000 who plays online and has a Game Review they never open. Three minutes a day on the phone, the morning after.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a board, his pieces at the bottom, and one line: "Last game, move 9. You played Nd5. Before it lands: what did Black's last move attack?" 0 to 10 s: he looks at his own position from yesterday, taps e6. "Yes, the e6 pawn hits d5. You played it anyway and lost the knight. Today, find the other move." 10 to 25 s: he plays a move; the engine checks that nothing of his is left hanging; "Good. Two more." 25 to 30 s: the second board loads. Thirty seconds in he has faced two of his own mistakes and fixed one. On day one, before any game exists, the first frame is still a board: three positions from beginner games with the line "Three to start with. Play a game and tomorrow these will be yours." and a "Paste a game" link, never an empty shell.
concepts.core_loop: 1. A game ends in the Hold-on page or a PGN is pasted. 2. The engine traces every move at depth 14 in the worker, 10 to 20 s, with a progress line ("checking move 9..."). 3. The rule picks candidate moments: cp loss of 200 or more with a capture or check refutation, free captures ignored, mates in one missed or allowed; positional losses are filtered out even when larger. 4. The rule-based three appear at once with templated questions; Claude's phrasing replaces them when its call returns. 5. He answers each by tapping squares and then playing the other move; the engine checks each answer at depth 12. 6. Next visit: R2, the same three with no highlights. 7. The visit after: R3, the same mistake in a new position built by Claude and confirmed by the engine, falling back to R2 if confirmation fails. 8. A moment closes when R3 is answered right; the category counts feed the memory line here and the opening line of the Hold-on page.
concepts.llm_role: Three calls. (1) After the trace, modelTier "default" with tools, 30 to 60 s behind "Reading your game...": the input is the PGN, the engine trace (cp per move and refutation lines), his colour, and his memory (categories and counts from db). Page tools: evaluate(fen, depth) and line(fen, sanMoves) on the in-page Stockfish, legal_moves(fen) from chess.js, and show(fen, highlight, arrows) to lay out a board. Claude picks the three moments that fit the band (hung pieces over anything positional, always), confirms each refutation with line (the page records the confirmation and drops any moment Claude did not confirm), and writes for each the question of at most twenty words naming squares, the expected squares, the follow-up, and the criterion for an acceptable other move. Example: "Move 9. Your knight went to d5. Before it landed: which black pawn attacked d5?" (2) For R3, "default" again: "Build a different position in a 1.e4 e5 opening with the same mistake available, a knight placed on a square a pawn attacks"; Claude returns a FEN and the tempting move; the page checks legality with chess.js and the refutation with evaluate and line, and on any failure shows the original position and logs the attempt. (3) The memory line is a "quick" call with the counts: "Four of your last six hung pieces were to a pawn." Without sample: the trace runs, the rule picks the three largest capture-refuted losses, the templated question shows ("Before Nd5 lands: what attacks d5?"), and R3 falls back to R2. The page works; it is only less personal.
concepts.engine_role: The depth-14 trace is the whole truth of the game; Claude never evaluates a position itself. The engine is also the gatekeeper of every claim: line confirms refutations, evaluate confirms that the other move exists and holds, chess.js confirms the legality of any generated position. During the review the engine checks each of his answers instantly at depth 12. The definition of a "moment" is the coach's band belief encoded as a rule: under 1000 only material lost to a one-move look, mates in one and free captures count; a 300-centipawn positional error is deliberately left out because it is not what loses his games.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: a "use last game" button reading the Hold-on page's record, a PGN paste box one tap away, the engine trace with a progress line, the rule-based selection of three moments, three boards with the templated question and tap-to-answer, the engine check of his other move, and a localStorage record of categories and results. Claude's call (1) with tools is the one LLM feature in the slice, stubbed in tests with a canned JSON of three questions. R2, R3 and db plus user are iteration two. Ships after Hold-on, because it needs games to exist.
concepts.delight: Seeing his own game from last time, move 9, his own knight, with the coach asking the question he should have asked himself, and getting it right today. The quieter second delight comes a week later, when the memory line says: "Pawns: none this week."
risks: It needs games; without them it is a demo, so it ships after Hold-on, never before.
Default tier with tools is 30 to 90 s; once per game is acceptable only if the rule-based three appear first and Claude's phrasing replaces them when it arrives, with honest progress copy in between.
Generated R3 positions: the engine can confirm a refutation but not that the position resembles his game; if many fail verification R3 silently reverts to R2 and the feature looks absent.
The PGN paste box is a text input and breaks "the board is the hero" if it sits on the first frame; it must be one tap away.

There is no notification mechanism in an artifact, so "tomorrow" is whenever he returns; the copy must say "last time", not "yesterday", and the memory must live in db plus user or it dies with the browser.

concepts.persona: Product designer: intuitiveness, craft and emotional design for the LLM-native chess coach, designing for Sambudh (under 1000, studied nothing, opens 1.e4, phone in hand) first.
concepts.perspective_summary: Product design cares that the first screen is a board with one line of text and nothing to learn, that the single primary action at every moment is "make a move" or "tap the board", and that the visual identity reads as chess rather than as an AI app: a tournament board (buff and green squares), the coach speaking in a book serif, no eval bar, no cards, no scores, both themes at 400 px with the board as the one hero. Above everything it cares how a blunder feels: here the piece is held before it lands and the player chooses, so a mistake becomes a question you answered instead of a red mark you received after the fact.

concepts.name: Hold On
concepts.one_liner: You play a game; when your move is about to lose a piece the board holds it in the air and asks you one question about the position, which you answer by tapping a square. Then you decide.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The board intercepts your move before it lands. On Lichess and Chess.com a blunder is discovered after the fact, as a red '??' and an eval bar that swung while you were not looking. Here, when the engine sees that the move you just dropped loses material to a one-move reply, the piece does not land: it floats over the destination square with a soft shadow, the square breathes amber, and one line of serif text above the board asks a question an LLM wrote for this exact position without naming the answer ('Hold on. That pawn on e4 has a friend. Tap what guards it.'). You answer by tapping the board, not by typing. The page already knows the true answer from the engine, so the coach can never be wrong about chess and can never spoil it. Then the choice is yours: Take it back (the piece slides home, nothing is recorded against you) or Play it anyway. After the game, Claude reads the game with page tools, sets the board to the move that mattered and writes 'One thing from this game', three sentences you can act on next game, and the holds in your next game refer back to it ('The c4 bishop again. Tap what it sees.'). No product combines a pre-commit hold, a question you answer on the board itself, a dignified take-back, and a coach with a memory of what you personally keep skipping.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh when he wants to play: a 10-20 minute game on his phone against an opponent that plays like a person at his level (it makes mistakes and punishes his). Secondary: anyone under about 1200 who learned the moves and loses to hanging pieces. Not for titled players, not for puzzle grinders.
concepts.first_30_seconds:
Visual frame (both themes): page background is a cool off-white in light (slate text) and a near-black blue-grey in dark; the board is the brightest, warmest object on the page in both: buff and green squares like a tournament vinyl board (light: pale sand #e9e5d8 and sage #8f9a7e; dark: dim buff #b8b4a0 and deep green #5c6b5a), pieces as an inline SVG set (the Unicode glyph board stays as fallback). Type: the coach's line in a book serif (Source Serif 4 or Literata with a Georgia fallback), UI labels in a plain grotesk (IBM Plex Sans), never Inter. Accent (coach ink) is a deep ink-blue in light and a pale ink-blue in dark; 'hold' is amber; nothing on this page is ever red. Layout at 400 px: a 44 px header with a tiny 'Game 1' label left and a theme/level dot right; one serif line (max three lines) above the board; the board at full width minus 16 px gutters (46 px squares); a 56 px action bar below that is empty until a decision is needed. No move list, no eval bar, no clock, no rating visible.

Second 0-5: the page opens mid-position, not on an empty board: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, White (Sambudh) at the bottom. Line: 'Your move. Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7.' He understands in five seconds: a board, my turn, one sentence.
Second 5-15: he drags Bxf7. The bishop does not land. It floats over f7, f7 breathes amber, the line reads 'Hold on. Check and a pawn, and then? Tap the piece that takes your bishop back.' (canned copy for this verified position: 4.Bxf7+? loses 3.7 pawns at depth 20, so no Claude call and no consent dialog yet).
Second 15-25: he taps the black king on e8. Line: 'The king takes. A bishop for a pawn: you are down two. Take it back?' Action bar: [Take it back] (primary, ink) [Play it anyway] (quiet). He taps Take it back; the bishop slides home in 180 ms.
Second 25-30: line: 'That is all I do. Now a real game. Your move.' The board resets to the start position. He plays 1.e4, the opponent's e5 slides in under a second. The first real hold, and with it the one consent dialog for Claude, arrives only when he actually needs it, after he already knows what a hold is.
concepts.core_loop:
1. 'Your move.' Drag or tap-tap a piece (both work on phone; legal squares show as faint dots on pickup).
2. On drop, the engine checks the move in under 300 ms (it pre-evaluated your position while the opponent was moving). Clean move: it commits, the opponent replies within a second with a 180 ms slide. If you captured something that was free: 'Free knight. You looked.'
3. Losing material to a one-move reply (cp loss >= 150 and the refutation is a capture, check or mate in two, never a positional loss): HOLD. The piece floats, one question appears, you answer by tapping a square. Right square: 'Yes, d3. The pawn takes back: a knight for a pawn. Still want to?' Wrong square: 'Not that one. Look at the pawns next to e4.' (one retry, then the answer is shown on the board with an arrow).
4. Decide: [Take it back] (piece slides home, 'Good. Your move.', nothing recorded against you) or [Play it anyway] (commits; if punished: 'There it goes. You saw it coming, that counts.'). A square you chose to play anyway is never held again that game.
5. Game over: 'Well played.' or 'That one got away.' Action bar: [One thing from this game] (primary) [New game]. Tapping it starts the one long Claude call; you watch the board jump to the position Claude is examining ('Reading your game...' then 'Setting up move 9...'), then three sentences appear under the board. Saved to db with the game.
6. Next game: the holds know your one thing ('The c4 bishop again. Tap what it sees.'). A small 'Games' sheet (tap 'Game 4' in the header) lists past games, each with its one thing and a PGN download.
concepts.llm_role:
Claude is called at exactly two moments, both from explicit viewer actions, and the page plays fully without it (sample null or not_granted: holds fall back to templated questions and the post-game call becomes an engine-only 'Your three biggest swings'; copy: 'The coach is not available here; the board still holds on.').

Call 1, the hold question: quick tier, sample.json, 1-2 s, no tools, fired by the drop that triggered the hold. Input is a stable instruction block plus compact facts the engine already established: FEN, the attempted move in SAN, the hanging piece and its attacker (from chess.js: attacked and undefended, or attacked by a cheaper piece), the three-ply refutation in SAN, the eval before and after, whether the player has been held for the same piece or square earlier this game, and the saved one-thing from the last game. Rules in the prompt: ask ONE question of at most 25 words that points at the look the player skipped (what did their last move attack / what can be taken / what checks exist / what can they take after your move), never name the answer square, name the squares that count as a correct tap, and give the two follow-up lines. Output: {question, answer_squares, yes, no}. Example for the position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Nxe4?? facts (knight on e4 attacked by the d3 pawn, undefended; 5.dxe4; +3.9): question 'Hold on. That pawn on e4 has a friend. Tap what guards it.'; answer_squares ['d3']; yes 'Yes, d3. The pawn takes back and you have traded a knight for a pawn. Still want to?'; no 'Not that one. Look at the pawns standing next to e4.' Example for 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 Nc6 3.Bc4 with Black to move, after the player tries 3...Nf6 (facts: 4.Qxf7# mate in one): 'Hold on. Their queen and bishop are both looking at the same square. Tap it.' answer ['f7']. The page validates: answer_squares must be real squares and a subset of the engine's own answer set, the question must not contain any of those squares, else the template is used. The template appears instantly under the floating piece and Claude's version replaces it only if it arrives within 2.5 s; the hold never waits for Claude. Why an LLM and not templates: the question has to point at the attacker's intent in prose without naming the answer, pick which of the three looks to ask about, and vary with the position and the player's history; templated questions become wallpaper after five games, and this question is the product.

Call 2, 'One thing from this game': default tier, with tools, 30-90 s, fired by the button, with a Stop button and progress copy driven from inside the tools' execute. Input: the PGN, per-move cp loss from the engine (computed during play), every hold with its outcome, the player's level and the last three one-things from db. Tools (two, small results): show_position({ply, highlight, arrow}) sets the board to a position FROM THIS GAME ONLY (the page refuses any ply outside the move list, so Claude cannot show a position that did not happen) and returns 'ok'; check({ply, move}) returns the engine's cp and best reply for that move so every claim is grounded. Output: two or three short sentences in the coach's voice plus the board left on the moment that mattered. Example: 'Twice this game a bishop sat on c4 looking at f7, and twice you looked past it. On move 4 you took the pawn on e4 with your knight, and the pawn on d3 took the knight back; that is the position on the board now. Next game, before every move, find the pawn next to the square you are landing on. That is the one thing.' Stored in db and reused by Call 1.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish 18 lite in a Web Worker plus chess.js, and they do everything that does not need language, all instantly: legality, SAN, FEN, game over (chess.js); the pre-move evaluation of your position at depth 14 while the opponent 'thinks' so the hold decision after your drop is a single depth-12 search (under 300 ms); the hold trigger (cp loss >= 150 AND the refutation is a capture, check or mate in two whose material swing chess.js can count along the PV; positional losses never hold, this is what keeps the coach inside the under-1000 band); the facts for the question (the hanging piece, its attacker, the three-ply refutation, the squares that count as a correct tap); the 'free piece' detection when the player captures an undefended piece; the opponent's moves (Skill Level 1-4 by the Easier / Like me / Harder setting, depth 6 with multipv 3 and a weighted pick so it makes human-shaped mistakes within one second; UCI_Elo cannot go below 1320 so skill level is the lever); per-move cp loss for the whole game as input to the post-game call and as the engine-only fallback; and the grounding for Claude's check tool. The engine never speaks to the player; it decides when the coach is allowed to.
concepts.mvp_slice: Recommended MVP, one page (app/index.html + vendor files), a day's build: the board (tap-tap and drag, legal-square dots, 180 ms slides, reduced-motion static), the tournament board identity in both themes at 400 px, the opening canned hold on the verified 3...Nf6 position, play against the Worker engine at one 'Like me' level, the hold with the templated question and tap-to-answer validated by chess.js facts, Take it back / Play it anyway, 'Free piece' lines, game over lines, and Call 1 wired through sample.json with the 2.5 s swap rule and window.__stubSample for tests. Explicitly NOT in the slice: Call 2, the Games sheet, db persistence (localStorage holds the current game and the tutorial-seen flag), level settings, PGN download. The slice proves the new interaction: a piece that will not land, a question answered on the board, a take-back with no shame.
concepts.delight: The first time the piece refuses to land. It floats, the square breathes amber, and a sentence asks you something you can actually answer. You tap the right square, it says 'Yes. Still want to?', and you realise you are being asked, not corrected. Then you tap Take it back and the piece slides home with 'Good. Your move.' Relief, not shame; most beginners have never had that feeling at a chessboard.
risks: Over-holding turns the coach into a nag: the trigger must be strictly 'material lost to a one-move reply' (cp loss >= 150 with a capture/check refutation), never positional, with a per-game cap, Play it anyway always one tap away, and a 'Hold on: off' setting for the brave.

Opponent calibration: Stockfish's UCI_Elo floor is 1320, so a believable ~900 opponent needs Skill Level plus a weighted top-N picker that makes human-shaped mistakes (hanging pieces, missed one-move threats); it must be tuned against Sambudh's real games, not guessed.

Quick-tier latency during the hold (1-2 s, longer on the first call because of the consent dialog): the floating-piece illusion must never wait on Claude, so the template shows instantly and Claude's question swaps in only if it arrives within 2.5 s.

Claude spoiling or mis-answering: it may name the answer square in the question or return a square the engine does not accept; the page validates against the engine's answer set and falls back to the template silently.

The post-game call is 30-90 s and uses tools: needs visible progress driven from the tools, a Stop button, show_position restricted to plies from this game, and copy for rate_limited / not_granted; a viewer who declines Claude must still get an engine-only review.

Piece rendering: Unicode glyphs render inconsistently on Android and look like text, so the craft bar needs an inline SVG piece set with a license that can ship (cburnett, CC BY-SA) or hand-drawn paths; the glyph board remains the fallback.
Scope discipline: the temptation to add an eval bar, a move list, a rating and a dashboard is exactly what makes this feel like Lichess; the MVP keeps one serif line, one board, one action bar.
Licensing: shipping Stockfish inside the page means the page's source should be GPL-compatible; flagged, not solved, in the MVP.

concepts.name: Chairs
concepts.one_liner: A five-minute daily drill where you make a move, the board turns around, and you try to punish your own move from the other side with your own hands.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Every chess trainer shows you a position and asks for the best move. None makes you play both sides of your own decision. Here the loop is literal: you are White, you make any move you like; the board turns around (a 400 ms rotation, with 'Now you are Black' as the caption), and the line reads 'Now you are Black. Punish that, if you can.' If you find a capture of the piece you just moved, you have discovered your own blunder with your own fingers, which no eval number can teach. The engine grades your Black reply instantly, the board turns back, and you choose a different White move until one survives your own best effort against it. It is the chess master's 'change chairs' from lesson 0001 made physical. Claude is the voice from the other chair when you are stuck, and the author of tomorrow's five positions from your own games.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh between games: five positions, five minutes, phone in one hand, on the bus. Also for the player who does not have twenty minutes for a game but wants the blunder check to become a reflex.
concepts.first_30_seconds: Same identity as Hold On: tournament buff-and-green board, serif coach line, plain sans labels, no cards, no scores. Header: 'Today, 1 of 5' as five small dots (filled when done; a hollow dot is a position you needed to be shown). Second 0-5: the page opens on a verified beginner position from the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7 5.O-O O-O 6.Nc3 d6, White to move). Line: 'You are White. Make a move.' Nothing else. Second 5-12: he plays 7.Nxe5 (it takes a pawn; it is the move most beginners play). The board turns around; the pieces are now seen from Black's side with coordinates kept. Line: 'Now you are Black. Punish that, if you can.' Second 12-25: he looks, sees the knight on e5 and the pawn on d6, plays dxe5. Line: 'You just caught yourself. That knight was free: a pawn took it.' Action bar: [Take it back] (primary). Second 25-30: the board turns back to White, the knight is home on f3, line: 'Your move again. Something that survives this time.' He understands the whole product without reading a word of instructions.
concepts.core_loop:
1. 'You are White. Make a move.' (engine-verified position from the set; later, from your own games).
2. The board turns. 'Now you are Black. Punish that, if you can.' You play Black's reply.
3. The engine judges your reply in under a second. Three outcomes: CAUGHT ('You just caught yourself. That bishop was free.' [Take it back]); SAFE, your White move had no one-move punishment and your Black reply was reasonable ('Nothing to punish. That move stands.' [Next]); MISSED, there was a punishment you did not find ('There was something. Keep looking?' [Keep looking] [Show me]; Show me draws the engine's reply as an arrow and the dot for this position stays hollow).
4. Stuck from Black's chair: tap 'I do not see anything' and Claude gives a hint from Black's side without naming the move.
5. Caught: the board turns back, you choose a different White move, loop until SAFE. Then 'Why did that work?' is one tap away.
6. After five: 'Done for today. You caught yourself three times before I had to.' The next day's five are composed from your own games if you have any (from Hold On's db) or from the verified set.
concepts.llm_role:
Three calls, all on explicit taps; the drill runs fully without Claude (hints become the engine's arrow after one more try).

(a) Hint from the other chair: quick tier, sample.json, 1-2 s, no tools. Input: FEN after the White move, the engine's best reply and what it wins in material, which White piece became undefended and by what, plus the rule 'one sentence under 20 words, from Black's point of view, name no move and no square'. Output {hint}. Example (after 7.Nxe5 in the Italian: dxe5 wins the knight): 'Something of White's just stepped onto a square one of your pawns can reach.'

(b) 'Why did that work?' after CAUGHT or SAFE: quick tier, sample.json, Output {say, highlight}. Example after dxe5: 'The pawn on e5 was guarded twice, by the d6 pawn and the knight on c6, and the knight that took it was guarded by nothing. Counting the guards before you take is the whole trick.' with highlight ['e5','d6','c6'] drawn on the board. The page only draws squares that exist and only accepts text that does not contradict the engine's material count it passed in.

(c) Tomorrow's five (only when the player has games in db): default tier with tools, 30-90 s, fired by tapping 'Make tomorrow's five from my games', with progress and Stop. Tools: candidates() returns the ten moves from the player's games with the largest one-move material loss (ply, FEN, cp loss, refutation), small plain data; check({fen, move}) returns engine cp and best reply. Output: five {ply, caption} entries, captions under twelve words in the player's own story ('Move 9, the one where the bishop came to g4'). The page verifies each chosen position has a one-move punishment of at least 150 cp before it enters the set. Why an LLM: picking the five most instructive moments out of a week of games and captioning them in the player's own narrative is editorial judgement grounded in engine facts; the engine alone produces a sorted list of numbers.
concepts.engine_role: chess.js for legality, the board flip and material counting; Stockfish at depth 12-14 for: whether the White move is punishable (best reply gains >= 150 cp and is a capture or check, so it is visible in one look), grading the player's Black reply (within 50 cp of best counts as found), the arrow for Show me, the facts behind every hint and every Why, and the verification gate for tomorrow's five. The MVP position set is the engine-verified positions already in the lessons (scripts/engine_check.py comments are the evidence) plus a dozen more checked the same way.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: the board with a turn animation (reduced-motion: instant with caption), twelve verified positions baked in as data, the three outcomes with their copy, Take it back, the five dots, and call (a) through sample.json with the stub for tests. No db, no tomorrow's five, no Why. Proves the chair-switch as a loop a beginner can run alone on a phone.
concepts.delight: The board turning around with 'Now you are Black. Punish that, if you can.' and, a few seconds later, taking your own knight and reading 'You just caught yourself.' It is the first time most players laugh at their own blunder instead of flinching.
risks: Flipping the board disorients beginners; coordinates stay, the rotation animates, and the caption says who you are now, but this needs testing with Sambudh before it is trusted.

It can read as 'just puzzles' if the both-sides framing is not loud in the copy and the turn; the positions must be the player's own as soon as possible, which depends on games existing in db (from Hold On) or a pasted PGN.
Show me becomes a crutch; it leaves the dot hollow and the coach says so at the end of the day, which is a social cost without a score.
Position supply: every position must be engine-verified (a hallucinated 'punishment' would destroy trust); the verification gate must run in the page, not only in authoring.
Claude hints that accidentally name the move; the page scans the hint for square names and move text and falls back to the arrow.

concepts.name: Ghost Moves
concepts.one_liner: A playground where any move you pick up is shown as a ghost before it lands: what it attacks, what it leaves hanging, what they would play back, drawn on the board, with 'Why?' one tap away.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Analysis boards show you an evaluation after you commit; DecodeChess explains the engine's move. Nobody draws what YOUR idea does before you commit it. Here, tapping a piece colours its legal squares by consequence (plain, green ring for a free capture, amber ring for a square where the piece would be taken; never red), and tapping a destination places a translucent ghost of the piece there without moving it: arrows show what it now attacks, small amber dots mark any of your pieces it stopped guarding, and a dashed arrow shows what they would play back. Tap again to commit, tap elsewhere to cancel. 'Why?' asks Claude to explain your idea in two sentences and to draw its answer on the board (it returns squares and arrows, not just words). Long-press a piece and the coach tells you its job ('This bishop has one job: it guards e4. Move it and the pawn is free.'). 'Teach me this position' lets you watch the coach try two or three ghost moves on your board, thinking out loud, each one checked by the engine before it is drawn.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh when he is curious rather than competitive: after a game, on an opening he keeps meeting (1.e4 e5 2.Qh5), or when a friend sends a position. Also for sharing: a position in the link, a friend opens it and asks Why on the same board.
concepts.first_30_seconds: Same identity: buff-and-green board as hero, serif coach line, one quiet action bar. Second 0-5: opens on the start position with the line 'Pick up any piece. See what happens before it happens.' Second 5-12: he taps the e2 pawn; e3 and e4 show as plain dots; he taps e4; a translucent pawn appears on e4, two faint arrows point at d5 and f5, nothing is amber. He taps again and the move commits; the coach line says nothing, because nothing needs saying. Second 12-25: 'You move both sides' is on by default in the playground, so he plays e5 for Black, then taps his queen and sees h5 as a plain dot; he places the ghost on h5: arrows to e5 and f7, and a dashed arrow back from Black (...Nc6 or ...Nf6 as the engine prefers) with the caption 'They would play this.' Second 25-30: he taps Why? and in about a second reads: 'The queen is out early and attacks e5 and f7, but every reply that develops a piece also chases her away. Tempting, and it costs you time.' with e5 and f7 highlighted. He has learned the product and one idea with no instruction.
concepts.core_loop:
1. Tap a piece: legal squares appear, coloured by consequence (instant, chess.js static: attacked-and-undefended or attacked-by-cheaper = amber; capture of an undefended piece = green; else plain).
2. Tap a square: the ghost is placed; arrows for what it attacks, amber dots for pieces it left hanging, the engine's dashed 'They would play this' arrow after about half a second at depth 12.
3. Tap again to commit (or drag to commit directly), tap elsewhere to cancel. With 'You move both sides' off, the engine plays the other side.
4. Why? on any ghost or any committed move; What is this piece doing? on long-press; both answer in a second or two and draw on the board.
5. 'Teach me this position' for a 30-60 s guided tour with ghost moves the coach tries and the engine checks.
6. Set up: start position, a few named beginner openings (Italian, Scholar's attempt, Spanish), paste FEN or PGN, flip. The position is in the link, so sharing is a copy of the URL.
concepts.llm_role:
All calls on explicit taps; the playground is complete without Claude (ghosts, rings, arrows and the engine's reply arrow are engine work and need no language).

(a) Why?: quick tier, sample.json, 1-2 s, no tools. Input: FEN, the ghost move, what the moved piece now attacks, which own pieces became undefended and by what, the engine's best reply and cp before/after, and the rule 'two sentences, plain words, use only these facts, then list the squares and arrows to draw'. Output {say, highlight, arrows}. Example for a ghost Nxe4 after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3: 'Your knight would be standing where the d3 pawn can take it, and nothing of yours guards e4. A knight for a pawn.' highlight ['e4','d3'], arrows ['d3e4']. The page draws only legal squares and only arrows between real squares.

(b) What is this piece doing? on long-press: quick tier, Output {say, arrows}. Input: the piece, what it attacks, what it defends (chess.js), whether it is pinned, whether anything it defends becomes hanging if it moves (computed by chess.js by removing it). Example: 'This bishop has one job: it guards e4. Move it and the pawn is free.' arrows ['c2e4'] (illustrative).

(c) Teach me this position: default tier with tools, 30-60 s, Stop button, progress from inside the tools. Tools: ghost({move, say}) places a ghost with a one-line caption and returns the engine's cp and best reply (so Claude learns whether its idea holds before it keeps talking); clear(). The page caps it at four ghosts. Output: a closing sentence. The player watches the coach try ideas on the board and get corrected by the engine in real time; that is the thinking-partner moment. Example closing line: 'So the pawn grab fails and the quiet move keeps everything. In this opening, the boring move is the strong one.'
concepts.engine_role: chess.js does the instant work: legal moves, attackers and defenders for the ring colours and the amber dots, what a piece attacks and defends, pins, the 'what becomes hanging if this piece leaves' simulation. Stockfish at depth 12 provides the dashed 'They would play this' arrow after a ghost (about half a second), the cp before and after for Why?, and the grounding result inside the ghost() tool so the coach's guided tour cannot teach a losing idea. No eval number is ever shown; the engine's output is always drawn as an arrow or a ring.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: board with tap-to-ghost and tap-to-commit (drag commits directly), consequence rings and amber dots from chess.js, the engine's reply arrow, 'You move both sides' toggle, start position plus paste-FEN, and Why? through sample.json with the stub for tests. No long-press, no guided tour, no openings list. Proves 'see it before it happens' as a direct-manipulation idea a beginner understands without reading.
concepts.delight: Placing a ghost and watching the dashed arrow appear half a second later, pointing at exactly the piece you were about to lose. It feels like x-ray vision, and it is yours to use, not the engine's to lecture with.
risks: It is a crutch if used during real games: keep it a separate mode from Hold On (or allow one ghost per game as a hint that costs something).
Rings on every legal square are noise; show them only after a piece is tapped, with most squares plain, and never red.
It can collapse into a Lichess analysis board if restraint is lost: the rule is fewer things drawn, no eval bar, no engine lines in text.
Claude contradicting the drawing: the Why prompt is restricted to the facts passed in and the page refuses highlights outside the facts' squares.
Phone gestures: long-press conflicts with drag on some browsers, so What is this piece doing? may need a tap on an already-selected piece instead; test on a real Android and iPhone.
Reading a position from a photo is tempting (sample images exist) and unreliable for chessboards; out of scope, say so.

concepts.perspective_summary: Claude earns its place only where language and memory matter: turning an engine threat into one sentence a beginner feels, asking the question a coach would ask, grading a reason rather than a move, and remembering what this player keeps doing; every chess fact it utters must be computed by chess.js and the in-page Stockfish, placed in the prompt as a fact sheet before the call, and checked again on the way out (every square and SAN token in the reply validated against the fact sheet, else the page's own template line shows). Quick tier with zero tool rounds for anything that happens during a move, default tier once per game while the player is already looking at a result screen, calls only from the player's own actions, and the page must play, talk and drill fully from engine-derived templates when `claude.use("sample")` is null or any call rejects.

concepts.name: Open Hand
concepts.one_liner: Play against an opponent of your own level who tells you, in one sentence, what it is about to do to you, so you learn to see it before it says it.
concepts.the_new_interaction: An opponent that plays with its hand open. After each of its moves, when and only when the engine finds that it has a real threat (material or mate) or that you have left something for free, a speech bubble by the board says what it intends, in the opponent's voice: "If you do nothing, my knight takes on f7 and your rook has to give itself up." Lichess and Chess.com bots are silent and their coaching speaks after the game; here the look from the other chair that the blunder-check lesson teaches is performed by the other chair, out loud, during the game, and you answer it on the board, never in text. When you answer a telegraphed threat the bubble ticks "Answered."; when you hang a piece anyway it takes it and says one line. After five answered threats in a row the opponent goes quiet and only speaks when you tap its name ("What are you planning?"), which is the moment the habit has moved from the page into your head.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh and every under-1000 player who loses to one-move threats and hanging pieces; someone who wants to play, not study, and would never open a lesson.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a board already set up, white at the bottom, the sides labelled "You" and "Mira"; one line above the board: "Your move. Mira plays at your level and says what she is planning." No menu, no settings. 3 s: you play 1.e4 by drag or tap-tap; Mira answers 1...e5 in under a second (Stockfish depth 8, Skill Level 3); no bubble, because a quiet position says nothing. 10 s: 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, still silent: the engine finds no threat worth a sentence. 20 s: you play 4.Ng5 (natural for a 1.e4 player); Mira plays 4...d5 and about a second after her move lands the bubble streams in: "That pawn hits your bishop. Move it or I take it." The d5 pawn and the c4 bishop glow. (On a first visit this is where the platform's consent dialog appears; if the viewer declines, the same moment shows the page's own phrasebook line, flatter: "The d5 pawn attacks your bishop on c4.") 30 s: you move the bishop; the bubble fades with a small tick, "Answered." The whole first half-minute was playing chess.
concepts.core_loop: 1. You move (chess.js validates; an illegal drag snaps back). 2. Mira answers in under a second (depth 8, Skill Level 2-6 tuned by results and blunder count). 3. While her move animates, the page builds the fact sheet for the new position (depth 12 multipv 3, attackers/defenders per square, and the "if you pass" probe) in about 1.5 s. 4. If a moment exists (threat gaining 150 cp or more, a mate-in-one threat, or something of yours left for free), one quick-tier JSON call turns the facts into Mira's one sentence; the bubble streams in and the involved squares glow; otherwise nothing is said and nothing is spent. 5. You answer on the board; the page re-checks the threat move at depth 10 on the new position and marks "Answered." if it no longer wins material, or lets Mira collect and say a phrasebook line ("You left it there."). 6. The answered-threat streak is counted; at five Mira goes quiet and the "What are you planning?" tap appears on her name. 7. Game over: one quick call writes Mira's closing line from the game facts, then "Play again"; the result and the hung-piece count go to db for the next concept.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is Mira's voice and nothing else: it never chooses a move, never evaluates one, never sees a position without the fact sheet. It is called from the player's move handler (an explicit action) only when the fact sheet flags a moment, so roughly 6-12 calls in a 40-move game, each `sample.json(prompt, {modelTier: "quick", cache: false, signal})` with a fresh AbortController that the next move handler aborts (a bubble that arrives after you moved on is cancelled, not shown). No tools in the MVP. The input is one string of about 1.5 KB in three blocks. Persona: "You are Mira, a friendly rival who plays at the same level as the person across the table. You talk like a person, never like a commentator. One sentence, at most 22 words, in your own voice: say what you will do if they ignore it. Use only the facts below. Name only the squares and pieces listed. Never give an evaluation number. Never tell them what to play." Facts (computed by the page): "Board after your move 4...d5; you are Black. Your pawn on d5 attacks their bishop on c4, which nothing defends. If they do nothing, your best move is dxc4, winning a bishop for a pawn. Their bishop can go to b3, b5, d3, e2 or f1, or they can take with exd5. Nothing of yours is left for free. No checks for either side." Contract: "Reply with only JSON: {\"say\": string, \"squares\": [up to three squares from the facts]}." Example reply: {"say":"That pawn hits your bishop. Move it or I take it.","squares":["d5","c4"]}. On the way out the page validates: every square in `squares` must be in the fact sheet's allowed set, and `say` must contain no SAN-shaped token (regex `\b([KQRBN]?[a-h]?[1-8]?x?[a-h][1-8](=[QRBN])?|O-O(-O)?)\b`) outside the fact sheet's listed moves; a violation discards the reply, shows the phrasebook line, and increments a counter so the stub tests can measure the violation rate. After a hung piece is taken there is no call: a rotating phrasebook line ("Free knight, thank you."). The closing line is one quick call from the game-end handler with the result, threats telegraphed, threats answered and the biggest swing move: "You answered every threat I told you about and missed the two I did not mention. Next game I will say less." Iteration 2 adds the "What are you planning?" tap (same contract, on an explicit tap) and one tool, `look({move})`: plays the move on a chess.js copy, runs depth 12, returns `{legal, evalAfter, bestReply, hangsAfter}` under 200 bytes, described as "Use only if the facts above do not already say what happens after a move", offered only when `sample.limits()` reports `tools`, with `cache` omitted on those calls as the contract requires. Error branches: `not_granted`, `sampling_disabled`, `not_declared`, `capability_disabled` set a view flag, never call again, phrasebook everywhere, no message to the player; `rate_limited` means phrasebook for the next three moments, then one more try on a later moment; `refused`, `invalid_json`, `empty_completion` mean phrasebook for this moment only; `cancelled` shows nothing; `upstream_error` keeps `e.text` if it streamed, else phrasebook. With Claude absent the game is identical minus the voice.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish 18 lite in a Web Worker does four jobs. (1) Mira's move: `setoption name Skill Level value N` (start 3; up one after a win, down one after two losses or a game with three or more hung pieces; floor 1, ceiling 8) then `go depth 8`, bestmove well under a second. (2) The fact sheet after every Mira move: chess.js gives legal moves, captures, checks and `attackers(square, colour)` per square, from which the page lists hanging pieces for both sides (attacked and undefended, or attacked by a pawn), what Mira's last move newly attacks, and each threatened piece's safe squares; `go depth 12 multipv 3` gives the best moves and evaluation; a second search on the FEN with the side to move flipped (skipped when the player is in check) gives Mira's threat, "what I do if you pass", and the material it wins. A moment is a threat gaining 150 cp or more, a mate threat, or a free capture of 150 cp or more available to the player. (3) Threat resolution after the player's move: the threat move is re-searched at depth 10 on the new position; if it no longer wins material the threat was answered. (4) On the result screen a pgn trace (eval after every move at depth 12) stored for the drill concept. Everything in (2)-(4) is the ground truth Claude is handed; the engine answers instantly and silently, Claude only speaks.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page, one board, one opponent (Mira, Skill Level 3), the player as White, no accounts: a full legal game with move highlighting and promotion; Mira's telegraph bubble on moments through the quick-tier JSON call with the square and SAN validator; the phrasebook fallback wired so the game runs unchanged when `claude.use("sample")` is null or `window.__stubSample` is installed; the "Answered." tick and the free-piece line; the closing line and "Play again". Not in the slice: the fade-out streak, the "What are you planning?" tap, playing Black, db, personas beyond Mira. Playwright drives it end to end with canned stub replies, including one that names an illegal square to prove the validator discards it and shows the phrasebook line.
concepts.delight: The first time Mira says "Move it or I take it," you move it and she says "Answered." The threat was real, you handled it, and someone noticed. The second delight comes later: the first game where she goes quiet and you realise you were already looking from her chair.
risks: A one-second quick call can land after the player has already moved in a fast game; the next move handler must abort the controller, and the call must be fired in parallel with the move animation, with the timing tuned on a phone.
The flipped-side threat probe is undefined when the player is in check; the page must skip it then and build the moment from the check facts alone.

If the moment threshold is set too low Mira says true but useless things ("I will improve my knight"); keep the threshold at material or mate and measure usefulness with a handful of real calls before widening it.

The consent dialog appearing mid-game at the first moment may confuse; consider making the very first bubble an explicit tap ("Mira wants to say something. Hear it?") so the dialog has a visible reason.
Skill Level 3 may still be too strong on a bad day; the adaptive step must respond to hung-piece count, not only results.
Telegraphing every threat can teach dependence; the fade-out is not in the MVP slice and must ship in iteration 2 before a second week of use.

concepts.name: The One Thing
concepts.one_liner: After each game your biggest mistake becomes one question in a coach's words, graded on your reasoning, and the page remembers which mistake you keep making.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Game review products show a list of mistakes with evaluations; nobody under 1000 learns from a list. Here the result screen slides the board to the one position where the game turned and asks one question about it ("You played Nxe4 here. Before letting go, what should you have looked at?"), grades what you type against the engine's verified answer for the reasoning rather than the move, and tells you the one idea in plain words. The drill is kept, re-asked three games later without the glow ("Do you remember this one?"), and after a few games the page says the sentence no product says: "Four of your last five games turned on a knight or bishop placed where a pawn could take it." Claude does the three things only it can: write the question from the engine's facts in the voice of a coach who watched the game, grade a free-text reason, and turn the page's motif counts into one sentence about you. The engine owns which position, which move was best, and by how much.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh after his first games on the page; anyone who plays and never reviews because review screens are lists of numbers.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the game just ended (lost on move 31); the board slides to move 12 and a line appears: "This is where it turned." Your knight on e4 shows, the d3 pawn glows; a thin progress bar along the move list shows the review finishing. 5 s: below the board: "You played Nxe4 here. Say, in a sentence, what you should have looked at before letting go." One text field, placeholder "Type your answer", a small "Skip" link; no evaluation shown yet. 15 s: you type "the pawn could take it back" and tap "Check". 17 s: one second later: "Yes: the pawn on d3 was guarding e4, so the knight was never free. A knight for a pawn." The engine's preferred 4...Bc5 appears on the board with the words "Any safe move was fine; this one develops." 25 s: a card slides in: "The one thing from this game: before you take something, look at what takes it back." Then "Play again" and, smaller, "Two more moments from this game".
concepts.core_loop: 1. A game ends (from the play loop or a pasted PGN); the page's review runs (depth 12 per move, progress bar visible) and finds the three biggest centipawn drops by the player; each is tagged with a motif code computed from the fact sheet before and after the move: hung_to_pawn, hung_undefended, missed_free_piece, missed_mate_in_1, allowed_mate_in_1, other. 2. One default-tier JSON call, no tools, everything precomputed, writes the drill cards and the one-thing sentence; it starts while the board slides so the first card is ready in about ten seconds. 3. You answer the first drill in text, or tap Skip, or tap a move on the board. 4. One quick-tier call grades the text against the rubric; feedback shows with the engine's preferred move. 5. Drill, motif code, verdict and the game go to db (per person, private, survives republishes). 6. On later result screens a due drill from an earlier game is re-asked first, without the glow. 7. After the fifth game the about-you line appears, written by Claude from the page's motif counts.
concepts.llm_role: Two prompts, two tiers, both from explicit actions. Drill writing: `sample.json(prompt, {modelTier: "default", cache: {gcTime: 86400000}, signal})` from the game-end handler, with a Stop link on the card; the game id in the prompt keys the cache. Input about 3 KB: role block "You are a chess coach who just watched this game by a player rated under 1000. Write for them. Use only the facts given; never add a move, square or evaluation that is not listed. No tactic names such as fork or pin. One idea per card."; then, per swing, the engine's review: "Swing 1, move 12 for White. FEN before: r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1n3/3P1N2/PPP2PPP/RNBQK2R. You played: Nxe4. Engine: this loses 3.8 pawns of advantage (+0.4 to -3.4, depth 14). The pawn on d3 defended e4; nothing of White's defended e4 after the capture; Black replied dxe4. Moves that kept everything safe: Bc5 (+0.3), d6 (+0.2), Be7 (+0.2). Motif: missed_defender."; then the contract: {"one_thing": string of at most 18 words, "drills": [{"swing": number, "question": string, "idea": string of at most 25 words, "hint": string, "full_answer_must_mention": [strings]}]}. Example reply: {"one_thing":"Before you take something, look at what takes it back.","drills":[{"swing":1,"question":"You played Nxe4 here. Before letting go, what should you have looked at?","idea":"The d3 pawn was guarding e4. The knight was never free: it cost you a knight for a pawn.","hint":"Look at the pawns next to e4.","full_answer_must_mention":["the d3 pawn defends or takes back on e4","nothing of yours defended e4"]}]}. Grading: `sample.json(prompt, {modelTier: "quick", cache: false})` from the Check button; input is the question, the facts, the rubric and the player's text, with the rule "Grade the reasoning, not the move name; 'full' only when every rubric point is present in substance; answers under five words are at most 'partial'"; output {"verdict": "full" | "partial" | "low", "say": string of at most 35 words}. Example: {"verdict":"full","say":"Yes: the pawn on d3 was guarding e4, so the knight was never free. A knight for a pawn."}. About-you line after five games: quick tier, `cache: {gcTime: 3600000}`, input is the page's own counts ("hung_to_pawn: 4 of the last 5 games; missed_free_piece: 1; allowed_mate_in_1: 0"), output one sentence: "Four of your last five games turned on a knight or bishop placed where a pawn could take it. Before the piece lands, look at the pawns." Validation on the way out: every SAN token in `idea`, `hint`, `say` and `one_thing` must be in the swing's listed moves, else that card falls back to the page template ("You played Nxe4. The pawn on d3 took it back. A safe move here was Bc5."); `truncated: true` shows the cards that parsed; `invalid_json` shows a "Try again" link (the viewer's click, never a loop). With Claude absent the drill still runs: template question "Find the move that keeps everything safe", answered by tapping a move on the board, graded by the engine (within 50 cp of best is full, within 150 partial).
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish runs the whole review on the result screen: `go depth 12` after every move of the game (a 31-move game is under 20 s on a phone, shown as the progress bar sliding along the move list), the three largest centipawn drops by the player re-searched at depth 14, and for each: `go depth 14 multipv 3` on the position before the move to list the safe alternatives with evaluations, the engine's reply to the mistake as the refutation, and the chess.js fact sheet (attackers, defenders, hanging pieces before and after) that yields the motif code by fixed rules, never by Claude. For the absent-Claude grading path the tapped move is scored against the same multipv list. Re-asked drills need no new engine work: the facts are stored in db beside the drill. Swings all under 150 cp mean no drill is shown at all ("Nothing turned this game; well played.").
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: paste a PGN, or tap "Use the demo game" so the first frame is never empty; run the review with a visible progress bar; show the single biggest swing with the board, one question, one text field, one grade, one one-thing card. The default-tier drill call with the JSON contract and SAN validation, the quick-tier grade call, the template fallback when `sample` is null, and `window.__stubSample` answering both prompts. No db yet (localStorage keeps the last three drills as a convenience), no re-asking, no about-you line.
concepts.delight: Typing "the pawn could take it back" and reading, one second later, that you were right and why, about the move that actually lost you the game twenty minutes ago. Then, three games later, the same position comes back and you remember.
risks: A default-tier call on a 3 KB prompt takes 10-30 s; the result screen must give the player something to look at (the board sliding, the progress bar, the position itself) or they leave before the card arrives.
Quick-tier grading of free text can be lenient; the rubric must come from the drill card itself and the page should default to partial for very short answers.

The motif rules are hand-written and will mislabel some swings (a sacrifice that is good at depth 20 and bad at depth 12); re-search chosen swings at depth 14 and show nothing when the swing is under 150 cp.
Players under 1000 may not want to type reasons; Skip must not feel like failure, and the tap-a-move answer may become the primary form.
Without db the memory story is a promise, not a feature; iteration 2 must add db and user before the about-you line is shown.
Caching the drill call for 24 h means a changed prompt format must change the prompt text, or stale cards replay during development.

concepts.name: Point at It
concepts.one_liner: Tap any piece and ask the only three questions a beginner has about it; the answer is one sentence drawn on the board, never wrong, and sometimes a question back.
concepts.the_new_interaction: No chat box. On any position, during a game or a review, you tap a piece and the page offers two or three question chips computed from the facts for that piece: "Is it safe?", "What is it doing?", "Why not take on f7?" (only when that capture exists), "What should I do with it?". The answer is one sentence that arrives with arrows and glows the page has verified before drawing ("No. The pawn on d5 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it. Move it, or it is gone next move." with d5 to c4 drawn). In quiz mode the answer opens with a question back ("First: tap the piece that attacks your bishop."), you answer by tapping, the page checks the tap against its own attack map instantly, and then the sentence follows. Engines give you a number; DecodeChess gives you paragraphs; chat-with-the-engine apps talk and get squares wrong. Pointing at the board as the question, one sentence as the answer, and a Socratic tap-back keyed by the page, is the new part.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh in the middle of a game when he is unsure whether a piece is safe or what it is for; later anyone reviewing a game who wants to understand one piece, not the whole position.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: a game is in progress on the Open Hand board, or a demo position loads with the line "Tap a piece to ask about it."; your bishop on c4 wears a thin ring because the page already knows it is attacked. 4 s: you tap the bishop; three chips slide up under the board: "Is it safe?", "What is it doing?", "Why not take on f7?". 6 s: you tap "Is it safe?"; the chip becomes a bubble reading "Looking..." and the d5 to c4 arrow appears at once, drawn from the fact sheet before any call. 7 s: the sentence streams in: "No. The pawn on d5 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it. Move it, or it is gone next move." 15 s: the bishop's safe squares glow (computed by the page) and you play Bb3. 20 s: you tap Mira's knight on c6 and "What is it doing?": "It guards e5 and keeps your pieces off d4. Nothing is attacking it." 30 s: you notice the small "Quiz me" toggle; the next answer will open with a question.
concepts.core_loop: 1. Tap a piece; chips appear from the fact sheet, no call. 2. Tap a chip; the page draws what it already knows (attackers, defenders, the engine's best move for that piece) and fires one quick-tier call. 3. The sentence streams into the bubble; the reply's squares and arrows are validated and drawn. 4.
