In quiz mode the reply carries an `ask` of a type the page can key (tap_attacker, tap_safe_square, tap_guarded); the page shows the question, checks the tap locally, says "Yes" or "Not that one, look again", then reveals the sentence. 5. Tap elsewhere or move; the bubble clears. A repeat of the same piece and chip in the same position within an hour replays from cache without a call.
concepts.llm_role: One call shape from one explicit action, the chip tap: `sample.json(prompt, {modelTier: "quick", cache: {gcTime: 3600000}, signal})`; the prompt embeds the FEN and the chip so the cache hits exactly when a replay is right. No tools in the MVP; iteration 2 offers `look({move})` (chess.js copy, depth 12, returns `{legal, evalAfter, bestReply, hangsAfter}`) for the "What should I do with it?" chip only, with `cache` omitted on those calls, "call look at most twice" in the prompt, and only when `sample.limits()` reports `tools`. Input under 1.5 KB: role block "You are a chess coach answering a player rated under 1000 who tapped one piece. One sentence of at most 25 words, optionally one more. Use only the facts below. Name only squares and pieces that appear in the facts. No evaluation numbers. No tactic names."; piece facts "Piece: White bishop on c4. Attacked by: pawn d5. Defended by: nothing. Safe squares: b3, b5, d3, e2, f1. It attacks: b3, b5, d3, d5, e2, f1, f7 (f7 is defended by the king). Engine best move here: Bb3 (+0.1); exd5 is also fine (0.0); leaving the bishop loses 3.0."; the question "Is it safe?"; and the contract {"say": string, "squares": [...], "arrows": ["d5c4"], "ask": null | {"type": "tap_attacker" | "tap_safe_square" | "tap_guarded", "prompt": string}}. Example reply: {"say":"No. The pawn on d5 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it. Move it, or it is gone next move.","squares":["c4","d5"],"arrows":["d5c4"],"ask":null}. In quiz mode the prompt adds "Open with a question the player answers by tapping a square; choose the type from the list; the page knows the right answer" and the reply is {"say":"Right. Nothing of yours covers c4, so after the pawn takes, the bishop is simply gone.","squares":["c4"],"arrows":["d5c4"],"ask":{"type":"tap_attacker","prompt":"First: tap the piece that attacks your bishop."}}; the answer set (d5) is keyed by the page from the fact sheet, never taken from Claude, and an unknown `ask.type` is dropped. Validation: squares and arrows must be in the fact sheet's allowed sets; `say` must contain no SAN token outside the listed moves; a failed check shows the template answer ("Attacked by the pawn on d5. Not defended.") with the same arrows. Error handling as in Open Hand; `rate_limited` turns the chips into template answers for a minute with no message beyond "Coach is resting." With Claude absent the chips still appear and give template answers built from the facts, and the quiz toggle is hidden.
concepts.engine_role: chess.js computes the per-piece facts instantly on tap: `attackers()` by colour for the square, the piece's legal destinations and which of them are attacked (the safe-square glow), every square the piece attacks, and the captures available to and against it. Stockfish `go depth 12 multipv 3` on the position gives the best moves and evaluation, and a `go depth 10 searchmoves <the tapped piece's legal moves>` pass ranks that piece's own moves so "What should I do with it?" comes from the engine, not Claude. The answer key for every quiz type is computed here. All of it runs before the call so the arrows appear at tap time, not at answer time, and the fact sheet is cached per FEN so re-taps cost nothing.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page with the demo position and a board you can also move pieces on freely (both sides, chess.js rules only); tap-a-piece chips with "Is it safe?" and "What is it doing?"; the quick-tier JSON call with validation and drawn arrows; the attack ring on threatened pieces; template fallback and `window.__stubSample` with one canned reply that names an off-list square to prove it is dropped. No quiz mode, no third chip, no tools.
concepts.delight: Tapping a piece you were worried about and seeing the arrow from the pawn that threatens it appear before the sentence finishes: the page saw what you felt. And the first quiz turn where you tap the right attacker and it says "Right."
risks: Every first tap on a chip is a paid call and a curious player can tap thirty times in a game; cache by position and chip, show the template sentence for repeat chips, and keep the call for the first tap only.
"What is it doing?" has no single engine fact; the answer is Claude's reading of the attack map, grounded but sometimes bland.
At 400 px the chips, bubble and board must fit without pushing the board off-screen; the bubble must overlay the board edge, not stack below it.
The chip set is limited by design; the moment a player wants a fourth question a text box is the obvious next request, and that is exactly the chatbot this concept refuses.
The quiz keying covers three question types only; Claude must be told to use ask: null for anything else and the validator must drop any other type.
A chip answer during Open Hand play competes with Mira's bubble for the same space and the same quick-call slot; only one bubble may be live, and the chip tap must abort any pending telegraph call.

concepts.persona: The beginner: Sambudh's stand-in. Rated under 1000 once, studied nothing, opens 1.e4, lost most games to pieces taken for free without knowing why, and has closed every chess app that showed him an evaluation bar.
concepts.perspective_summary: I do not want a number, a label or a line of moves; I want one plain sentence and a lit-up square at the exact moment it matters, which is the second before I let go of a piece and the second after I lose one. I will come back tomorrow if the thing being counted is one I understand and can feel going down (pieces I gave away today, not an ELO estimate), and I will send it to a friend if there is a single moment I can hand them with "can you see it?"

concepts.name: Hold On
concepts.one_liner: A game against a bot where the board catches your hand before you give a piece away, and lets you argue back.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The half-placed move. In every app I have used, my move is either played or not, and the only help is an arrow (Hint) or a red label afterwards. Here, when I drop a piece on a square that gives something away for free, the move does not go through: the piece hovers on the target square at half opacity, the enemy piece that would take it glows, and one sentence appears under the board: "Hold on. That pawn can take your knight, and nothing of yours protects it." I then have three thumb-sized choices: "Show me" (his pawn slides over and takes, pauses, slides back; no words), "Take it back" (the piece returns, no penalty, no label), "Play it anyway" (counted, never nagged). And I can push back: tap "But..." and say in my own words "I'm attacking his king", and the coach answers my plan, not an engine number: "You are, and it's a good idea. But it's his move first, and he takes the knight before you get there. Is there a square for the knight that still looks at f2 but no pawn can reach?" No product holds the move and talks about my intention while the piece is still in my hand. The engine makes it correct; Claude makes it about me. This is not a chatbot next to a board because Claude never speaks unprompted, never speaks about anything but the move in my hand, and speaks through the board (lit squares, ghost moves) in two sentences at most.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh and anyone under 1000 who loses pieces for free and wants to stop without reading a book; also anyone who turned off Chess.com's Game Review because it felt like a report card.
concepts.first_30_seconds: Screen "Play": a board, white at the bottom, a bot with a plain name at the top, one line above the board: "Your move. I'll only speak up if a piece is about to be lost." Nothing else: no eval bar, no move list, no clock, no rating. 0-5 s: I drag e2 to e4 (or tap the pawn, tap the square). It snaps; the bot replies e5 in under a second with a soft slide. 5-20 s: three more move pairs (Nf3 Nc6, Bc4 Nf6); the bot plays like a human beginner, and the coach is silent; the only text that changes is "Your move" / "Thinking...". 20-30 s: I try to take his pawn on e5 with my knight because it looks free. The knight hovers on e5 half-transparent, his knight on c6 glows, and under the board: "Hold on. His knight on c6 takes yours back. You'd get a pawn and lose a knight." Buttons: Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway / But... I tap Show me: his knight slides to e5 and takes, a small "-2" floats up (pawn 1, knight 3), a beat, everything slides back. I tap Take it back and play d3. The coach says nothing. That silence is the first lesson. (The position and the loss are the ones verified in chess-study/lessons/0001-blunder-check.yml, phase 3: 4.Nxe5?? Nxe5, cp_loss 335.)
concepts.core_loop: 1. "Your move": while I think, the engine quietly scores every legal move in the background so the drop can be judged instantly. 2. I drop a piece. If it gives nothing away (loss under 200 cp, or not something a one-move look would catch), it plays, silently; silence is the reward. 3. If it hangs something: half-placed piece, glowing attacker, one templated sentence, Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway / But... (the last two words open Claude). 4. The bot replies in about a second; its reply sometimes hangs a piece too, and the "what can I take?" look is mine to run; no hint is pushed, but tapping any enemy piece tells me what guards it. 5. Game ends with one card: "Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4). Times you held on: 3." plus the single worst moment, which opens Rewind if that concept exists. 6. "Play again"; the bot goes a notch harder only when I gave away zero pieces.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is NOT called on ordinary moves and NOT for the standard hold-on sentence; code templates that from the engine's facts (attacker square, victim, defenders, material delta). Claude is called, modelTier "quick", only from two explicit taps on the hold-on card: "Why?" and "But..." (a one-line box). Input is one prompt string: FEN before and after my move, my move in words and in SAN, the engine's best reply and the 2-ply line with the material swing, the list of my pieces attacked after the move, my last three moves, my typed "But..." text if any, and the rules: "Two sentences at most. Call pieces by name and square in words, never bare notation. Never say blunder, mistake, inaccuracy, or give an evaluation number. Never contradict the engine facts given. If the player pushed back, end with a question." Tools handed in: highlight({squares}) to light up what it is talking about, and play_ghost({moves}) that animates up to 2 plies on the board and reverts (the page checks legality with chess.js; nothing commits). Example, after I typed "but I'm attacking f2": "You are, and your bishop on c4 already points there. But it's his move first: his pawn on d3 takes your knight before you get to f2. Can you find a square for the knight that still looks at f2 but no pawn can reach?" with highlight(["d3","e4","f2"]). A third optional call at game end, "quick", sends this game's hold-on and given-away events as one fact line each plus the last five games' lines from db, and asks for "one sentence about what to watch next game, in the player's words". Example: "Three of the four pieces you lost this week were a knight landing where a pawn could take it. Next game, before the knight lands, look for the pawns." If claude.use("sample") is null or the viewer declines (not_granted), Why and But... are hidden and the template sentence stands alone; the page is fully playable without Claude.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish in a Web Worker does three jobs. (a) Opponent: Skill Level 0-3 with a sprinkle of its own second and third choices (multipv 3, weighted random) so it plays like a 700-900 human and gives pieces away sometimes, which I need, because otherwise I never get to practise "what can I take?"; replies at depth 6-8, under a second. (b) Referee, ahead of time: during my think time it runs go depth 10 with multipv set to all legal moves on the current position, so when I drop a piece the cp loss of that move is already known and the hold-on decision is instant; if the pre-compute has not finished it falls back to go depth 12 on the position after my move (about 1 s) while the piece visibly settles. The hold-on rule is the lesson's rule: loss of 200 cp or more AND the engine's best reply is a capture, or a check that wins material within 2 plies; otherwise silence, because a positional loss is not my level. (c) Fact supplier: the reply line for the "Show me" ghost, the material delta, and (via chess.js) attackers and defenders of the target square, which both the template and Claude's prompt use, so nobody says anything the engine did not find.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/vendor: a board rendered from FEN in a CSS grid (same approach as chess-study/components/local/board.js, plus drag and tap-tap input), chess.js for legality, Stockfish worker as opponent (Skill 1) and referee (depth 12 after-drop check; the pre-compute can come in iteration two). Hold-on card for the capture case only (piece attacked and undefended, or attacked by a pawn, material delta of 2 points or more) with the templated sentence, Show me (ghost capture animation and revert), Take it back, Play it anyway. One "Why?" button that calls Claude on quick with the highlight tool, hidden when sample is null; window.__stubSample returns a canned two-sentence answer for the Playwright run. End card with pieces given away and times held on, kept in localStorage. Light and dark, 400 px, no eval bar, no move list, no rating anywhere.
concepts.delight: Tapping "Show me" and watching the future happen on my own board: his pawn slides over, takes my knight, a small "-2" floats up, a beat, and everything slides back as if nothing happened. The first time I see it I will laugh, because it is exactly the thing I never saw in my games until it was too late.
risks: Interrupting too often: if it holds every slightly worse move I stop trusting it and turn it off; the threshold must stay at "a piece for free" and nothing else, and that has to be enforced by tests, not taste.
The settle delay: a one-second pause on every move while the engine checks will feel like lag; the pre-compute during think time, or a visible settle, is not optional for long.

The bot's strength: a Stockfish that never gives anything away means I never practise taking free pieces and I lose every game anyway; the weakening (Skill Level plus random second choices) is untested on real beginners.
"Play it anyway" abuse: if I always press it, nothing is learned; count it on the end card, never nag about it.

The first Claude consent dialog appears the first time I tap "Why?"; if the page has not said in plain words beforehand that this asks Claude on my own account, I will decline out of fear and never see the feature.
Drift back to labels: every chess app says blunder and shows ??; the team will be tempted to add them "for clarity" and the copy rule needs a test that fails on those words.

Outside the Claude viewer (a friend's link, local testing) sample is absent, so Why and But... vanish; the template sentence has to carry the whole product on its own and must not look like something is missing.

concepts.name: Rewind
concepts.one_liner: After a loss, not a report card: the one moment it went wrong, a question instead of an answer, and the chance to play the game again from there.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The replayable mistake, with a question I answer by touching the board. Every review I have seen is a list: move 14, blunder, best was Ba4, +4.5, and three lines of moves I cannot read. Here, when the game ends (or when I lose a piece mid-game and tap the small "what just happened?" chip), the board rewinds by itself to the position before my bad move, his last move slides in again so I see it arrive, and the coach asks instead of tells: "That pawn just moved one step. Tap the piece of yours it is now attacking." I tap. Right: "Yes, the bishop. It had to move. Play from here." Wrong: "Not that one. Follow the pawn's next step diagonally." Then I re-enter the game I lost, at the exact position where I lost it, against the same bot, and if I keep the piece this time the moment is marked answered. The coach keeps these moments across days (db) and, in one line, names my personal pattern: not "you blunder in the opening" but "A pawn walking up to your bishop. Three times this week." Nobody else asks me the question and lets me answer with my thumb, and nobody else lets me step back into the game at the moment it went wrong. Not a chatbot: there is no text box on this screen unless I choose to type an answer; Claude writes one question and reads one answer.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh after a lost game, when he wants to know why without feeling stupid; any beginner who closed Chess.com's Game Review because it was a column of red labels behind a paywall.
concepts.first_30_seconds: Screen "That game" opens right after the end-of-game card or from a "Rewind" tap. 0-5 s: the board slides back move by move to the position before my mistake, fast then slowing, like a tape rewinding, and stops. One line above the board: "Move 4. This is where the bishop went." His last move, the pawn to a6, plays again slowly so I see it. 5-15 s: under the board: "That pawn just moved one step. Tap the piece of yours it is now attacking." Every square is tappable, nothing else is on screen. I tap my bishop on b5. 15-25 s: "Yes. The bishop had to move. You castled instead, and the pawn took it." The capture ghosts through: pawn takes bishop, pause, revert. 25-30 s: one button, "Play from here". The board turns live, it is my move at move 4, and I play the bishop back to a4. Silence. The bot replies. We are playing again. (This is the verified Ruy Lopez moment from lesson 0001 phase 2: 3...a6 4.O-O?? axb5, cp_loss 455; 4.Ba4 best.)
concepts.core_loop: 1. Finish a game, or lose a piece mid-game (a small "?" chip appears for one move, no interruption). 2. The engine scores the game and picks the single worst loss that a one-move look would have caught. 3. Rewind animation to the position before it; his last move replays. 4. One question, answered by tapping a square (or by typing a sentence if I prefer); one line of feedback, then the ghost of what actually happened. 5. "Play from here": the game resumes from that position against the bot, with the Hold On coach active if it exists. 6. If I reach the end without giving that piece away, the moment is marked answered; the end card says "Answered: the bishop on b5 moment." 7. The moment is stored per viewer (db) as one fact line: date, kind (attacker missed / took a defended piece / missed the coming check), pieces, squares; every few games the coach writes one sentence about my pattern.
concepts.llm_role: Claude writes the question and reads my typed answer; the engine and chess.js supply every fact and grade every tap. Call 1, modelTier "quick", sample.json, triggered by the explicit "Rewind" tap (one call per game, the input is fixed so it is cached): input is the FEN before the mistake, his last move, my move, the engine's refutation line, the attacker, victim and defender squares, the mistake kind as classified by code, and the rules: "Write one question for a beginner that is answered by tapping one square. Do not name the answer. Call pieces by name, never bare notation. Reply with only JSON: {question, answer_squares, if_right, if_wrong}." Example output: {"question":"That pawn just moved one step. Tap the piece of yours it is now attacking.","answer_squares":["b5"],"if_right":"Yes, the bishop. It had to move, and stepping back to a4 keeps it.","if_wrong":"Not that one. Follow the pawn's next step diagonally."}. Code checks answer_squares against the real attacked set from chess.js and overrides if Claude is wrong, and a fallback question ("Tap the piece of yours his last move attacks") exists so Rewind works with no Claude at all. Call 2, "quick", only if I tap "Type it instead": my sentence plus the same facts; "In one sentence, say whether the player has found the attacked piece and the reason; if not, one nudge, never the answer." Example: "Half right: the pawn is the attacker, but it is your bishop it reaches, not the knight. Look one square diagonally from the pawn." Tools for both calls: highlight({squares}) and play_ghost({moves}) (max 2 plies, reverts). Call 3, "quick", from the end card every third game with the last ten stored moment lines: "One sentence naming the player's pattern in plain words, with the count; if fewer than five moments, reply with an empty string." Example: "Three of your last five lost pieces were a knight stepping onto a square a pawn could reach. Next game, before the knight lands, look for pawns."
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish scores the finished game (go depth 14 per position, about 40 positions in 20-40 s in the worker while the end card is already useful, with the line "Looking back over the game...") and finds every move of mine that lost 200 cp or more; chess.js then keeps only the ones a one-move look catches (the reply is a capture of a piece that was attacked and undefended or attacked by a pawn, or a check that wins material within 2 plies). The engine picks the biggest of those as "the moment", supplies the refutation line for the ghost animation, confirms the acceptable rescue moves (within 60 cp of best, or any move that keeps the piece) so "Play from here" can judge the first move I play, and is the opponent from that position on. chess.js supplies the attacked set for grading taps. No evaluation number is ever shown.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page that takes a finished game (from Hold On if built; otherwise a built-in seed game of a beginner's 1.e4 e5 loss containing the verified 3...a6 4.O-O?? axb5 moment), runs the engine over it in the worker, picks the moment, rewinds with animation, asks the engine-only fallback question, grades the tap with chess.js, ghosts the capture, and offers "Play from here" against the bot. Claude call 1 (the written question) behind sample, with window.__stubSample returning a fixed JSON for the Playwright run. Answered moments kept in localStorage; db comes in the next iteration.
concepts.delight: "Play from here" and winning the game I lost, from the exact position where I lost it, with the exact move I missed. The board does not say anything special. I just know.
risks: The engine's biggest loss and the moment I felt was the problem can differ; the move number must be shown and a "show me another moment" must exist, or I will not trust the rewind.
Scoring 40 positions at depth 14 on a phone could take over 30 s; the end card must already be useful while it runs, or I will close the page before the question appears.
Claude's question could leak the answer or name a square that is not actually attacked; the page must validate answer_squares and fall back to the engine-only question silently.

If nothing was given away (I lost slowly, or to a mate I never saw) there is no moment to rewind; an honest state is needed: "Nothing was given away for free this game. It was lost slowly, which is a different lesson."
Replaying from the moment, the bot will play differently, so the game goes elsewhere; "answered" must mean I kept that piece, not that I won, or it becomes another way to lose.
Pattern sentences need enough stored moments; before five games the coach must say nothing rather than invent a pattern, and the prompt must say so.

concepts.name: Can You See It
concepts.one_liner: One position, one question, one tap, every day, from your own games; and a link that puts a friend in the same seat.
concepts.the_new_interaction: A position I can hand to someone. Puzzles exist everywhere, but they are "find the best move" with a rating attached, and I usually cannot. Here the first screen is a single position and a question about looking, not calculating: "His queen came out early. Tap the square she and the bishop both aim at." I tap f7. One line back, a ghost of what would have happened, done in forty seconds, Day 1. Once I have played games, the position of the day is from MY own game (a stored Rewind moment) and the question is rewritten for the daily form the way the lessons review: the second time it comes round, no hint about which piece moved; the third time, the same idea in a different position. And the share: "Send this one" makes a link carrying the position and the question; my friend opens it in any browser, same board, same question, taps, and only then sees "Want to play a game that stops you before you give a piece away?" No account, no app, no rating; the thing passed around is a moment, not a score. Not a chatbot: there is no text box at all unless I choose to type an answer; most days nothing is said to Claude.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh on a day he will not play a whole game; the friend he sends it to, who has never opened a chess app; beginners who find puzzle ratings humiliating.
concepts.first_30_seconds: Screen "Today" is the first thing on load: a board turned so my side is at the bottom (here Black, after 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 Nc6 3.Bc4), and one line under it: "His queen came out early. Tap the square she and the bishop both aim at." That is all: no puzzle number, no rating, no timer. 0-10 s: I look and tap f7. 10-20 s: "Yes. Two of his pieces on f7, and only your king guards it. Queen takes would be checkmate." The queen ghosts to f7 and back. Then: "Your move. What do you play?" I play the g-pawn to g6. "That closes her road. Done for today." 20-30 s: a small "Day 1", and two buttons: "Send this one" and "Play a game". Tapping "Send this one" copies the link and the page says: "Copied. They'll see the same board and the same question." (Position and acceptable replies verified in lesson 0001 phase 2: g6 best, Qe7/Qf6/Nh6 also hold f7; Nf6, Bc5, d6 allow Qxf7 mate.)
concepts.core_loop: 1. Open the page: today's position, from a seed set of engine-verified positions until I have five stored moments of my own, then from my own moments, spaced: the moment again after two days with the board hint, after a week without the hint, then the same idea in a different seed position. 2. One question, answered by a tap. 3. One line of feedback and a 2-ply ghost animation. 4. When the question was about an attack, a follow-up on the live board: "What do you play?", checked against the acceptable set (within 60 cp of best, or any move that keeps the piece). 5. "Day N" and a streak kept per viewer. 6. "Send this one" copies a link with the position, the question and the answer squares in the URL hash; the friend's page reads it, no Claude needed. 7. "Play a game" leads into Hold On.
concepts.llm_role: For seed positions Claude is not called at all: the question, answer squares, feedback and acceptable replies ship with the position, taken from the verified lessons. Claude is called, modelTier "quick", sample.json, only when today's position is one of MY stored moments and the question must be written for the daily form, triggered by opening the Today screen (one stable prompt per day, so it is cached): input is the moment's facts (FEN, his last move, my move, the refutation line, attacker, victim and defender squares, mistake kind, how many times this moment has been shown) and the review rule ("second showing: do not say which piece moved; third showing: the same idea, do not mention it is a repeat"), plus: "One question answerable by tapping one square, no bare notation, do not name the answer. Reply with only JSON: {question, answer_squares, if_right, if_wrong}." Example: {"question":"Something of yours can be taken for free right now. Tap it.","answer_squares":["b5"],"if_right":"The bishop. The pawn beside it stepped forward last move.","if_wrong":"Not that one. Look at the pawn that moved last and where it steps next."}. A second "quick" call only if I tap "Type it instead": my sentence plus the same facts, "In one sentence, has the player named the attacked piece and the attacker? If not, one nudge." Tool for both: highlight({squares}). Code validates answer_squares against chess.js's attacked set before anything is shown. Shared links never call Claude: the question text travels inside the link.
concepts.engine_role: For seed positions the engine confirms once at load in the worker (go depth 16) that the shipped answer is still best and the acceptable-reply set holds; if it disagrees the position is skipped, so a hallucinated line can never reach the screen. For my own moments the engine already scored them in Rewind; here it supplies the acceptable-reply set for "What do you play?", the refutation line for the ghost, and plays the 2-ply ghost. chess.js grades the tap. No evaluation is ever displayed, not even as a bar.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page with a data file of six positions lifted from the two existing lessons (Nxe4/dxe4, Ng4/hxg4, a6/Ba4, Qh5 and Bc4/g6, the Bxf7+ grab, the Nxe5 grab), each with question, answer squares, if_right, if_wrong and acceptable replies; the board with tap-to-answer; ghost animation; the "What do you play?" follow-up checked against the shipped set, with the engine confirming at load; a Day counter in localStorage; "Send this one" building a URL hash the page reads on load. Claude only for typed answers, stubbed with window.__stubSample. No db yet; my own moments arrive when Rewind ships.
concepts.delight: Sending a position to a friend and getting "I didn't see it either" back. Or, on day nine, recognising the position as one from my own game and tapping the right square in a second.
risks: Six seed positions last a week; before I have five moments of my own the daily goes stale, so a second seed batch has to be written and verified with scripts/engine_check.py early.
The share link opens outside the Claude viewer, so Claude is absent there; the daily is designed engine-only, but "Play a game" for the friend then lacks the Why button and must not look broken.
Tap-only questions get boring if it is always "tap the attacked piece"; the question kinds must rotate (what is attacked, what is free to take, the check that is coming, the piece that defends).
Streaks guilt people; a missed day must not scold, and "Day N" must count days played, not days in a row.
Positions from my own games are what make this personal and they do not exist on day one; the screen should say so plainly ("Your own positions start after five games") rather than pretend.
A malformed or edited link must fall back to today's seed position, never to a blank board.

concepts.perspective_summary: A game designer cares that the thing the player does every twenty seconds is itself the lesson, that the opponent is tuned so a beginner can win while losing exactly the way they need to lose, and that getting better is felt in the hands (a ring that shrinks, a chair that is no longer offered) before it is ever shown as a number. The coach is a voice inside the game that arrives at the moment it is asked for, points at the board, says one true thing in the player's words, and otherwise stays out of the way.

concepts.name: Both Ways
concepts.one_liner: Play an opponent that tells you what it is about to do, and learn to look before it has to.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Two things, neither in any chess product. First, the opponent is transparent on demand, in its own voice: after any bot move, one tap on the chip "What am I up to?" and the opponent answers in the first person and points at the board while it speaks: "I put my bishop on c4. It's looking at f7, and only your king is guarding it. Next move my queen comes to h5 and that's mate. Your turn." The facts are the engine's (the page computes what the moved piece now attacks, what is hanging, whether a mate-in-one threat exists, before Claude is asked, and hands them over in the prompt); Claude's job is to say them as an opponent would and to highlight the squares as it says them. Second, the hold: when you drop a piece the move waits about a second on a soft ring and the board shows their chair, so anything you have just left for free pulses under the enemy piece that would take it; you drag it back for free. The ring shrinks as you stop needing it and one day it is gone. Nothing is explained after the fact; the looking happens inside the move, which is the only place an under-1000 player ever loses a game.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh first: knows the rules, plays 1.e4, wants to play rather than study, and loses pieces to one-move threats. Then the millions like him under 1000 who have never opened a lesson and never will.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-3 s: the page opens on the starting position, white at the bottom, nothing else but one line above the board: "Your move. I'll tell you what I'm up to, if you ask." No login, no settings, no empty state. 3-8 s: he plays 1.e4 by dragging or by two taps; the move holds for a beat on a ring, nothing pulses because nothing is hanging, it commits with a soft tick; the bot replies 1...e5 in under a second (Stockfish depth 12 in the worker), and a small chip appears under its move: "What am I up to?" 8-20 s: 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, each bot reply instant. 20-27 s: he drags the bishop to f7, check and a pawn. The hold turns the board to their chair: his bishop on f7 pulses, a thin arrow runs from the e8 king to f7, and the ring reads "they take back, free". He drags the bishop home. Nothing is said; a one-word chip under the board reads "Looked." 27-30 s: he plays 4.d3, the ring is quiet and green, and he has run the blunder check without ever hearing its name.
concepts.core_loop: Every 20 seconds: (1) pick a move, (2) drop it, (3) the hold shows their chair for a beat, (4) commit or drag it back, (5) the bot answers instantly, (6) optionally tap "What am I up to?" and watch the opponent point. Every session (10-15 minutes): (1) one game of 25-40 moves against a bot that always takes what you hang and leaves two or three pieces of its own for you to catch, (2) at the end one card, "The moment that mattered": the biggest swing in the game with your side to move and the question "What did my last move attack? Tap the square.", (3) the card's one-paragraph note from Claude with memory of your last games, (4) "Again", with the bot hanging a little less if you caught its pieces and a little more if you missed them. Every week: (1) the clean-games streak (games with zero pieces hung) shown as marks on the board edge, (2) the hold's ring visibly smaller than last week, (3) one line: "Last week you hung 5 pieces in 4 games. This week 2 in 5. The hold is half the size it was."
concepts.llm_role: Claude is the opponent's voice and the memory, never the engine, and it is called only on taps. (1) The "What am I up to?" chip after any bot move: modelTier "quick", about a second, with onText so the sentence appears as it is written. The prompt carries the FEN, the last move, the facts the page already computed (the moved piece and every player piece on a square it now attacks, each hanging player piece with its attacker and defender counts, a mate-in-one threat and its square if the depth-3 search found one, the engine's best player reply at depth 12 so Claude knows what not to give away), the player's band, and the instruction: speak as the opponent in the first person, two sentences at most, never name the player's best move, and call the page tool point({squares, arrows}) for everything you mention. Tools given: point only. Example: "My knight on g4 is aiming at f2, together with the bishop. But before you worry about that, have a look at what your h3 pawn can reach." (2) "The moment that mattered" card at game end: modelTier "default", 10-30 s, the card and its board drawn first and the text streamed into it. The prompt carries the position, the move played, the engine's best move, the refutation line (2-4 plies of the depth-14 PV), the player's mistake tallies from the last five games in db (hung-to-pawn, took-a-guarded-pawn, ignored-last-move, walked-into-mate) and the three-looks vocabulary from the blunder-check lesson. Tools: show_line(moves) which animates the line on the card's board and returns the engine eval, and point. Example: "You asked what you could take and stopped there. The knight landed where my d3 pawn attacks it, and nothing of yours defends e4: a knight for a pawn. That is the third time this week a knight has gone to a square a pawn attacks. Next game, before you let go: what can they take?" (3) "Show me" inside the hold when the ring pulses: quick tier with show_line, and Claude plays the two-ply punishment as ghost pieces: "You take the pawn, I take your knight back with the bishop. See it?" If claude.use("sample") is null or a call rejects with not_granted, the chips are hidden and the hold still works, with the engine's facts as a plain line ("Your knight on e4 can be taken by the d3 pawn, and nothing defends it."); rate_limited shows "Ask me again in a minute" on the chip and the page never retries on its own.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/stockfish-18-lite-single.js in a Web Worker) and chess.js (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/chess.js) do everything that needs no words, instantly, so the game never waits. chess.js: legality, SAN, and the attacker and defender count of every square on drop, which is what the hold's their-chair pulse is drawn from in under a millisecond. Stockfish, depth 12 with multipv 8: the bot's move, with three rules that make it beatable and instructive: it always plays the top move when that move captures material worth two points or more or gives mate (so a hung piece is always punished), it never hangs its queen or walks into mate, and otherwise it samples among moves within 60 cp of best, except that at a tuned rate (10% of moves at first, lower as the player's catch rate rises) it deliberately plays a move from the multipv list that loses 200-400 cp, a minor piece left for free, so the player gets to be the one who looks and takes. Stockfish also evaluates every move at depth 12 during the game so the biggest swing is known the instant the game ends, runs a depth-3 search after each player move to detect a mate-in-one threat for the chip's facts, and produces the depth-14 refutation line handed to Claude so it never invents one. The engine, not Claude, grades the card's tap-the-square question.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page in app/: play white against the bot, with the hold and the their-chair pulse. The "What am I up to?" chip after each bot move backed by sample on quick with the point tool, and by window.__stubSample returning canned text under Playwright. At game end the one-moment card with tap-the-square (engine graded) and the Claude note (default tier, stub in tests). The hold's ring size and the clean-games count in localStorage for the MVP, moved to db + user once the loop is proven in Sambudh's hands. No black-side play, no daily, no sharing yet. The MVP is proven if he drags a piece back inside the hold at least once per game and finishes a game with fewer pieces hung than his first.
concepts.delight: The first time the hold catches his bishop on f7 and he drags it back himself, the opponent says nothing and a one-word chip reads "Looked." The silence is the smile, because he did it. The second smile is the end of his first clean game, when the ring under the board is visibly smaller than it was and the line reads "You did not need the hold for 31 moves."
risks: Cost: one quick call per tap is fine, one per move is not; if the chip is tapped three moves in a row the page shows the engine's plain fact first and offers the voice on a second tap, and every call runs on an explicit tap, never on the bot's move itself.

The hold can feel like friction to an impatient player; it must be a tap-to-confirm with a visible shrink, never a blocking modal, dismissable from the board edge, and shortened by prefers-reduced-motion.

A sampled-multipv bot can play silly moves that teach nothing; the hang rule (minor piece only, 200-400 cp, never queen, never mate) and a few hundred headless self-play games are needed to tune it before Sambudh sees it.
The their-chair pulse could become a crutch; the shrink is the answer, and only games played at the smallest ring count toward the clean streak.

Claude must never state a chess fact the page did not compute: the prompt gives it the engine's facts and tells it to point and speak, not to analyse, and the stub tests check that the chip's text names only squares the page highlighted.

concepts.name: Change Chairs
concepts.one_liner: When you hang a piece, the opponent stops the game and hands you its chair: take it yourself, feel it, then rewind.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The punishment becomes the player's own move. Every product in the world either plays the capture against you or marks your move with a red question mark afterwards. Here, when the engine sees that the move you just made leaves a piece for free, the bot does not reply. The board turns over half a second, you are sitting on the other side, and the opponent says: "Sit here a second. What would you take?" You make the capture with your own finger: the piece comes off, the material count on the board edge drops, and only then does the board turn back with "Still want to play it?" and a Rewind. The first games offer unlimited chairs; the budget shrinks as you stop needing them, and the first game with none is announced before it starts: "No chairs today. A real game." This is the blunder-check lesson's "change chairs" phase made physical, and no engine review or chatbot can do it because it happens before the move is final. Claude is not the mechanic; it says the one line that ties the swap to the look that was missed, with memory, and it answers "but what if I defend it?" by playing that out on the ghost board.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh: a player under 1000 who knows what a hanging piece is in words and cannot yet feel it before he lets go. Second, a parent teaching a child, because swapping chairs is a thing two people already do across a real table.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-3 s: the board, white at the bottom, one line: "Your move. If you hang something, I'll let you sit in my chair before I take it." 3-18 s: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, every reply instant. 18-23 s: he plays 4.Nxe5, a pawn in the centre. The bot does not reply. The board rotates, the pieces settle from Black's side, and the line reads "Sit here. What would you take?" 23-28 s: his own knight on e5 is the obvious thing; he taps the c6 knight, then e5; the white knight comes off with a soft thud and the count on the edge reads "-2". The board rotates back: "Still want to play 4.Nxe5? Rewind." He taps Rewind; the knight slides home; the count returns to 0. 28-30 s: one line arrives from Claude: "That pawn was guarded by the knight beside it. Before you let go: what can they take?"
concepts.core_loop: Every 20 seconds: (1) make a move, (2) most of the time the bot answers at once, (3) when the move hangs two points or more or walks into mate-in-one the chair swap fires: turn, take with your own hand, turn back, (4) Rewind or Play it anyway. Every session (10-15 minutes): (1) one game, (2) the chairs used this game shown as small chairs along the board edge, not as a number, (3) one line at the end and "Again". Every week: (1) games one to three have unlimited chairs, (2) then the budget is set to your average chairs used minus one, down toward zero, (3) the first zero-chair game is a named event with a different board frame: "No chairs today. A real game.", (4) after it, one chair a game can still be asked for and is counted, (5) clean games (no chair needed) chain into a streak drawn as a row of chairs turned to face away.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is called at three explicit moments and never to find a move. (1) Right after the board turns back, one line on modelTier "quick", no tools, about a second, streamed with onText. The prompt carries the position before the move, the move, the capture the player made in the other chair, the engine's attacker and defender counts on the landing square, the three-looks vocabulary, and the player's recent chair reasons from db (counts of hung-to-pawn, took-a-guarded-pawn, ignored-last-move, walked-into-mate). Instruction: one or two sentences in the second person, name the look that was skipped, never name the best move, and if the same reason has happened three or more times this week say so plainly. Example: "The e5 pawn was defended by the knight on c6. You asked what you could take; the question you missed was from this chair. That is the fourth guarded pawn you have taken this week." (2) The "But what if I..." chip on the swap screen: the player types a few words or picks one of three engine-generated candidate defences; modelTier "default", 10-30 s, with tools try(moves) which plays a ghost line on the board and returns the depth-14 eval, and point. Claude plays the player's idea out, the pieces moving as each tool call lands, and says in at most three sentences why it does or does not work: "Say you defend with 4...d6 instead. I take the knight anyway, and the pawn you were guarding is still there. See it?" (3) The end-of-game line on default tier from the game's chair moments: "Three chairs tonight, all of them guarded pawns. You never hung a piece to a one-move threat; that look is working." With sample null or not_granted, (1) becomes the engine's fact in a plain template ("e5 was defended by the knight on c6."), (2) is hidden, and the swap itself runs entirely without Claude.
concepts.engine_role: The swap trigger belongs to the engine, so it is never wrong and never late. After every player move chess.js (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/chess.js) counts attackers and defenders on each player piece, and Stockfish (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/stockfish-18-lite-single.js in the worker) compares the depth-12 eval with the previous one: a drop of 200 cp or more, or a mate-in-one for the opponent, fires the chair; drops of 100-200 cp do not, because at this level they are not the lesson, and a sacrifice the engine sees as sound never fires. Inside the swap the engine does not play; the player does, and chess.js checks that the capture made is the punishing one (take the wrong thing and the edge count shows the smaller gain while the right capture pulses: "There was a bigger one."). The bot's own moves use the same calibrated sampler as Both Ways: multipv 8 at depth 12, always taking free material, never hanging the queen or walking into mate, hanging a minor piece at a tuned rate so the player gets to be the one who punishes. The three candidate defences for the what-if chip are the engine's multipv moves for the player filtered to those that touch the hanging piece, so Claude never has to invent one.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page, white against the bot, unlimited chairs. The swap in full: trigger, rotate (fade under prefers-reduced-motion), capture by hand, count on the edge, rotate back, Rewind or Play it anyway. The one post-swap line from Claude on quick with window.__stubSample for Playwright, and the plain engine template when sample is null. No budget, no what-if chip, no end-of-game line. The mechanic is proven if a tester rewinds after a swap more often than not, and if the number of chairs per game falls across five games.
concepts.delight: The moment the board turns and he takes his own knight with his own finger. It is a small physical shock, the "oh" of the lesson's road-crossing analogy, and it is funny. The opponent is allowed exactly one joke per game, and it is this one: "Comfortable? Mine is the better chair, I think."
risks: The rotation on a 400 px phone must take under half a second and become a fade under prefers-reduced-motion, or it is nauseating and the mechanic dies on the first game.
A swap every third move in a bad game is a lot of stopping; the 200 cp trigger, a cap of one swap per two moves, and the shrinking budget keep the game a game.
Play it anyway must be a real, unscolded option, or the swap feels like a parent's hand on the wrist and the player leaves.

The budget's shrink must be felt as graduation, not as losing a safety net; the named "No chairs today" frame and the one-chair-a-game allowance after it are what make it kind, and they need testing with Sambudh before the budget ships.
The what-if call with tools is 10-30 s per use and must stay out of the MVP; without it the page must still answer "why" with the engine's plain fact and the pulsing capture.
Both this and Both Ways share the bot and the engine plumbing; the team should build the bot once and pick one of the two front mechanics for the MVP rather than ship both half-made.

concepts.name: Three Looks, Daily
concepts.one_liner: One position a day from a game like yours: tap what their last move attacks, what you can take, what checks there are; share your three squares.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Chess puzzles ask for the best move. This asks for the looks. The answer is not a move but three taps on the board in order: the square their last move now attacks, the piece you can take for free, the check that exists for either side. The engine knows all three exactly, so nothing is a judgment call and nothing is a chatbot. The opponent's last move replays before your eyes, so the first look is honest. Once the player has games in this page, the day's position is the moment that mattered from their own game of yesterday, and the page says so. The result is a three-square grid you can send like a word game's grid, and a friend who opens the link gets the same position before they see your answer. Claude's part is the one sentence that turns three taps into a habit and remembers which look you keep skipping.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh on the days he will not play a full game: two minutes on a phone. Anyone under 1200, and the friend they send the grid to, who has never seen the page before.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-5 s: the page opens on today's position with Black's last move still animating in (the knight lands on g4); under the board: "Their knight just moved. Tap the square it is attacking." 5-12 s: he taps f2; the square rings and the next question slides in: "Now, what can you take for free? Tap it." 12-18 s: he taps g4; the h3 pawn's arrow draws itself to g4; a second ring. 18-24 s: "Any checks on the board, theirs or yours? Tap the piece that could give one, or None." He taps None; the board confirms none; a third ring. 24-30 s: the grid fills in square by square with a small bounce, "Three looks in 24 seconds. Share.", and Claude's line arrives: "All three. The knight was never a threat you had to answer, because you could take it first."
concepts.core_loop: Every 20 seconds: (1) one look, (2) one tap, (3) a ring, or a soft cross with the real square shown and the reason drawn (the arrow, the attacker count). Every session (two minutes): (1) three taps on one position, (2) the grid, (3) an optional "Why?" that plays the refutation on the board with the words, (4) share. Every day: the streak drawn as a row of the three-square grids, not a counter; a missed day leaves a grey grid, not a broken chain. Every week: (1) the look you skip most, named ("You skip the third look most: checks."), (2) which then chooses next week's positions, (3) and once the player also plays games in Both Ways or Change Chairs, the day's position is theirs: "This is from your game last night."
concepts.llm_role: Claude writes words, never positions. (1) The result line after the third tap: modelTier "quick", about a second, no tools. The prompt carries the position, the three correct squares with the engine's reasons (which piece attacks which, attacker and defender counts, the mate threat if any), the three taps the player made, and the last fourteen days of results per look from db. Instruction: one sentence in the second person; if a look was missed name it; if the same look has been missed three days running say so plainly. Example on a miss: "You found the free knight but skipped what their move attacked; that is the third day in a row the first look went missing." (2) The "Why?" chip after a miss: modelTier "default", 10-20 s, tools show_line(moves) and point, the board animating as each tool call arrives so the wait is the show. Claude is given the engine's refutation line and plays it while explaining in two sentences: "Leave the knight and it takes on f2 next move, with the bishop behind it. Take it first and there is nothing left to defend." (3) Each seeded position's one-line caption is generated once at authoring time by this team with engine_check.py, not by the viewer's Claude, so the daily costs the viewer nothing unless they tap. With sample null or not_granted the grid, rings and streak all work and the lines fall back to the engine's plain facts ("Their knight attacks f2. The knight on g4 is free. No checks.").
concepts.engine_role: The engine is the author and the grader. chess.js (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/chess.js) computes the three answers from the FEN deterministically: the player pieces on squares the moved piece now attacks, the player's captures that win material (attacker and defender counts and the value of the lowest attacker), and the checks available to either side. Stockfish (/home/user/hello-world/app/vendor/stockfish-18-lite-single.js) at depth 16 confirms that the free piece is really free (no in-between tactic) and that a mate-in-one threat is real; a position where the three looks and the engine's best move disagree is rejected at authoring time, so the daily never teaches a wrong look. For positions from the player's own games, Stockfish picks the biggest-swing move from the game's stored evals and the same checks run before it becomes the day's position; if they fail, a seeded position is used. Grading is the engine's, instant, and accepts any correct square when several are correct, showing the rest after the tap.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page with a corpus of 30 seeded positions from beginner 1.e4 e5 games (authored by the chess-master agent and verified with /home/user/hello-world/scripts/engine_check.py like the lessons in chess-study/lessons), one per day by date. The three-tap flow with rings and crosses, the grid, a share button that copies the grid text and the link with the day's number (the friend opens the link and gets the same position; no db compare yet), the result line from Claude on quick with window.__stubSample, and the streak in localStorage.
concepts.delight: The third ring on a clean day and the grid bouncing in square by square, then the share text that is in his own hand: "Three looks, day 4: all three in 24 s."
risks: It has the shape of a puzzle app, and the world is full of those; the newness is the verb (tap the looks, not the move) and the memory, and that must be felt on day one or it is a daily puzzle with extra steps.

Positions from the player's own games are the strongest version and need the play loop from Both Ways or Change Chairs to exist first; on its own this is a layer, not the product Sambudh opens on day one.

The three looks have edge cases (several pieces attacked, several free captures, a check that is also the free capture) that must be handled by accepting any correct square and revealing the rest, or the grading feels unfair and the smile is lost.
The streak must never punish: a missed day is a grey grid, and the week's line speaks about looks, not about days missed.
Thirty verified positions are real authoring work with the engine before the first day exists, and a wrong one teaches a wrong look to everyone who opens the link that day.

concepts.perspective_summary: Stockfish facts turned into LLM prose with a follow-up chat is now a commodity: Chessiro, ChessGPT, LearnChess, Chesska, the Lichess AI Coach extension and Chess.com Game Review v2 all ship it, all post-game or hint-shaped, and a 2026 benchmark still finds about a fifth of commentary sub-claims wrong without tools, so engine grounding is the entry fee, not a feature, and "chat next to a board" is dead on arrival. What no product does is listen: the player says the check before the move, the engine supplies the facts in milliseconds, and the LLM's one necessary job is to find the false belief in the player's own sentence and ask the question that exposes it without naming the move; that reversal is the interaction a Lichess forum thread would call new, and the other two concepts here (the rationed look from the opponent's chair, the habit that whispers before the moment) are its best companions, not substitutes.

concepts.name: Say It Before You Move
concepts.one_liner: You play a bot that hangs pieces like an 800, and before each move you say your check in one line; the coach stays silent when your reasoning is complete and asks one question, never a move, when it is not.
concepts.the_new_interaction: The direction of the conversation is reversed: the player talks first and the coach listens. Every product on the market makes the player ask the AI ("why was my knight move bad?" in ChessGPT, follow-up chat in Chessiro, the Hint button in Chess.com Play Coach that "tells you what you need to achieve or highlights pieces") or shows the answer after the fact (Game Review v2's Coach recap and on-board explanations, Lichess "Learn from your mistakes", which hides the best move until asked but speaks no language, DecodeChess's threat and plan tabs, Aimchess's six-area stats, Noctie's colour-coded live grades and puzzles from your games). None of them grades the player's reasoning, only the move. Here, under the board, there is one line: "Say your check, then move." Sambudh types "knight and bishop both aim at f2, I will castle to be safe" and plays O-O; the page already knows from Stockfish and chess.js that his h3 pawn attacks the g4 knight and nothing defends it, and that O-O loses 323 centipawns to hxg4; Claude reads his sentence against those facts and says: "You saw the threat to f2. Before you guard it: what does your h3 pawn attack right now, and who defends that square?" It never names a move. If the sentence covers the facts and the move is clean, the coach says nothing at all and a small "Checked" mark appears. A YouTuber can demo it in twenty seconds; a forum thread would notice that the engine never speaks, the LLM never shows a move, and the thing being corrected is the player's belief, which no template and no engine can parse. Checked today via WebSearch (vendor pages and announcements, not hands-on; chess.com and chessiro.com could not be fetched directly from this container): Chess.com Game Review v2 https://www.chess.com/news/view/chesscom-launches-game-review-v2 and Play Coach https://support.chess.com/en/articles/10877257-how-do-i-play-against-the-coach and Vs Computer Assisted mode https://www.chess.com/announcements/view/new-vs-computer ; Lichess Learn from your mistakes https://lichess.org/blog/WFvLpiQAACMA8e9D/learn-from-your-mistakes (no official LLM coach on Lichess was found); Chessiro (Stockfish 18 in the browser, Gemini prose, post-game chat with arrows, admits roughly one explanation in five is wrong) https://chessiro.com/blog/inside-chessiro-game-review and https://chessiro.com/blog/can-ai-coaching-work ; ChessGPT iOS (Stockfish 17 classifies, LLM answers questions) https://apps.apple.com/app/id6481724799 ; Noctie (human-like bots from a billion Lichess games, live grades, SRS puzzles from your games, 4.7 on 604 iOS ratings) https://apps.appfollow.io/ios/noctie-chess-trainer/6444289077?country=us ; DecodeChess https://decodechess.com/new-feature-explaining-your-moves/ ; Aimchess https://playmagnusgroup.com/brands/aimchess ; Chessable MoveTrainer https://support.chess.com/en/articles/10319322-how-does-the-spaced-repetition-scheduling-work ; the hallucination benchmark https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2608.04240 ; the Lichess community on coaches that invent positions https://lichess.org/@/baskervile/blog/why-a-chess-coach-shouldnt-be-allowed-to-invent-the-position/MUo90GyJ .
concepts.who_for: Sambudh first: under 1000, opens 1.e4, has studied nothing, phone in hand, wants to play rather than read. Then every adult returner who knows how the pieces move and loses to hung pieces and one-move threats. Not titled players, and not children who cannot type a sentence (voice is a later iteration).
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-5 s: The page opens on a board, white pieces at the bottom, already at move 6 of a typical 1.e4 e5 Italian; the first five moves were played for him and are listed faintly above the board with the line "Both sides developed. Black just played ...Ng4." The last move's from and to squares are tinted. Above the board: "Your move." Below it: one input with the placeholder "Say your check: what did that attack, what can you take, any checks?" and a button "Move". Nothing else on the screen. 5-15 s: He types "the knight and bishop are both on f2, I will castle" and drags the king to g1. 15-18 s: The king moves; a quiet listening pulse under the input for about a second (the quick-tier call); then one line appears in the coach's voice: "You saw the threat to f2. Before you guard it: what does your h3 pawn attack right now, and who defends that square?" with a single button, "Take it back". The g4 square is not highlighted; he has to look. 18-30 s: He takes it back, plays hxg4, the knight disappears, and the coach says "That one was yours." The bot replies instantly and the line reads "Your move." again. He has not read a menu, a manual or a settings screen.
concepts.core_loop: 1. The opponent moves (Stockfish at Skill Level 0-3 with a page-planted free piece every six to ten moves, each verified free by the engine). 2. The page computes the facts for the new position in under a second: what the last move newly attacks, your hanging pieces, your free captures, checks for both sides, mate-in-one threats. 3. The player optionally types one line, then moves. 4. The page scores the move: cp loss at depth 12 against the best move, plus whether a one-move look would have caught it. 5. If the move is clean and the line covers the facts: silence, a "Checked" mark, and a streak line ("Five moves, nothing hung"). 6. If the line misses a fact or the move hangs something catchable: one quick-tier call returns one question that names no move; a free takeback is offered only now. 7. The player fixes it or plays on; the coach says "That one was yours" on a fix and nothing on a refusal. 8. Game over: one slower call reads the flagged moves and writes three sentences and one named habit; the player can send the page to a friend or download the PGN. 9. "Play again" starts in the same opening family with a different planted trap.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is called at most once per player move, only when the player presses Move (an explicit viewer action, as the sample contract requires), on modelTier "quick" (about one second), with no tools: every chess fact is computed in the page first and placed in the prompt, so there are no tool rounds and no 30-90 s waits during play. The call is sample.json with a fixed instruction, the facts as a numbered list (F1 "your h3 pawn attacks g4; the g4 knight is defended by nothing", F2 "O-O loses 323 cp; the best move captures on g4"), the player's sentence, and the move. Output schema: {heard: string, missed: null | {fact: "F1", question: string}, praise: null | string}. Rules in the prompt: refer only to listed facts by id, never name a move or a destination square the player has not named, one question of at most twenty words, written to the player ("your h3 pawn", not "White's"). The page validates: a missed.fact not in the list, or any square or SAN token not already in the player's sentence, discards the answer and falls back to the template question for the top engine fact. Example: sentence "the knight and bishop are both on f2, I will castle", move O-O; output {heard: "You saw the f2 threat.", missed: {fact: "F1", question: "Before you guard f2: what does your h3 pawn attack right now, and who defends that square?"}, praise: null}. When the sentence covers every fact and the move is clean, the page does not call Claude at all. Post-game, one "default" tier call (no tools, 10-30 s, shown while the game replays) turns the flagged moves and facts into three sentences and one habit label from a fixed list of five. Why an LLM and not templates: the thing being corrected is the player's stated belief ("I will castle to be safe", "my queen covers it"), and finding the gap between a free-text belief and a fact list is language understanding; this repo's old coach.py line "Your knight on g4 is undefended!" is what templates give, and it is exactly the answer we must not show. Without the capability (not_granted) the input hides and the engine's templated questions carry the loop; on rate_limited the move still plays and the coach stays quiet for the next three moves.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish 18 lite in a Web Worker plus chess.js do everything that is not language, and do it before Claude is asked. (1) The opponent: Skill Level 0-3 (Stockfish's UCI_Elo floor is 1320, above this band, so the page must weaken it further) with a planted free piece every six to ten moves: the page picks a legal move that leaves a minor piece capturable, then confirms with a depth-12 search that the capture really wins material and is not a trap. (2) Facts per position, chess.js for geometry and depth 10-12 multipv 3 for values: squares the last move newly attacks and which of your pieces stand on them, attacked-and-undefended pieces, pieces attacked by a lower-value piece, free captures with net value, checks available to each side, mate-in-one threats. (3) The move audit: eval before, eval after the candidate at depth 12, cp loss, the two-ply refutation, and whether the refutation is an immediate capture or check; only those "one-move look" mistakes trigger the coach, deeper mistakes are let through at this band. (4) Every highlight, arrow and takeback decision comes from these numbers; Claude's text is never allowed to put anything on the board. (5) Post-game, the same audit list is the only material the summary call receives, so the summary cannot invent a mistake that did not happen.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus the vendored files: the board (chess.js, drag or tap-tap, phone width), the Stockfish worker as a planted-blunder beginner opponent, the facts computer, the move audit, the one-line input with "Move", the quick-tier sample.json call with the validator and the template fallback, the "Checked" mark and streak line, the takeback-after-question rule, light and dark tokens, and window.__stubSample so Playwright can drive the coach. It starts at a fixed Italian position with a known planted threat so the first frame is the product working. No accounts, no db, no post-game summary, no habits, no voice, no PGN download: those are iterations two and three.
concepts.delight: The first time he takes the move back after the question, plays the capture himself, and the coach says only "That one was yours." The second is the silence: five clean moves with no coach text and the line "Five moves, nothing hung" appearing without ceremony.
risks: Typing before every move is friction and most players will skip it. Mitigation: the line is optional, the coach only speaks on engine-flagged moves, the sentence is graded only when given, and the facts list makes an empty sentence still produce a good question. If the skip rate stays above 80 percent after real use, this is Chess.com Play Coach with better questions and should pivot to voice input or to Their Chair.

The LLM can still misread a fact list and ask a question pointing at the wrong thing; the roughly 20 percent sub-claim error rate measured for tool-free commentary applies to free prose, not to fact-matching, but it is not zero. Mitigation: outputs reference facts by id only, token validation against the facts, template fallback, and a log of every discarded answer for the next iteration.

The beginner opponent is the hard engineering: Stockfish at low skill plays strangely rather than like a beginner, and planted blunders must be verified free. A bot that never hangs anything teaches only defence; a bot that hangs everything teaches nothing.
Quick-tier latency variance: one second is fine, four seconds breaks the move rhythm. Mitigation: the move always plays immediately and the coach's line arrives after; never block input on the call.

The silence is a feature only if the player trusts it; early on he may want confirmation. A single "Checked" mark and a streak count are the compromise; a chatty coach turns this back into the commodity product.

Evidence caveat: WebSearch was available and used; chess.com and chessiro.com could not be fetched directly from this container (DNS blocked), so their feature claims come from search snippets of their own announcements, not hands-on use. Lichess Learn and Practice are described from knowledge; the search confirmed no official LLM coach exists there.
Licence: shipping Stockfish inside the page means the page's own source should be GPL-compatible; flagged, not solved, as the brief asks.

concepts.name: Their Chair
concepts.one_liner: Before you commit a move, tap once, the board turns round, and your opponent tells you in one sentence what it would do to that move; you get three such looks a game, and a clean look is refunded.
concepts.the_new_interaction: A pre-mortem in the opponent's voice, rationed. Everything on the market shows the current position's threats (Chess.com Assisted mode's red threat arrows and green suggestion arrows, Play Coach's Hint) or explains the move after it was played (Game Review v2, Chessiro's post-game arrows, the engine line on a Lichess analysis board). Nothing lets a beginner hover a candidate, turn the board, and hear the other side say what happens next in words a beginner can follow. Here the player drags the bishop to f7; it sits there as a ghost, not yet played, with two buttons: "Play it" and "Their chair (3 left)". Tap the second and the board rotates (instantly under reduced motion), the opponent's pieces are now nearest him, and the bot speaks: "Thanks. I take it with my king. Your knight check on g5 I answer with Kg8, and now you are a bishop down for a pawn." The three-ply refutation came from Stockfish; Claude only turned it into one first-person sentence. Tap "Back" and the ghost is still there, with "Play it anyway" or drag another. The ration is what makes it a product rather than a hint button: three looks is three decisions, and the pedagogy (the Steps Method's "change chairs", already in this repo's blunder-check lesson, phase 3) is the player learning to do the look in his head because he cannot afford to spend one on every move. A YouTuber would film the flip; a forum thread would say the ration and the refund are the clever part.
concepts.who_for: The players who will not type: Sambudh on a phone, one thumb, ten minutes between things. Also the returner who knows the rule "look at what they can do" but has never practised it from the other side of the board.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-5 s: Board, white at the bottom, a live Italian position after 3...Nf6, the moves so far listed faintly. Above the board: "Your move. Three looks from their chair." with three small filled circles. 5-12 s: He drags the c4 bishop to f7. It lands as a translucent ghost; the move is not played; two buttons appear under the board: "Play it" and "Their chair". 12-16 s: He taps "Their chair". The board rotates 180 degrees in 400 ms (no animation under prefers-reduced-motion), one circle empties, and a line appears in the opponent's voice while the engine's three-ply reply animates as ghost moves on the flipped board: "Thanks. I take it with my king. Your knight check on g5 I answer with Kg8, and now you are a bishop down for a pawn." 16-22 s: He taps "Back". The board rotates home; the ghost bishop still sits on f7 with "Play it anyway" and the hint "or drag another move". 22-30 s: He drags d2-d3 instead; a new ghost; he presses "Play it" without spending a look; the bot replies at once; the line reads "Your move. Two looks left."
concepts.core_loop: 1. The opponent moves (the same planted-blunder beginner bot as Say It Before You Move). 2. The player drags a candidate; it becomes a ghost, uncommitted. 3. Either "Play it" (commits, the bot replies instantly) or "Their chair" (spends one of three looks). 4. On a look: the engine computes the best reply line to the ghost move at depth 12 and the material change over three plies; the board flips; Claude writes one first-person sentence from that line; the ghost plies animate on the flipped board. 5. "Back" restores the player's view with the ghost intact; he plays it anyway or chooses another. 6. When the look finds nothing ("Nothing for me there. I would probably just bring a piece out."), the look is refunded, so a clean look costs nothing and he learns that most of his moves are safe. 7. When the ration is spent, the button turns into "Do the look in your head" and the game continues without it. 8. Game over: the page shows the three looks he spent and the moves he hung without looking, side by side, and asks "Which three would you spend next time?" 9. Play again with a fresh ration.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is called only when the player taps "Their chair" (an explicit action), on modelTier "quick", no tools, cache false (allowed without tools; avoids a stale replay if the same line recurs). Input: a short instruction plus the engine's data: the candidate move in SAN, the refutation line in SAN with piece names spelled out, the material balance before and after, and whether the line ends in check or mate. Output via sample.json: {line: string}, at most twenty-five words, first person, present tense, as the opponent, mentioning only the squares and pieces in the given line. Example input: candidate Bxf7+, line "Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8", material for White minus two after; output {line: "Thanks. I take it with my king. Your knight check on g5 I answer with Kg8, and now you are a bishop down for a pawn."} The page checks every square token in the sentence against the line and the position; a sentence containing a square not in the line is discarded and replaced by the template rendering ("Kxf7, then Ng5+ Kg8: you are down a bishop for a pawn"). Why an LLM: a template can print "Kxf7 Ng5+ Kg8", which an 800 cannot read, and cannot say what the opponent wants ("I just take it with the king and wait"); compressing a multi-ply line into intent in beginner English is the one thing the engine cannot do and a template does badly. Honestly, this is the weakest LLM necessity of the three concepts: about 60 percent of looks could be served by a careful template, and the page must ship with that template as the no-capability path.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish in the worker with chess.js: (1) the opponent, Skill Level 0-3 with planted free pieces verified by a depth-12 search; (2) on every look, "position fen <current> moves <ghost uci>" then "go depth 12" for the best reply and its principal variation, plus the eval before the ghost move, giving cp loss and a three-ply refutation; chess.js converts to SAN, computes material before and after, and flags check or mate at the end of the line; (3) when cp loss is under 50 and nothing of the player's hangs after the line, the look is reported clean and refunded, so the engine decides refunds, never Claude; (4) the ghost plies drawn on the flipped board are the engine's line, animated by the page; (5) at game end, the move audit finds the moves where a look would have shown a hung piece, for the "which three would you spend" screen. The engine answers in under a second, so the flip and the sentence arrive together.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: board with ghost-move commit, flip animation with the reduced-motion fallback, the three-look ration with refunds, the planted-blunder bot, the depth-12 look computation, one quick-tier call with token validation and the template path, light and dark tokens, phone width, window.__stubSample. Start on a fixed Italian position where Bxf7+ is the tempting trap. No post-game screen, no accounts, no habits.
concepts.delight: The flip itself with the opponent saying "Thanks." when he was about to give up a bishop, and the refund line "Nothing for me there" when a look comes back clean, which is the moment he learns that most of his moves are fine.
risks: It is a hint machine wearing a costume; without the ration it collapses into Chess.com Assisted mode (threat arrows and engine on). The ration and the refund rule carry the whole pedagogy and must be tuned on real play.

LLM necessity is the weakest here: templates can render most lines, so if the sentence is not noticeably better than the template in a blind test with Sambudh, drop Claude from this loop and keep the flip.
Beginners may not follow even a worded three-ply line; the ghost animation on the flipped board is what makes it legible, and that is the hardest UI piece to get right at 400 px.
Rotating the board on a phone disorients some players; reduced-motion must be honoured and a "never flip, just tell me" setting may be needed, which weakens the idea.
A YouTuber would call it a gimmick after five minutes unless the post-game "which three would you spend" screen lands; that screen is where the learning is and it is not in the MVP slice.

concepts.name: What You Keep Doing
concepts.one_liner: The coach remembers your last games as up to three named habits, in your own words, and in the next game whispers the habit before the moment it usually happens, not after.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Memory that changes what the coach says during play. Every incumbent with memory uses it after the fact: Aimchess scores six areas and offers a Blunder Preventer drill, Chessiro's Replay Mistakes rebuilds old errors as puzzles and "surfaces a prompt to practise" when a review hits a recurring weakness, Noctie turns your slips into flashcards with spaced repetition, Chessable schedules moves to memorise. None of them carries a habit into the next live game and times a single warning to the engine detecting that habit's precondition before the player moves. Here, after three games, the page holds per person lines such as "You put pieces on squares a pawn can reach: g4, e4 and b5 this week." In the next game, the moment the facts show that a pawn now attacks one of his pieces, one quiet line appears above the board before he touches anything: "Your habit. A pawn can reach something of yours." Nothing is highlighted; he has to find it. When a habit stays clean for three games the coach retires it: "You stopped doing that." A forum thread would notice two things that are new: the warning is personal and arrives before the move, and the memory is a sentence a coach would say, not a radar chart.
concepts.who_for: The returning player in week two: Sambudh after his first three games, and anyone who has played a hundred online games and been told "work on tactics" by a stats page without ever being told what they, personally, keep doing.
