concepts.first_30_seconds: 0-5 s: A new player has no games, so the first screen is the first of three placement positions from this repo's 0000-placement lesson (already engine-verified at depth 20): the Italian after 7...O-O, white at the bottom, caption "Black just castled. Your move, and in one line, why." 5-15 s: He plays Nbd2 and types "develop". 15-18 s: Facts: h3 attacks the g4 bishop, defended only by the f6 knight; hxg4 wins a bishop for a pawn; Nbd2 loses 285 cp. One quick-tier call returns: "Developing is right in a quiet position. What did your seventh move, h3, attack, and did Black ever answer it?" He looks, takes it back, plays hxg4. 18-30 s: Positions two and three follow (the Morphy mate in two and the king-and-pawn opposition), each a single move and a line of reasoning. At 30 s the page has three engine-audited answers and shows one sentence: "First thing I will watch for: you answer the plan and miss the attack. Now play a game and I will whisper before it happens." with one button, "Play".
concepts.core_loop: 1. Play a game against the planted-blunder bot with the live coach (the Say It Before You Move loop). 2. The engine audits every move: cp loss, refutation, and the type of fact a one-move look would have caught. 3. Game over: the board replays while one slower call labels each flagged move with one of five fixed labels (walked-into-pawn, ignored-last-move, missed-free-piece, missed-their-check, grabbed-defended) and writes one player-facing sentence per habit with two or more instances. 4. The page rejects any label inconsistent with the engine fact (walked-into-pawn requires a pawn capture in the refutation) and stores the surviving habits per person (db plus user; localStorage in the MVP). 5. Next game: before each player move, the facts are matched against the active habits' preconditions; a match shows the habit's sentence once per game per habit, before the move, with nothing highlighted. 6. Each audited game updates the counts; a habit with zero instances in three consecutive games is retired with "You stopped doing that." 7. The page can be sent to a friend; the friend starts at step 1 with their own placement and their own habits.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is used in two places and never for the whisper itself. (a) During the placement and the game, the quick-tier audit of the player's one-line reason, exactly as in Say It Before You Move. (b) After each game, one "default" tier call, no tools (the facts are in the prompt; a tools call would cost 30-90 s for nothing), taking 10-30 s and shown as the game replaying move by move, via sample.json. Input: the flagged moves, each with its position, the move, the cp loss, the refutation and the engine's fact type; the five allowed labels with definitions; the player's own sentences from those moves. Output: {habits: [{label, sentence, examples: [moveNumbers]}], summary: string}. Example output: {habits: [{label: "walked-into-pawn", sentence: "You put pieces on squares a pawn can reach: g4 on move 5, e4 on move 11 and b5 on move 19.", examples: [5, 11, 19]}], summary: "Three pieces went to a pawn. Everything else was fine for this level: you castled by move 8 and took the free knight on move 14."} The whisper in the next game is that stored sentence's first clause plus the precondition phrase ("A pawn can reach something of yours"), chosen by the engine match, zero Claude calls, instant. Why an LLM: counting fact types is arithmetic, but naming the pattern across three different positions in the player's own words, and knowing that "walking into a pawn" and "rushing at f7" are different habits even when both lose a bishop, is pattern naming over language, the one job a stats page cannot do. Without the capability, the page falls back to counts by fact type and a templated sentence per label: less personal, still a working loop.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish and chess.js do all in-game work and all detection: (1) the move audit for every player move (eval before and after at depth 12, cp loss, refutation, and the fact type of the catchable error); (2) the precondition check before each player move, pure chess.js geometry: is one of his pieces attacked by a pawn, did the last move newly attack a piece, is there a free capture on the board, does the opponent have a check that wins material next move (enumerated by swapping the side to move, verified at depth 8); (3) verification that each flagged mistake was catchable by a one-move look, so only band-appropriate mistakes ever reach the habit call and the coach never nags about a six-ply tactic; (4) the three placement positions are already engine-verified in the repo and are reused as they are. The engine decides when a whisper fires; the LLM only wrote the words days earlier.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page: the three placement positions with the quick-tier reason audit, one game against the planted-blunder bot, the move audit, one post-game default-tier labelling call with the five-label validator and a template fallback, habits stored in localStorage for the MVP (db plus user in iteration two), the whisper matcher for the five preconditions, the retirement rule, light and dark tokens, phone width, window.__stubSample. One day is tight; if it slips, cut the placement to the first position only.
concepts.delight: "You stopped doing that." The habit line crossing itself out after three clean games, still showing the three move numbers it used to cite, is a progress bar that reads like a person noticing.
risks: Cold start: the value shows only after two or three games; the placement is the mitigation, and because it is borrowed from the lesson engine it must feel like play, not a test.

Whispers become nagging fast. One per habit per game and no highlight is the rule, and it still needs tuning with Sambudh; a whisper that fires when the precondition is met but the move was fine teaches him to ignore it.

The five-label vocabulary is a bet on the chess master's under-1000 band beliefs; if his real mistakes do not fit, the LLM will force-fit and the validator will reject, leaving no habits. Keep an "other" label that stores the sentence but never whispers.

Mislabelling by the LLM despite the facts; the validator checks label against fact type, but the sentence can still over-generalise from two examples. Require three instances before a habit whispers, two before it is shown.

Persistent per-person state needs the db and user capabilities and the viewer's consent; localStorage is per-browser and silently loses the habits when he switches from laptop to phone, which is exactly his case.
This is a layer on Say It Before You Move, not a standalone product; shipping it first would be a memory feature for a game nobody is yet playing.

concepts.perspective_summary: The board is the whole interface: every answer, from the engine or from Claude, has to land on the squares (a held piece, a pulsing square, a ghost line, a square turning green) within a frame on a 400 px phone with one primary action, which means pieces as an absolutely positioned inline-SVG layer animated by transform, pointer events handling tap and drag in one code path, and the Stockfish Worker warmed at load so the player never waits on it. The second thing I care about is seams: plain ES modules with one engine.js command queue, one coach.js where `sample` resolves to `window.__stubSample` before `claude.use('sample')`, and one store.js that is `db`+`user` inside the viewer and localStorage everywhere else, so the page plays fully with no Claude at all and the existing headless checker (scripts/app_check.js) can drive, assert and screenshot every flow.

concepts.name: Hold On
concepts.one_liner: Play a game against a soft Stockfish; when a move would hang something, the piece is held on the board instead of landing, and the coach asks one question you answer by tapping a square.
concepts.the_new_interaction: A move held in mid-air. Every existing product lets the blunder land and marks it afterwards (a red ??, 'best was Ba4', an eval bar). Here the piece sits on its new square dimmed to 60% with a small 'Hold on' chip, the game pauses, the two or three squares that matter pulse, and the coach asks ONE of the three looks as a question: 'Before this goes: after they take back with the king, what can you take?' The player answers by tapping a square, not by reading. chess.js already knows the set of correct squares, so the tap is graded instantly and the move can be taken back or played anyway with one button. Claude is what makes it personal: it chooses which look was skipped, phrases the question in this player's words, points on the board with highlight/arrow tools, and across games names the habit ('third hold this week where you moved the piece that was guarding something'). Nobody ships a board where a blunder is a question you answer by touching the square, grounded by an engine, with memory of your own holds.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh and every under-1000 player whose games are lost to hanging pieces and one-move threats; someone who plays on a phone in ten-minute slots and has never read a chess book.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a board with his white pieces at the bottom, 'Your move' above it and one muted line below: 'Play. When something is about to go wrong, I will hold the move.' No menu, no setup, no empty shell. The 7 MB engine is loading in a Worker behind the board (about 1 s desktop, 2-4 s phone); his own first move never waits on it. 3 s: he taps e2, the pawn lifts (scale 1.08 and a soft shadow), dots appear on e3 and e4; he taps e4 and the pawn slides there in 150 ms. 5 s: Black's reply (Skill Level 2, depth 6, ~300 ms) slides in and the from/to squares tint. 10-25 s: 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, then he taps Bxf7+, the move every beginner plays. 26 s: the bishop lands on f7 but dimmed, a 'Hold on' chip appears above the board, e8 and f7 pulse, and under the board one line: 'Before this goes: after they take back with the king, what can you take?' The board is waiting for a tap. 30 s: he taps around, nothing lights up, and he taps the one big button 'Nothing. Take it back' (next to a quiet 'Play it anyway'). The bishop slides home. He has done the look from Black's chair himself, with no paragraph to read.
concepts.core_loop: 1. Player moves (tap-tap or drag). 2. chess.js validates and applies the move on a scratch board; the engine has already analysed the pre-move position at depth 12 MultiPV 2 while he was thinking, so the verdict needs only the post-move eval (~0.3-0.6 s). 3. cp loss under 150: commit, animate, engine replies in ~0.5 s. 4. cp loss 150 or more AND chess.js can name the mechanism (a piece of his now attacked and undefended or attacked by something cheaper; a free capture missed; a check or mate-in-1 allowed): HOLD. The piece is shown but not committed, squares pulse, one question is posed, the board accepts a tap as the answer. 5. Tap graded by chess.js against the correct-square set. Right: 'Yes.' plus Take back / Play it anyway. Wrong: the pulse narrows to a second hint, then the answer is revealed. 6. The hold is logged: {fen, played, better, look: 'their-threat' | 'free-capture' | 'checks' | 'from-their-chair', outcome, tapsToAnswer}. 7. Game ends on one screen: '0 pieces hung. Two holds, both taken back.' plus the coach's three lines. 8. 'Play again' with colours swapped.
concepts.llm_role: Claude is NOT called on every move. The hold, the pulsing squares, the correct-tap set and the fallback question copy are all engine plus chess.js. Claude is called (a) when the player taps 'Why?' inside a hold, quick tier, with tools, and (b) once at game end, quick tier, no tools, cache {gcTime: 24 h} keyed by the game id. Prompt for (a): the coach instructions (the three looks from lesson 0001, under-1000 voice, two sentences, no move lists, no evaluation numbers unless asked, speak from the player's side), the FEN before and after, the move in SAN, the engine's best move with both cp numbers, chess.js facts as plain data ('after Bxf7+ Kxf7: your pieces attacked and undefended: none; you can take: nothing; your checks: Ng5+ (king goes to g8)'), the last six moves, and the hold history summary ('last 5 games: 7 holds, 5 were from-their-chair, 2 free-capture'). Tools: highlight({squares}) which pulses squares and returns 'ok'; arrow({from, to}) which draws one arrow; evaluate({fen}) which returns {bestMove, cp, mate, pv} from the Worker at depth 12, for when Claude wants to check a line the player might wonder about. Two rounds is typical, about two seconds. Example output, streamed into the caption line under the board with 'Thinking...' until the first delta and a small Stop: 'You gave a bishop for a pawn. Check and a capture both feel like progress, but switch chairs: after the king takes back you have nothing to take and your only check is the knight on g5, which the king simply walks away from.' with arrow c4 to f7 and highlight e8, f7. For (b) the prompt carries this game's hold log and the running totals; the output is three lines in second person naming the look he skips most and one thing he did right. If claude.use('sample') is null or the call rejects not_granted, the 'Why?' button is hidden and the engine-grounded fallback sentence stands ('Your bishop can be taken by the king, and nothing of yours defends f7.'); the product stays fully playable.
concepts.engine_role: Stockfish 18 lite in one Worker behind a serialized command queue (uci, isready, setoption, position, go, stop; a line parser for info/bestmove). Three jobs. (1) Opponent: setoption Skill Level 2 (confirmed in the wasm's option table) plus go depth 6 gives roughly 800-strength play that still punishes hung pieces; a strength slider is a later iteration. (2) The verdict: eval of the best move versus eval after the player's move, depth 12 MultiPV 2, precomputed during his think time so a hold is instant; the cp-loss threshold is what makes a hold honest, because chess.js can say 'attacked and undefended' but cannot say whether the capture actually wins (the recapture might be bad). (3) The evaluate tool for Claude. chess.js (attackers, isAttacked, moves({verbose:true})) supplies legality, the legal-move dots, promotion detection, and the mechanism data in words-free form.
concepts.mvp_slice: One page app/index.html plus app/src/{main,board,game,engine,coach,store,ui}.js, app/styles.css and app/pieces.svg (twelve inline <symbol>s used by <use>; Unicode glyphs would be tofu in headless Chromium and vary by phone), no build step, served by python3 -m http.server, published with `files`. Board: a static 64-cell CSS grid for squares; a separate absolutely positioned piece layer where each piece is a <button class=pc data-square> placed by transform: translate(file*100%, rank*100%) with a 150 ms transition, so moves, takebacks and flip animate for free and prefers-reduced-motion sets the duration to 0; overlay layers for last-move tint, legal dots and the hold pulse; one SVG for arrows; the hold is a data-hold attribute on the board root that CSS turns into the dimming and the pulse. Input: pointer events only (one path for mouse and touch), tap-to-select then tap-to-move as the primary path, drag with setPointerCapture and touch-action:none as the enhancement; promotion is a four-button strip overlaid on the target file with Enter/Escape bound. Phone: the board is min(100vw - 32px, 62vh), a sticky bottom bar holds the ONE primary action (Your move / Take back / Play again). State: a single state object and render(state) after every mutation; store.js exposes {get, set, append, list} backed by db+user when claude.use('db') resolves (read the artifact-capabilities skill for its exact API before writing it) and by localStorage otherwise. Testing: window.__app = {play(san), fen(), state(), waitEngine()}; coach.js resolves sample as window.__stubSample ?? await window.claude?.use?.('sample'), so scripts/app_check.js drives it unchanged; a scenario plays 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Bxf7+ through __app.play, asserts [data-hold] is set, the pulse set is {e8, f7}, zero sample calls so far, clicks Why and asserts __sampleCalls[0].opts.tools equals [highlight, arrow, evaluate] and the caption contains the stub text; then the four screenshots with no horizontal overflow. Cut for day one: drag polish on touch (tap-tap is enough), the strength slider (fixed Skill Level 2), the game-end Claude note (ship the engine counts), the cross-game habit memory (log the holds, show counts, let Claude narrate in iteration two), PGN download, sound.
concepts.delight: The piece that will not land. He taps Bxf7+, it sits there dimmed with a tiny 'Hold on', two squares pulse, the question is about his own move, and when he taps 'take it back' the bishop slides home and the game simply goes on: no red ??, no evaluation bar, no shame.
risks: Thresholds: a 150 cp loss at depth 12 sometimes has no mechanism chess.js can name (a positional loss); rule: no nameable mechanism, no hold, just commit. The product only holds what a one-move look would catch, which is the whole thesis.
Engine warm-up on a slow phone is 3-5 s and the first opponent reply may wait; show 'Warming up the engine...' in the status line and never block the player's own first move.
The SVG piece sheet costs an afternoon of drawing or vendoring, and any vendored set needs a licence check next to stockfish.COPYING.txt.
The quick tier may ignore the two-sentence rule; the caption clamps to three lines with a 'more' toggle, and the prompt states the limit twice.
A viewer who declines consent must never see a dead control: hide on not_granted and make the fallback copy good enough that the product is still good (it is engine-grounded, so it can be).
The db capability's exact API is not in the brief; until the builder reads the artifact-capabilities skill, store.js runs on localStorage behind the same interface.

concepts.name: Show Me
concepts.one_liner: Tap a piece and ask 'what if this takes?'; Claude tries your idea with Stockfish and answers by playing the line out on your board as ghost pieces, then puts everything back.
concepts.the_new_interaction: A question answered by moving the pieces. In every existing product the 'why' is a sentence, or an engine line in notation he cannot read. Here he taps a piece and one of three chips ('What if this takes?', 'Is this piece safe?', 'What are they threatening?'); Claude is handed try_line (a scratch chess.js plus the Worker) and show_line (plays SAN moves on the real board as translucent ghost pieces 600 ms apart with a one-sentence caption per move, then rewinds) and it answers by SHOWING: the ghost bishop takes on f7, the ghost king takes back, the ghost knight checks, the ghost king steps away, each with a line of caption, then the ghosts fade and the real position is back. The LLM is needed because it turns a vague human question into concrete lines to test and chooses the one worth showing; the engine is needed because the page refuses to show any line as 'good' that it has not evaluated, so what the board shows cannot be wrong chess.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh in the moment of doubt on his own turn ('can I take that?'), and anyone who has opened Lichess analysis and closed it again because the arrows meant nothing.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: the page opens on a real position, not an empty board: the Italian after 3...Nf6 (verified in lesson 0001), white to move, his pieces at the bottom, and the line 'Your move. Or tap a piece and ask.' 4 s: he taps the c4 bishop; the legal dots appear AND three chips slide up under the board: 'What if this takes f7?', 'Is this piece safe?', 'What are they threatening?'. 6 s: he taps the first chip. The caption reads 'Trying it...' and a faint ledger line appears as the tool runs: 'tried Bxf7+ Kxf7: you are down a bishop for a pawn'. 10 s: the ghost bishop slides to f7 ('Check, and a pawn.'), the ghost king takes it ('They take back. Now what do you have?'), the ghost knight goes to g5 ('Your only check...'), the ghost king to g8 ('...and it steps away. A bishop for a pawn.'). 18 s: the ghosts fade, the real position is back, the chips are gone, the status reads 'Your move.' 20-30 s: he plays 4.d3 instead, Black replies, and the game goes on.
concepts.core_loop: 1. Play against the same soft engine opponent, or start from one of the five verified lesson positions (later: positions from his own game log). 2. On his turn, at any time: tap a piece to get the three chips for that piece, or tap 'Ask' for the same chips without a piece. 3. One quick-tier call with tools; progress is rendered from inside execute (each try_line appends a faint ledger row; that ledger IS the thinking indicator). 4. show_line plays the chosen line as ghosts with captions while the real pieces dim to 35%; the real game state is untouched because the ghost layer reads from a scratch Chess instance. 5. The board rewinds; 'Your move.' 6. The question, the line shown and its eval go to the store so the game-end note can say 'you asked about f7 twice and then played it anyway'. 7. He moves, the engine replies, repeat.
concepts.llm_role: Quick tier, called only on a chip tap, tools present so no cache (omit the cache option). Prompt: 'You are at the board with a player rated under 1000. Answer only by trying lines with try_line and then showing ONE line with show_line. Captions are one short sentence per move from the player's side, naming squares, never notation, never evaluation numbers. If the player's idea is good, show it and say so. If show_line refuses a line, show the engine's best reply instead.' plus the FEN, the side, the last six moves, the legal moves in SAN, chess.js facts (which pieces of each side are attacked and by what, checks available) and the chip text with the tapped square. Tools: try_line({moves: string[]}) applies SAN on a scratch board and returns {legal, finalFen, cpForPlayer, mate, bestReply, hanging} from the Worker at depth 12 (~0.4 s); show_line({moves: string[], captions: string[]}) validates legality, plays the ghosts, and resolves 'shown' when the animation ends; evaluate({fen}) returns {bestMove, cp, pv}. A typical call is two try_lines and one show_line, four rounds, about five seconds on quick. Example final text, rendered under the board after the rewind: 'Your bishop takes with check, but after the king takes back you have nothing on f7 and your only check is the knight, which the king walks away from. Keep the bishop; d3 keeps everything safe.' If sample is null, the chips never appear and tapping a piece only shows legal dots; if limits() reports no tools, the chips call a plain quick prompt that answers in words from the chess.js facts and never claims a line.
concepts.engine_role: The same Worker with a two-slot queue: slot A is the opponent (Skill Level 2, depth 6), slot B is analysis for try_line and evaluate (depth 12, MultiPV 1), with 'stop' issued to A when B is requested so a question never waits on the opponent. Every ghost line has an engine number behind it before Claude may show it: show_line throws 'Error: that line loses 3 pawns for the player; show it as the refutation or try another' if Claude presents as good a line the engine scores more than 100 cp below the best move. That grounding lives in the page, not in the prompt. chess.js plays the scratch lines, validates every SAN in show_line, and supplies the attacked/hanging data in try_line's result.
concepts.mvp_slice: Shares board, engine, game, store and coach modules with 'Hold On' (one codebase, one page, a mode flag). New for this concept: ghost.js (a second piece layer at 50% opacity fed by a scratch Chess, a playLine(moves, captions) promise with 600 ms steps that aborts on Stop, on context.signal, or on any tap, and always rewinds) and ask.js (the chips, the three tool definitions, the prompt builder, the 100 cp guard). Positions: app/data/positions.json holds the five verified FENs from lesson 0001 so the first frame is a real position with a real question available. Tests: a scenario taps c4, asserts three chips, clicks the first and asserts __sampleCalls[0].opts.tools equals [try_line, show_line, evaluate] and modelTier is quick; a second scenario calls window.__app.tools.show_line({moves:['Bxf7+','Kxf7'], captions:['a','b']}) directly, asserts the ghost layer moved twice and the real FEN is unchanged afterwards; a third asserts show_line throws for a losing line presented as good. Cut for day one: typed questions (chips only; typing mid-game on a phone is the part I do not trust yet), positions from his own games, the tried-lines ledger (a single 'Trying Bxf7+...' line instead), arrows during ghost playback.
concepts.delight: The pieces move by themselves to answer him: the ghost bishop takes, the ghost king takes back, a line of caption per move, and then everything slides back to where it was, as if a friend had reached over the board, shown him, and put the pieces back.
risks: Latency: four quick rounds is four to six seconds and the consent dialog adds to the first; the 'Trying...' line and the ledger must fill that time or the chip feels broken.

The quick tier may call show_line without trying first; the page-side guard stops wrong chess from being shown but can make the final text apologetic, so the prompt tells Claude what to do when show_line refuses.
Ghosts over real pieces on a 400 px board are busy; the real layer must dim to 35% while a line plays, and captions must sit in the same fixed line under the board, never in a growing bubble.
A Stop or an aborted context.signal mid-animation must rewind the ghost layer and release the input lock; this is one function with one test, but it is the function that will be forgotten.
tools_unavailable on some viewers: ship the words-only prompt variant and never let the board claim a line it did not verify.

concepts.name: Say It First
concepts.one_liner: On the moves that matter, you say the three looks in one line before you move; Claude reads what you meant, the board checks it against the truth, and the move unlocks when your looking was honest.
concepts.the_new_interaction: Grading the thinking, not the move. Every app grades the move after it lands. Here, when chess.js sees that something is at stake (a piece of his is attacked, or a free capture exists; it fires on roughly one move in four), a thin 'Look first' band appears and the board refuses the drop until he has written one line: 'their bishop hits f7, I can take nothing, no checks'. One quick-tier sample.json call turns that sentence into {attacks:['f7'], canTake:[], checks:[]}; the page compares it with the truth from chess.js; the squares he named correctly light green, the one he missed pulses amber ('You missed: the pawn on e5 is free'), a false claim gets a grey strike, and then the board unlocks. The move he chooses is still his. Only an LLM can read 'their bishop hits f7' and map it to squares; only chess.js knows whether it is true; the product is the join, and it is the MISSION's own 'blunder check said aloud before every move' made real.
concepts.who_for: Sambudh and beginners who know the habit exists and cannot make it run by itself; people who want to practise looking, not memorise answers.
concepts.first_30_seconds: 0 s: board, his pieces at the bottom, 'Your move.' and a muted 'On moves that matter I will ask you to look first.' 3-12 s: 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 Nc6 3.Bc4 (the opponent plays from a tiny beginner-trap book for the first moves of this mode, so a moment that matters arrives early). The band under the board tints amber: 'Look first.' with one field, placeholder 'Their last move attacks...', and two chips 'nothing to take' and 'no checks'. 15 s: he types 'bishop and queen both look at f7, nothing to take' and taps the 'no checks' chip. 17 s: the field reads 'Checking...'. 18.5 s: f7 lights green, a quiet 'All three looks, honest. Your move.' appears, and the pieces accept his touch again. 25 s: he plays ...g6, or ...Nf6 and the queen mates on f7, and the end screen says 'You looked, you saw the threat to f7, and then you moved a different piece. Next game, the move has to answer the threat you found.'
concepts.core_loop: 1. Opponent moves. 2. chess.js builds the truth table for the new position: threats (his pieces now attacked, and by what), freeCaptures (their pieces attacked and undefended, or attacked by something cheaper), checks (his legal checking moves, and theirs next move via a side-to-move swap on the FEN). 3. All empty: silent, normal move. 4. Otherwise the band appears and the drop is refused with a gentle shake; legal dots still show so he can look. 5. He writes one line and taps 'Checked' (the explicit action that makes the one quick call). 6. The page marks each claim on the board: green for true, amber pulse for a miss, grey strike for a false claim. 7. The board unlocks; he moves; the engine scores the move at depth 12 and replies. 8. The store appends {fen, said, extracted, truth, missed, thenPlayed, cpLoss}. 9. Game end: 'Looks honest: 6 of 8. The look you skip: what can I take.' from the store alone, plus Claude's three lines.
concepts.llm_role: Quick tier, sample.json, no tools, one call per 'Checked' tap, cache false (a repeated sentence must be read again). Prompt: 'A chess player under 1000 is doing the three-look check before moving. Here is the position as FEN and a map of every occupied square to its piece and colour, so names resolve (their bishop = c4). Read the player's sentence and reply with ONLY {"attacks": string[], "canTake": string[], "checks": string[], "unclear": string}: the SQUARES of the pieces the player says are attacked by the opponent, can be taken by the player, and give check. Do not correct the player and do not add anything they did not say. Sentence: «...»'. Example reply: {"attacks":["f7"],"canTake":[],"checks":[],"unclear":""}. The page, not Claude, decides right and wrong and writes the feedback from a small table of sentences keyed by miss type (that copy is the chess-master partner's job). The only place Claude writes to the player is the game-end note, a second quick call with the look log, cached per game: 'Six honest looks out of eight. The two you skipped were both what-can-I-take, and both times a pawn was free. Look at their pawns first next game.' If sample is null the band still appears as a three-tap version (tap the squares instead of writing; chess.js grades the taps directly), so the product degrades to Hold On's tap-the-square and stays fully playable.
concepts.engine_role: Opponent at Skill Level 2, depth 6, with a twenty-line beginner trap book (data/traps.json) for the first six moves so that moments that matter come early; evaluate after each of his moves (depth 12) to record cp loss beside the look log, which is the evidence MISSION.md asks for to close Pattern 1 ('the check runs by itself in his games'). chess.js does the truth table (attackers, isAttacked, moves({verbose:true}), the side-swap trick for their checks next move). The engine is needed to separate an honest look that still led to a bad move from a dishonest look; the truth table alone cannot tell them apart.
concepts.mvp_slice: Shares board, engine, game, store and coach modules; new look.js (the truth table, claim grading, the band UI and its square marks) and data/traps.json. The field is a single <input> with enterkeyhint=done, autocomplete off, and the chips 'nothing to take' and 'no checks' as one-tap inserts so the common case on a phone is one short phrase plus two taps; the OS keyboard's mic gives dictation for free. The page shows what it understood ('I read: attacks f7') with a 'Fix' link that reopens the field, so a wrong read is visible, never silent. Tests: a scenario drives __app.play to 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 Nc6 3.Bc4, asserts the band is visible and that a drop is refused; sets window.__stubReplies to ['{"attacks":["f7"],"canTake":[],"checks":[],"unclear":""}'], types the sentence, clicks Checked, asserts f7 carries the green class and the board is unlocked; a second stub reply claiming canTake e5 in a position where e5 is defended asserts the grey strike; a third asserts an invalid JSON stub reply shows 'Try again' and makes no second call. Cut for day one: the trap book (play from the lesson FENs instead), the per-game Claude note (show the counts), partial credit for piece names without squares (resolve by the map; if ambiguous, ask once), any trigger on checks (threats and free captures only).
concepts.delight: Typing 'bishop hits f7' and watching f7 light green on the board: the page understood what he meant and the board agreed with him, the first time his own reasoning has ever been visible on the squares.
risks: Typing on every triggered move is friction on a phone; the trigger must be strict (a piece of his attacked, or a free capture; not checks) or it fires too often and he stops reading what he types.
Extraction can mis-resolve ('their knight' when two knights exist); the square map in the prompt plus the visible 'I read:' line and a Fix link make a wrong read recoverable, never hidden.
The first quick call happens mid-game and raises the consent dialog; the band must say in one line why Claude is being asked before the first 'Checked'.
A player can type 'nothing, nothing' to unlock; the amber marks make the lie visible and the store records it; this is a habit tool, not a lock, and the copy must not scold.
invalid_json from sample.json must surface as 'Try again' on the band with no automatic retry; rate_limited keeps the band and offers the three-tap fallback.

reviews.persona: Chess coach: master-strength player, twenty years coaching club players from their first games to 2000+. Judging every concept by one test: does it make an under-1000 player stop leaving pieces where they can be taken, and does the scaffold come off once the habit runs by itself.

critiques.strengths: The interrupt lands in the only half-second that matters at this band, before the piece touches the square. The gate is the coach's judgment encoded and strict (200 cp AND a capture or check refutation, suppressed when already five down), silence on the ninety percent, a scripted first game so a hold exists by move five, the play-anyway cap so the coach shuts up when the student has decided, and a close that shows the hold moments as boards rather than numbers. Claude is asked only how to ask, never whether.
critiques.weaknesses: It is my own concept and its holes are mine. The scripted beginner tree is fragile: if he opens 2.Bc4 or 2.d4 the tree breaks and a careful first game may contain no hold at all, so he never learns what the page does. There is no reward for the look done right: the only feedback is a hold, so a clean game feels like nothing happened. There is no fade, so the hand stays on the wrist forever and the habit never has to run alone. The opponent persona is hand-waved (Skill Level 1 plays alien moves and rarely hangs anything, so the free-capture look gets no reps). And 'Show me' as a ghost line is weaker than the game designer's version where he takes his own piece.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The free-capture look in both directions. Half of under-1000 is not failing to defend, it is failing to take: the bot must leave a minor piece for free every six to ten moves (engine-verified free), the page says 'You looked.' when he takes it and holds the move when he ignores it ('Hold on. Before that: is anything of theirs free?'). Plus a per-game hold budget that shrinks as clean games accumulate, borrowed from Change Chairs.

critiques.strengths: Punish, then prevent, is the transfer step every puzzle app lacks: the second half makes him see his own move from the other side, which is the look beginners never run on their own. Positions from real beginner games verified at depth 20; acceptance decided by the engine, never by prose; one in six positions with nothing to punish keeps the look honest.
critiques.weaknesses: It is a drill, and drills at this band transfer badly unless the position is his. Ten positions last two sessions. The prevent half is fuzzy (many moves save the bishop) and the student can pass it by playing any quiet move without having looked at anything. It decays into 'find the capture' pattern matching within a week.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Reverse the order on the second showing: prevent first, then punish. R1 is punish-then-prevent so he feels it; R2 gives him the position one move earlier with no setup line and asks for a move that survives, and only if he plays the losing move does the board turn so he can punish himself. The habit is pre-move; the drill must end up pre-move too.

critiques.strengths: R1, R2, R3 of his own mistakes is exactly how I run a lesson: same position next week, then the same idea in a fresh position, until it is gone. The moment definition is band-correct (only what a one-move look catches; positional losses deliberately excluded) and the memory line by category ('four of six were to a pawn') is the sentence no app says.
critiques.weaknesses: It needs games and ships as a review screen, which beginners do not open. The 30-90 s default-tier call sits between the game and the lesson. R3 generation by Claude will fail verification often enough that the feature looks absent. And in R1 the squares are already highlighted, so the first return is reading, not looking.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Move the returns into the game instead of a screen: R1 happens inside the close of the same game (one tap on the small board), R2 is the opening question of the next game before he touches a piece, and R3 is live: when the same category's precondition appears in a later game, the hold whispers 'This one again.' with nothing marked. Memory should change what the hand does, not fill a page.

critiques.strengths: The best product spec of the Hold On family. The tutorial hold on the verified 3...Nf6 position before the first consent dialog means he knows what a hold is before anyone asks him anything. 'Free knight. You looked.' rewards the look, which my own version forgot. 'A square you chose to play anyway is never held again that game' is the right no-nag rule. The one-thing memory feeding the next game's question ('The c4 bishop again. Tap what it sees.') is coaching, not review. The 2.5 s swap rule keeps the hold a beat, not a stall.
critiques.weaknesses: 150 cp is too low for this band: a 150 cp loss is often a pawn plus position, and a hold must be a piece or it becomes a nag. 'Mate in two' as a refutation is beyond a one-move look. The opening question 'Check and a pawn, and then?' is a two-ply question whose right answer is 'nothing', and there is no square to tap for nothing. The opponent calibration is named as a risk but not designed, and there is no gate for a free capture he ignored, only praise when he takes one.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Raise the gate to 200 cp with a one-ply capture or check refutation, add a 'Nothing' answer button for the from-their-chair question (the correct answer after 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 is 'nothing to take, no useful check'), and add the missed-free-capture hold. Then the first-30-seconds opener is the one I would ship.

critiques.strengths: 'You just caught yourself' is the right emotional note, and the SAFE outcome teaches the thing beginners most need to hear: most of your moves are fine. The five dots instead of a score; the hollow dot for a shown answer is a quiet, honest cost.
critiques.weaknesses: He moves first in a vacuum: there is no opponent's last move, so look one ('what did their move attack') does not exist in this drill. The loop is gameable: play a quiet move every time, get SAFE, tap Next, learn nothing. Twelve positions. The board turns on every move, which on a phone is a lot of turning for very little looking.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Animate the opponent's last move in before he moves so the first look is real, and on MISSED never let the arrow do the work: after 'Show me' he must play the punishing move with his own hand before Next appears. A drill where the hand does nothing teaches nothing.

critiques.strengths: Direct manipulation, restraint (no eval bar, nothing red), and the 'they would play this' dashed arrow is a beautiful way to show the from-their-chair look. The guided tour where the coach tries ideas and the engine corrects it is a real thinking-partner moment.
critiques.weaknesses: It is x-ray vision, and a beginner with x-ray vision never learns to look. Rings on legal squares by consequence do all three looks for him before he has done one. In twenty years I have never seen a student get stronger from an analysis board; they get stronger from being asked. This is a playground for the curious, not a coach for Sambudh, and used during games it undoes the habit.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Prediction before revelation: the ghost may be placed only after he has tapped the squares he thinks it attacks and the pieces he thinks it leaves hanging; the ghost then shows the truth and marks what he missed. Keep it out of the game page entirely; it belongs in the post-game review.

critiques.strengths: A threat in the opponent's own voice is honest and vivid, 'Answered.' is a real reward, and the fade after five answered threats is pedagogically correct: the author understood that the voice must go quiet. The validator discipline (fact sheet in, SAN regex out) is the best engineering in the set.
critiques.weaknesses: The opponent performs the student's second look for him. I spend lessons removing exactly this crutch: a student who is told the threat reads threats, he does not find them. The fade is not in the MVP, so a second week of use teaches dependence. The free-piece line after it is taken ('Free knight, thank you') is after the fact, like every product in the brief. And the bot does not hang pieces on purpose, so the one look he most needs reps on never comes up.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make Mira ask before she tells: 'Something of yours is in trouble. Tap it.' graded by chess.js, and if he taps right she says nothing at all. Add the planted free piece so he gets to be the one who looks and takes.

critiques.strengths: One position, one question, graded on the reasoning rather than the move, which is what a coach actually grades. The motif codes computed by rule, not by Claude. Re-asked three games later. 'Nothing turned this game; well played.' is the honest empty state nobody else wrote.
critiques.weaknesses: Post-game only, so the habit is built after the fact. Typing a reason on a phone after a loss is the moment a beginner closes the app. A 10-30 s default-tier call between the game and the lesson. The motif list lacks the second most common error at this band, taking a defended piece (the 7.Nxe5?? dxe5 class), and grading free text on quick tier will be lenient.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Add the grabbed-defended motif, and make the re-ask live rather than on a result screen: the next game's first hold in the same category says 'This again.' Then 'Play from here' from Rewind, so the one thing is replayed in the same session, not remembered.

critiques.strengths: No chat box, chips computed from facts, arrows drawn before the sentence arrives, and the quiz mode with the tap-back is genuinely Socratic: the page keys the answer, Claude only phrases the question.
critiques.weaknesses: 'Is it safe?' is the look I want him to run in his own head. During play the chips are a hint button with better manners; a student who can ask the board whether a piece is safe never learns to ask himself. 'What is it doing?' has no engine fact behind it and will be bland. In a review the chips are fine; in a game they outsource the second look.
critiques.what_i_would_add: In play, the chip is locked until he has guessed: tap the piece, then tap what you think attacks it; only then does the chip confirm or correct. Free chips in the post-game review only.

critiques.strengths: The floating '-2' when the ghost recapture plays is the clearest 'feel it' in the whole set: a beginner understands minus two before he understands centipawns. 'But...' answering his plan rather than the engine's number ('You are, and it's a good idea. But it's his move first') is exactly what I say across the table. Counting pieces given away rather than a rating, and silence as the first lesson.
critiques.weaknesses: The hold sentence tells him the answer ('That pawn can take your knight') before he has looked, so the look is done for him and the hold becomes a notification. 'Why?' and 'But...' both lead to explanation, not to looking. No reward for taking a free piece, and no fade.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Turn the template into a question answered by tap before 'Show me' is offered: 'Hold on. What can they take?' and only after a wrong tap does it name the pawn. Keep the '-2' and the 'But...' exactly as written.

critiques.strengths: 'Play from here' is the single best post-game idea on the table: going back to the move and playing it again against the same opponent is what I do on a real board in every lesson. His last move replays before the question so look one is honest. 'Nothing was given away; it was lost slowly, which is a different lesson' is the kind of honesty that keeps a student's trust.
critiques.weaknesses: One moment per game and it needs a game to exist. Forty positions at depth 14 on a phone is a long wait after a loss. 'Answered' meaning he kept the piece is fragile because the bot plays differently from the moment, so the issue may never recur in the replay.
critiques.what_i_would_add: 'Play from here, and this time I hold the move': the replay runs with the hold active and the moment's category primed, so the hand is on the wrist at the exact spot it was missing. And the moment comes back as a live whisper in a later game (R2) rather than only on a screen.

critiques.strengths: The question is about looking, not calculating, which is the right question for this band. Seed positions engine-confirmed at load. A moment you can hand to a friend. No rating, no streak guilt.
critiques.weaknesses: One tap a day is not enough reps: a habit takes twenty games with the hand on the wrist, not twenty taps. The share link is marketing more than learning. Six positions go stale in a week and the own-moments version depends on a play loop that does not yet exist.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Rotate the question kinds across the three looks and include their-chair positions where the right answer is 'nothing is free, play quiet', or it becomes a tap-the-attacked-piece reflex. Feed it from the hold log of the play loop, never from a separate authoring queue.

critiques.strengths: The bot design is the best in the set and it is how I play my own students: always punish a hung piece, never hang the queen or walk into mate, hang a minor piece at a rate that falls as the catch rate rises. The hold shows their chair, the ring shrinks as he stops needing it (the only concept besides Change Chairs with a fading scaffold), 'Looked.' is the perfect one-word reward, and the one-moment card is graded by the engine.
critiques.weaknesses: The their-chair pulse appears automatically on every hold, so the board looks for him: he does not have to find the hanging piece, it glows. A beat on every move is friction for a player who already looks. 'What am I up to?' is a first-person statement, a crutch on tap. One moment per game at the close.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Pulse after the tap, not before: the hold turns the board to their chair with nothing marked and he taps what he thinks hangs; the ring pulses only after his tap, right or wrong. And the chip becomes a question: 'What did my last move attack? Tap it.' That is the difference between a hint and a coach.

critiques.strengths: Taking your own knight with your own finger is the strongest 'feel it' on the table and it is the lesson's phase three made physical. The budget shrinking toward 'No chairs today. A real game.' is the fading scaffold everything else lacks; the first zero-chair game as a named event is graduation, not a lost safety net. 'There was a bigger one.' when he takes the wrong thing. One swap per two moves.
critiques.weaknesses: Rotation on a phone, which the author flags. The swap skips the question: he takes, but he is never asked which look he skipped before he is shown. The Claude line after the take-back reads as a verdict. And the chair fires on every hang, so a student who would have found it himself with one question still gets the full theatre.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One tap in his own chair before the board turns: 'Hold on. What can they take?' If he taps right the board does not turn, the chair is saved, and the coach says nothing. The chair becomes the consequence of not looking, which is what it is at a real table.

critiques.strengths: It asks for the looks instead of the move: the right drill shape for under 1000 and a real departure from puzzle apps. The opponent's last move replays, any correct square is accepted, the grid is honest about which look he skips.
critiques.weaknesses: It has the shape of a puzzle app, and daily reps without a game transfer badly. Thirty verified positions is real authoring before day one. The third look (checks) is 'None' most days and becomes a reflex tap rather than a look.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the third tap the from-their-chair look on a candidate move: 'You want to play Nxe5. Tap what they could take after it.' That is the look beginners never run and the one a daily can drill without a game.

critiques.concept: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)
critiques.strengths: The only concept that catches the false belief rather than the move: 'I will castle to be safe' is wrong for a reason the engine cannot name and a coach can. Silence when the reasoning is complete; 'That one was yours.' when he fixes it; the planted-blunder bot; validation by fact id. This is what I do in a live lesson when I make a student say the check aloud.
critiques.weaknesses: Nobody types before every move on a phone. I do not even make students say every move aloud in a lesson, only the moves that matter, and the saying-aloud is a scaffold I remove within a month. No fade, so the sentence is forever. If the skip rate is high it is Play Coach with better questions, as the author admits.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ask for the sentence only when the facts say something is at stake, and in the placement; and after three honest sentences in a row stop asking and start holding. The hand replaces the voice as the habit forms. Keep the typed sentence as the diagnostic tool it is, in the post-game 'But...' and the placement, not as the per-move gate.

critiques.strengths: The ration and the refund teach two true things: a look costs something, and most of your moves are fine. 'Which three would you spend next time?' at the close is the learning moment. The first-person line is readable where a notation line is not.
critiques.weaknesses: A hint button in a costume, as the author says. The student never looks himself; he asks, and the refund rewards asking a clean question, not looking. A worded three-ply line is beyond this band's reading, and the flip plus the line is a lot of theatre for a beginner on a phone.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A look is refunded only if he first taps his own prediction of what they would take and is right; a wrong prediction spends it. Prediction before revelation turns the ration into practice.

critiques.strengths: The whisper before the precondition is the 'remember what we said' a coach gives at the moment, and 'You stopped doing that.' is the best progress line in the set. Five fixed labels validated against engine facts, including both walked-into-pawn and grabbed-defended. The placement reused as play.
critiques.weaknesses: Cold start; it is a layer on a loop that does not yet exist. A whisper when the precondition is present but the move would have been fine teaches him to ignore whispers. The whisper is a statement before the move, so once again the look is done for him. Two instances is too few to call a habit.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The whisper is a question keyed to the habit ('Your habit. Where is the pawn?'), fires only when the engine says the precondition is also a real loss on the move he is about to make, and needs three instances. Then it is the memory I would want inside Hold On.

critiques.strengths: 'Nothing. Take it back' is the right answer button for the from-their-chair look, because the correct answer after 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 is 'nothing to take, no useful check'. The hold log by look category is the data a coach needs. 'No nameable mechanism, no hold' is the thesis stated as a rule. The engineering seams (stub, store, worker queue, scenarios on the verified positions) are what make the day's build real.
critiques.weaknesses: The first question in the example is two-ply on the first hold. No scripted or tutorial hold, so a careful first game may show nothing. 'Why?' with tools inside a hold costs two seconds and gives an explanation at the moment he should be looking. 150 cp again.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Let the log drive the question: the look he skips most gets asked first next time. Replace 'Why?' inside the hold with 'Show me' (ghost or chair), because at this band showing beats explaining every time, and keep 'Why?' for the close.

critiques.strengths: The pieces move to answer him, which a beginner can read when notation is noise. The engine refuses to show a losing line as good, so the board cannot lie. The ledger as the thinking indicator is honest about the wait.
critiques.weaknesses: 'What if this takes?' asked by the student on his own move is the look I want him to run in his head; a chip that runs it for him is a hint. Four quick rounds is five seconds in the middle of a move. The chips invite asking instead of looking.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Available only as the 'Show me' of a hold or in the post-game, and before the ghosts play he taps his guess of the recapture square; the line then marks 'you saw this' and 'you missed this'.

critiques.strengths: Triggered only when something is at stake (about one move in four), with the three-tap fallback when there is no Claude. His reasoning lit green on the squares is the first time a beginner has seen his own thinking on the board. 'I read: attacks f7' with a Fix link makes a wrong read visible.
critiques.weaknesses: Refusing the drop until he writes is a lock, and locks get gamed ('nothing, nothing'). Typing mid-game on a phone. It grades the sentence and not the hand: he can look honestly, be told so, and then hang the piece anyway, and nothing stops him.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The sentence is the look and the hold is the hand: an honest sentence unlocks the board, and the hold still fires if the move hangs something. Then fade the sentence to three taps, then to nothing, across games, as the habit shows up in the hold log.

ranking: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)

merged_proposal.name: Hold On
merged_proposal.one_liner: A game against an opponent that plays like an 800 (it hangs pieces, and it always takes yours) where the board catches your hand before a piece is lost, asks you one question about the look you skipped, lets you answer by touching the board, and takes its hand off your wrist as you stop needing it.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction: The hand on the wrist, and the hand coming off. When you drop a piece on a square that hands over material to a one-move reply, the piece does not land: it hovers at half opacity, the board dims one shade, and one line in the coach's voice asks for the look you skipped, never the answer: 'Hold on. After this lands: what can they take?' Nothing on the board is marked. You answer with your thumb, by tapping the square you think is in trouble (or a 'Nothing' button when the honest answer is nothing); only after your tap does the board show you were right, or pulse the square you missed with one more hint ('Not that one. Look at the pawns next to e4.'). Then you choose. 'Take it back': the piece floats home and the coach says nothing, because silence is the reward. 'Show me': you feel it; in the MVP their reply ghosts across the board, the capture happens, a small '-2' floats up, a beat, everything slides back; in iteration two the board turns and you take your own knight with your own finger, which is the lesson's change-chairs phase made physical. 'Play it anyway': counted, never nagged; the opponent takes at once and the coach says one sentence ('There it goes. A knight for a pawn. You saw it coming, that counts.'), and that square is never held again this game. The looks are the lesson's three, encoded as the only things that fire a hold: a piece of yours left where it can be taken (from their chair), their last move's attack ignored, a free piece of theirs ignored, a mate in one allowed or missed. A quiet positional loss, however large, never holds, because it is not what loses games under 1000. And the hand comes off: the hold budget per game shrinks as clean games accumulate, the first game with no holds is announced before it starts ('No holds today. A real game.'), and what the hold would have caught is shown only at the close. The opponent is built the way I play my own students: it always punishes a hung piece, never hangs its queen or walks into mate, and leaves a minor piece for free every six to ten moves so you get to be the one who looks and takes, rewarded with two words, 'You looked.' Claude's one job in the moment is to ask the question a coach would ask in this exact position, in this player's words, and to answer the squares he tapped; the engine decides everything else. Nothing in the world holds the move, asks the look rather than naming the square, grades the answer on the board itself, lets the student feel the punishment on his own board, and then fades.
merged_proposal.core_loop: Every move (about twenty seconds): 1. 'Your move.' While he thinks, the Worker has already searched the current position (depth 12, multipv 3), so the best move, its eval and any free capture available to him are known. 2. He taps or drags. chess.js applies the move on a scratch board; the engine searches the resulting position at depth 10 for the reply (about 0.3 s), giving cp loss and the refutation. 3. Clean (cp loss under 200, or no mechanism chess.js can name): the piece lands, the opponent replies in under a second with a soft slide, silence. If he just took a free piece: 'You looked.' 4. Hold, in this priority: G1 his move leaves a piece of his attacked and undefended or attacked by a pawn or cheaper piece, cp loss 200 or more, refutation a capture ('Hold on. After this lands: what can they take?'; for a capture of a defended piece, 'Hold on. Before you take on e5: what takes back?'); G2 the same test, but the piece was already attacked by their last move and he moved something else ('Hold on. Their last move. What did it attack?'); G3 the engine's best move is a capture winning two points or more and he played something else with cp loss 200 or more ('Hold on. Before that: is anything of theirs free?'); G4 his move allows a mate in one, or a mate in one was available ('Hold on. Checks. What check do they have?'). Suppressed when he is already five points down, after the second play-anyway of the game, and when the budget (iteration two) is spent. 5. 'Hold on.' and the templated question appear instantly from the rule; Claude's phrasing (quick tier, no tools) swaps in only if it arrives within 2.5 s. 6. He answers by tapping a square or 'Nothing'. chess.js grades against the engine's answer set: right, 'Yes, the d3 pawn. A knight for a pawn. Take it back?'; partial, 'The c6 knight does guard e5. Is that the only defender? Look at the pawns.'; wrong, one more hint, then the square pulses. 7. Take it back (silence) / Show me (the ghost recapture with the floating material count; iteration two, the chair flip where he takes his own piece) / Play it anyway (the opponent takes, one sentence, counted). 8. The hold is logged: {fen, move, category, tapsToAnswer, outcome}. Every game (ten to fifteen minutes): the opponent (Stockfish Skill Level 1-3, depth 6, multipv 3 weighted so it makes human-shaped mistakes; forced to play the top move whenever it wins two points or mates; a planted free minor piece every six to ten moves, verified free at depth 12) resigns a queen down so games end. The close is one card in the player's units: 'Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4). Holds: 3, two taken back.' and the hold moments as small boards; two sentences from Claude in the coach's voice ('Both holds today were a pawn you did not see. Before the piece lands, look at the pawns.'); then 'Again', and 'Play from here' on the worst moment (iteration two) with the hold active and that category primed. Every week (iteration two and three): the hold budget is the average of the last three games minus one, down toward zero; the first zero-hold game is a named event; clean games chain into a streak drawn on the board edge, not a counter. The worst moment of the last game is the opening question of the next game with nothing marked (R2), and when the same category's precondition appears live in a later game the hold whispers 'This one again.' (R3). After five games, one memory line from the category counts: 'Four of your last six holds were a pawn. Pawns are the ones you don't see.' The whole loop runs with Claude absent: templated questions, the same taps, the same ghosts; Claude only makes it personal.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/src modules, app/styles.css, an inline SVG piece set and the vendored chess.js and Stockfish worker; no build step; light and dark through tokens; the board as the hero at 400 px with one serif coach line above and one action bar below; no eval bar, no move list, no rating, no chat box. First thirty seconds: the page opens on the verified Italian position after 3...Nf6 (FEN r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/RNBQK2R w KQkq - 4 4), white at the bottom, with the line 'Your move. Most beginners take on f7 here. Go on, try it.' He plays 4.Bxf7+; the bishop hovers, the board dims, 'Hold on. After the king takes back: what can you take?' He taps around, nothing lights, he taps 'Nothing'. 'Right. Nothing to take, and your only check is a knight the king walks away from. A bishop for a pawn. Take it back?' He takes it back; the bishop slides home; 'That is all I do. Now a real game. Your move.' This canned hold uses no Claude call, so the one consent dialog arrives at his first real hold, when he already knows what a hold is. Then a real game as White from move one against the bot (Skill Level 1, depth 6, multipv 3 weighted pick; forced top move when it wins two points or mates; one planted free minor piece between moves 6 and 12 verified free at depth 12; resigns a queen down). Gates G1, G2, G3 and G4 as above, strictly 200 cp with a capture or check refutation and a chess.js-nameable mechanism, suppressed at five points down and after the second play-anyway; hold counter shown at the close, budget not yet enforced. The hold UI: hover state, 'Hold on.' plus the templated question instantly, Claude's question on the quick tier through sample.json with the schema {question, answer_squares, if_right, if_partial, if_wrong}, validated (answer_squares a subset of the engine's set, no answer square named in the question) and swapped in within 2.5 s, stubbed through window.__stubSample in tests; tap-to-answer with a 'Nothing' button; 'Show me' as the ghost recapture with the floating material count and rewind (reduced-motion: static with the count); 'Take it back' (silence) and 'Play it anyway' (one templated sentence, counted). 'You looked.' when he takes a free piece. The close card with pieces given away, holds, outcomes, the moments as small boards, and two sentences from one quick call (templated counts when sample is null), then 'Again'. localStorage for the last five games' counts. Acceptance tests, all from positions verified at depth 20 in lessons 0000 and 0001: Italian after 6...d6, 7.Nxe5 holds (G1, tapping d6 is right, c6 is partial), 7.Bxf7+ holds, 7.h3 passes silently; Ruy after 3...a6, 4.O-O holds (G2, tap b5), 4.Ba4 passes; Italian after 4.d3 Nxe4, 5.Nc3 holds (G3, tap e4) and 5.dxe4 passes with 'You looked.'; placement position after 7...O-O, 8.Nbd2 holds (G3, tap g4); after 5...Ng4, 6.O-O holds and 6.hxg4 passes; the Bxf7+ tutorial hold accepts 'Nothing'; zero sample calls in a clean game; a stub reply naming an off-set square is discarded and the template shows. Not in the slice: the hold budget and fade (counter only), the chair flip (ghost only), 'But...' pushback, 'Play from here', R2 and R3, db plus user, playing Black, PGN download, settings.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: Novelty: no product holds the move, asks for the look instead of naming the square, grades the answer by a tap on the board, lets the student feel the punishment on his own board and then fades; every incumbent in the brief marks the blunder after it lands or draws the threat for you. Beginner value: this is the only thing that moves a rating under 1000, the half-second before the piece lands, and the loop gives him twenty to forty reps of it per game against an opponent that both punishes every hung piece and hands him free ones to find, with the free-capture look and the from-their-chair look getting equal reps, which no bot and no puzzle set does. The fade is what makes it coaching rather than a crutch: a hand that never comes off never teaches a habit. Feasibility: one page, one loop, everything that needs no words done by chess.js and the Worker in under half a second, Claude called zero times in a clean game and two to six times in a typical one on the quick tier with no tools, the whole thing playable and testable without Claude on five positions already verified at depth 20 in this repo. Delight: the piece that will not land, the question he can actually answer, 'You looked.' when he takes the free knight, the '-2' floating up when he asks to see it, the bishop sliding home with no red mark and no shame, and a few games later the line 'No holds today. A real game.'

reviews.persona: Product designer: intuitiveness, craft and emotional design for the LLM-native chess coach, designing for Sambudh (under 1000, studied nothing, opens 1.e4, phone in hand) first. I judge every concept by the first screen, the single primary action, the visual identity (board as hero, tournament buff-and-green, serif coach voice, both themes at 400 px, never red), and by how a blunder feels here versus on Lichess.

critiques.strengths: The strictest silence in all twenty-one concepts: "Your move. I'll stay quiet unless it matters." is a promise the page can keep, and silence as the reward is emotionally exactly right for someone who has closed every app that showed him a bar. Answering by tapping squares, never typing. The scripted beginner tree that guarantees something hangs by move five solves the first-session problem without a tutorial. The bot resigns a queen down, so games end and the close arrives. "That's it." and "That's the one." are the right size of praise. The next game opening with one line that names the thing ("Watch the pawns today.") is memory as a sentence, not a chart.
critiques.weaknesses: The first frame is an empty start position plus a promise, so for twenty seconds the product looks like every play-the-computer page, and a beginner who leaves at fifteen seconds never saw the hold. "Before you let go of the knight: what defends e5?" uses coach vocabulary ("defends") that reads as homework under 1000; the lesson's own plainer phrasing ("a pawn can take it back") is better. The close screen with "hold-on moments as small boards" is a dashboard sprouting from a page that promised none, and the badge "Black: Beginner" labels the opponent with a rating word. Streaming the question in "within a second" after an instant "Hold on." means the line changes while he is reading it, which is the one craft sin a held piece cannot afford.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Open game one three moves in, at the Italian after 3...Nf6 (verified: 4.Bxf7+ and 4.Nxe5 both lose a piece, 4.d3 is clean), with the line "Your move. The first three moves are the usual ones." so the hold is one tempting tap away in the first fifteen seconds without telling him to blunder. And a fixed beat rule: "Hold on." plus the amber square instantly, then exactly one question at 1.5 s, Claude's if it has arrived, the template if not, and the line never changes after it is shown.

critiques.strengths: Punish-then-prevent is a real loop, and the second half is what no puzzle app does: he sees his own kind of mistake from the seat that profits from it. Two decisions in thirty seconds, both his, nothing read. The acceptance rules are the engine's, so a verdict is never arbitrary once the top three are shown.
critiques.weaknesses: It is a drill, and he said he wants to play. As a first screen, a board already flipped with "You're Black" is the most disorienting opening possible for someone who has only ever sat on the white side. Sets of ten with a count is puzzle-rush shape with a serif font. Ten built-in positions is two sessions of content, and the fuzzy "prevent" judgement risks a wrong-feeling verdict in his first minute.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Never open the product here. Offer it from the end screen of a game, using the game's own moment ("Sit in their chair for the one you missed"), and give the flip a 400 ms rotation with a side badge pinned to the bottom board edge reading "You are Black" in the serif, never a toast, static under prefers-reduced-motion.

critiques.strengths: The honest version of Game Review: three, not thirty; a question before any evaluation; harder on return (no highlights, then a fresh position). The memory line ("Four of your last six hung pieces were to a pawn.") is the one sentence no product says. Falling back to the original position when a generated one fails verification means a hallucinated puzzle never reaches him.
critiques.weaknesses: Needs games, so day one is seed positions pretending to be his. A 30-60 s default-tier call behind "Reading your game..." is the longest wait proposed, at the moment he is most likely to close the page. A PGN paste box is the only text input a beginner would ever see here, and its presence says the screen was designed for someone else. Three small boards on a phone is a list, and lists are what he closes.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One board, never three: the three moments as three small marks under the board that he steps through, the current one always full width. And the rule-based moment with its templated question must appear the instant the game ends, so there is never a spinner between the last move and the first question; Claude's phrasing replaces the template only if it arrives before he taps.

critiques.strengths: Shows the product working by second fifteen with a canned hold on a verified position, before any Claude call or consent dialog. The identity is decided: tournament buff-and-green board, serif coach voice, amber for the hold, nothing ever red, action bar empty until a decision is needed. "Take it back" with nothing recorded against him is the emotional thesis in one button. The 400 px layout is specified to the pixel.
critiques.weaknesses: Honestly: "Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7." instructs him to blunder, which is a tutorial in disguise and slightly patronising, and his first move is not his own. The 2.5 s swap rule lets the question change under his eyes. "One thing from this game" is a 30-90 s wait at the end of a ten-minute game. Two Claude calls, a Games sheet and db are a week, not a day. The Unicode glyph fallback board is a craft risk I waved at instead of solving.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Drop the instruction and let the position do the tempting; replace the swap with the 1.5 s beat; and make the end screen a rewind to the moment rather than a paragraph, so the game ends with a board, not a card.

critiques.strengths: The loop is literal: make a move, the board turns, punish yourself. "You just caught yourself." is the first laugh a beginner has at his own blunder. Five dots, no score.
critiques.weaknesses: A flip on every move is five rotations in five minutes on a phone, which is nauseating and tiring. The dot row with hollow dots for Show-me is a score by another name. It reads as puzzles with extra steps and needs a corpus. Nothing here happens inside a game, which is where his rating is decided.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold the chair switch into Rewind's "Play from here" as a single, story-bearing flip at the moment that mattered, not a standalone mode.

critiques.strengths: Direct manipulation: see it before it happens. The dashed "They would play this" arrow appearing half a second after a ghost is x-ray vision he can use without reading. Nothing is ever a number.
critiques.weaknesses: Consequence rings on legal squares are noise even when most are plain. It is one lost argument away from a Lichess analysis board. A playground is for the curious, and he is not curious yet, he is losing. "You move both sides" and paste-FEN are controls on the first frame of a page that promised one action.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep exactly one ghost: the "Show me" inside the hold, which plays the engine's refutation and rewinds. No playground until he asks for one.

critiques.strengths: A named rival (Mira) is better emotional design than "Black: Beginner": an opponent with a name is a person to beat, and "Answered." is the quietest possible way to say the threat was real and you handled it. The validators, abort-on-next-move and error branches are the most careful in the set, and the game is identical with Claude absent.
critiques.weaknesses: The opponent speaks unprompted six to twelve times a game in a bubble beside the board: that is the chat-next-to-board the brief rejects, in costume, and the eye goes to the bubble instead of the squares. The consent dialog appears mid-game at Mira's first sentence. Telegraphed threats teach dependence, and the fade-out is iteration two.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Mira speaks only when her name is tapped. Her sentence lives in the coach-line slot above the board, in the serif, not a speech balloon. Keep "Answered.", but draw it as the amber leaving the threatened piece rather than a word.

critiques.strengths: The board sliding to "This is where it turned." is the right first frame for a result screen: a position, not a list. Grading the reasoning rather than the move is new. "Nothing turned this game; well played." is an honest empty state.
critiques.weaknesses: A text field with the placeholder "Type your answer" on the result screen of a phone game is the moment he leaves. A 10-30 s wait for the card, then a card that slides in, then a "Two more moments" link: three things where there should be one. Typing is the act beginners like least, and Skip will be the primary action.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Answer by tap first (the squares are the vocabulary he has), with "Type it instead" as a small link; the card becomes one serif line above the board, no card.

critiques.strengths: Question chips computed from the facts, never a text box, is the best anti-chatbot pattern proposed. The arrow is drawn from the fact sheet before the sentence arrives, so the page answers before Claude does. "Coach is resting." is the kindest rate-limit copy in the set.
critiques.weaknesses: A layer, not a loop. At 400 px chips, bubble and board compete for the same inches and the board loses. A curious player taps thirty times a game. "What is it doing?" has no engine fact behind it and will be bland.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One chip only, on a second tap of an already-selected piece on your turn: "Is it safe?", answered first by the board (ring and arrow) and then by one sentence in the coach line. It belongs inside the game, not on its own page.

critiques.strengths: "Show me": the enemy pawn slides over and takes, a small "-2" floats up, a beat, everything slides back. That is the best single moment anyone proposed, and it needs no words. "But..." is the only place the player gets to argue with the piece still in his hand, and the coach answers his plan, not a number. The template sentence by default and Claude only on taps is cheap and honest. "Play it anyway: counted, never nagged."
critiques.weaknesses: Four buttons (Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway / But...) will not fit a 56 px bar at 400 px, and four choices is three too many for someone who was mid-move. The sentence tells ("His knight on c6 takes yours back") instead of asking, so he reads instead of looks. "-2" is a number, even if it is one he understands.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Two buttons and two links: [Take it back] [Play it anyway] in the bar, "Show me" and "But..." as text links at the end of the coach line. The sentence becomes a question with the answer squares tappable, and "Show me" is what he taps when he cannot find it.

critiques.strengths: The tape rewind, fast then slowing, with their last move replaying so he sees it arrive, is cinema: it tells the story of the loss with no words. A question answered by tap. "Play from here": the chance to win the game you lost from the move you lost it is a feeling no product has given a beginner. The honest empty state ("Nothing was given away for free this game. It was lost slowly, which is a different lesson.").
critiques.weaknesses: Scoring forty positions at depth 14 after the game is a 20-40 s gap on a phone, and the concept does not notice that the play loop already evaluated every move as it was made. The "what just happened?" chip mid-game competes with the hold for the same slot.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Reuse the in-play verdicts so the rewind begins within a second of the last move, and make Rewind the end screen of the hold game rather than a separate page: one board, one game, one ending that is a beginning.

critiques.strengths: A moment you can hand to a friend, who sees the board and the question before any pitch. "Day N" counting days played, never days in a row.
critiques.weaknesses: Six positions last a week. A daily for someone who does not yet have a daily habit. The share link opens outside the viewer, so the friend's "Play a game" lacks the coach and must not look broken. Another first screen that is not a game.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make "Send this one" a link on the Rewind screen, sharing the moment from his own game, and skip the daily until there are moments worth sending.

critiques.strengths: The ring that shrinks as you stop needing it: progress felt in the hands before it is ever a number, and "You did not need the hold for 31 moves." is the best clean-game line in the set. "Looked." is the quietest praise. The bot tuned to hang a minor piece at a tuned rate, so he gets to be the one who looks and takes.
critiques.weaknesses: The their-chair pulse on every drop shows the hanging piece without asking anything: it is a crutch and it over-draws. A one-second hold on every move is friction on the ninety percent of moves that are fine. "What am I up to?" is a second permanent control. Nothing is asked of the player, so nothing is learned by him.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Pulse only when something is actually lost, and ask instead of show. Keep the shrinking ring as the product's only progress indicator, drawn under the board edge, never as a counter.
