critiques.strengths: Taking your own knight with your own finger is a small physical shock, and funny. The one joke per game ("Comfortable? Mine is the better chair, I think."). The budget as graduation, with "No chairs today. A real game." as a named event, is kind design.
critiques.weaknesses: A rotation mid-game on a phone at every blunder is a context switch, and in a bad game that is every third move. The material count on the board edge is a number. The budget needs testing before it is trusted, and it is the part that makes the mechanic kind.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Use the chair swap once, at Rewind, where the flip has a story and the capture is the one that actually happened.

critiques.strengths: The grid you can send, square by square with a bounce, is the sharpest social artifact proposed. The verb is the lesson: tap the looks, not the move. A missed day is a grey grid, never a broken chain.
critiques.weaknesses: It has the shape of a puzzle app. Three questions in sequence with a "None" button is a quiz. Thirty engine-verified positions is real authoring before day one exists. On its own it is a layer; his rating is decided in games.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Steal the grid for the end-of-game share (holds as filled and hollow squares) and leave the daily for after the play loop has games to draw from.

critiques.concept: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)
critiques.strengths: The reversal, player talks and coach listens, is the most genuinely new idea in the set, and the market evidence behind it is the strongest. "That one was yours." is the best praise line anyone wrote. "Checked" and "Five moves, nothing hung" as the only feedback is the right amount.
critiques.weaknesses: A text input under the board on the first frame is a chatbot's chair even when the coach never speaks, and the placeholder "Say your check: what did that attack, what can you take, any checks?" is a form. Typing before moves on a phone, with an 80 percent skip rate expected by its own author. The question arrives after the king has already moved, so he reads a correction, not a hold.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold the reversal into the hold's "But..." link: he argues only when he wants to, with the piece still in the air, which is where the belief lives, and the coach's answer ends with a question. The input appears only then and disappears after.

critiques.strengths: Ration and refund are clever game design, and "Nothing for me there." teaches the thing most important for a nervous beginner: most of your moves are fine. The opponent saying "Thanks." when you were about to hand it a bishop is good character.
critiques.weaknesses: A hint machine in a costume, by its own admission. Two buttons appear under every ghost drop, so every move becomes a two-step. The flip per look, three times a game, on a phone. The LLM is the weakest necessity here and the author says so.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Nothing on its own; the refund's lesson belongs to the hold's silence, which teaches the same thing for free on ninety percent of moves.

critiques.strengths: "You stopped doing that." with the habit line crossing itself out is the best progress indicator anyone proposed: a sentence a person would say. The whisper before the moment is memory used during play, which nobody does. The five-label vocabulary with a validator is honest engineering.
critiques.weaknesses: Cold start: three placement positions on day one is a test with a serif font. A whisper that fires when the precondition holds but the move was fine teaches him to ignore it. The whisper lives in the same slot as the hold's question, with nothing highlighted, so it reads as the coach nagging in advance. Typing a reason is required for the placement.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The whisper as the opening line of a game, once ("Watch the pawns today."), never per move; and "You stopped doing that." as the end-of-game line on the day a habit retires, with the old move numbers still showing.

critiques.strengths: Buildable in a day with the seams right, and it reads as designed: the piece dimmed to 60 percent with a small chip, the hold as a data attribute CSS turns into dimming and pulse, the piece layer's transforms giving the take-back slide for free, reduced-motion as a duration of zero. "Nothing. Take it back" as the button when the honest answer is nothing is a lovely piece of copy. One primary action in a sticky bottom bar.
critiques.weaknesses: "Before this goes: after they take back with the king, what can you take?" is a two-clause hypothetical; an 800 reads it twice. The first frame is a start position and a promise line. "Why?" inside the hold with tools is two seconds of waiting in a moment that must feel like a beat. The end screen is counts.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Question copy from the lesson's three looks, one clause each, keyed by category, with the answer squares as the vocabulary. And the first frame three moves in.

critiques.strengths: Answering by moving the pieces: ghost bishop takes, ghost king takes back, one caption per move, then everything slides home. The 100 cp guard in the page, not the prompt, means the board can never show wrong chess as good.
critiques.weaknesses: Four to six seconds of waiting after a chip tap, mid-game. Three chips under every picked-up piece is three controls on every move. Ghosts over real pieces at 400 px are busy even with the real layer dimmed.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep show_line as the mechanism behind "Show me" inside the hold: the engine's own two-ply refutation, 600 ms a ply, the "-2" floating up, no Claude needed, always rewinds.

critiques.strengths: Typing "bishop hits f7" and watching f7 turn green on the board: his own reasoning visible on the squares for the first time. The "I read: attacks f7" line with a Fix link makes a wrong read visible, never silent. The OS keyboard's mic for free.
critiques.weaknesses: The board refuses the drop until he types: a lock on one move in four, with a gentle shake that is still a refusal. The amber "Look first" band with a field and two chips is a form on a page that promised a board. The first quick call raises the consent dialog mid-move.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Only as the optional "But..." path inside the hold, where the green square on a correct claim is the reward for arguing well.

ranking: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)

merged_proposal.name: Hold On
merged_proposal.one_liner: A real game on a tournament board against an opponent at your level; when the piece you are letting go of would be lost, the board holds it in the air and asks you one question you answer by tapping a square, then you take it back or play it anyway; when the game ends the board rewinds to the one moment that mattered and lets you play it again from there.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction: Three things, in one page, that no product has: (1) the pre-commit hold, answered on the board: a move that would lose a piece to a one-move reply does not land; it floats at 60 percent over its square with a soft shadow, the square breathes amber, the board dims one shade, a small chip reads "Hold on", and one serif line asks a question written for this exact position ("Hold on. That pawn on e4 has a friend. Tap what guards it."). He answers by tapping a square, never by typing; chess.js already knows the right squares, so the tap is graded instantly and the coach can never be wrong about chess. (2) The dignified take-back: [Take it back] slides the piece home in 180 ms with "Good. Your move." and nothing is recorded against him; [Play it anyway] is always one tap away and never nagged; "Show me" plays the enemy's capture as a ghost with a small "-2" floating up, a beat, and everything slides back. (3) Rewind: the end screen is not a card but the board itself rewinding, fast then slowing, to the position before the moment that mattered, their last move replaying so he sees it arrive, one tap question ("That pawn just stepped forward. Tap the piece of yours it is now attacking."), and [Play from here], so the game he lost resumes at the move he lost it. Across games the hold gets visibly rarer: holds are drawn as small marks under the board edge, a clean game earns "You did not need the hold for 31 moves.", and the next game opens with one remembered line ("Two holds last game, both a pawn you did not see. Watch the pawns."). The engine does everything that needs no language and does it before Claude is asked: Stockfish 18 lite in a Worker is the opponent (Skill Level 2, depth 6, multipv 3 weighted so it hangs a minor piece now and then but always takes what he hangs), the silent gate (depth 12 pre-search of his position while he thinks, a depth 10-12 check of the pending move on drop, under 300 ms), and the ghost line; chess.js names the mechanism and the answer squares. Claude does the one thing only an LLM can do here: turn the engine's facts into a question that points at the look he skipped without naming the answer, varying with the position and with what he personally keeps doing, so the question never becomes wallpaper. The hold fires only on what decides games under 1000: cp loss of 200 or more where the refutation is a capture or a check and chess.js can name what is lost, a free capture ignored, or a mate in one allowed; positional losses never hold; after the second "play it anyway" in a game the hold stays quiet until the end. How a blunder feels: on Lichess it is a red "??" discovered afterwards, alone; here it is a question you answered with the piece still yours and the choice still yours. The only red on Lichess is the only colour this page never uses.
merged_proposal.core_loop: One screen, the board, in both themes at 400 px: page off-white (cool, slate text) in light and near-black blue-grey in dark; the board the warmest, brightest object on the page, buff and green like tournament vinyl (light: #e9e5d8 / #8f9a7e, dark: #b8b4a0 / #5c6b5a), inline SVG pieces; the coach's line in a book serif (Source Serif 4 or Literata, Georgia fallback), labels in IBM Plex Sans; accent ink-blue, hold amber, nothing ever red. Layout: a 44 px header ("Game 1" left, one small dot right for theme and level), one serif line of at most three lines above the board, the board full width minus 16 px gutters (46 px squares), a 56 px action bar below that is empty until a decision is needed. No move list, no eval bar, no clock, no rating, no text field. States and their copy: OPENING (game 1 only): the Italian after 3...Nf6, his white pieces at the bottom, line "Your move. The first three moves are the usual ones."; both tempting grabs (4.Bxf7+, 4.Nxe5) are one tap away and 4.d3 is clean; later games start from the start position with the remembered line. YOUR MOVE: tap a piece (or drag), legal squares as faint dots, tap the square; the opponent replies within a second with a 180 ms slide, from and to squares tinted; nothing is said. HOLD (the gate fired): the piece floats, the square breathes amber, the board dims, chip "Hold on"; at 1.5 s exactly one question appears, Claude's if it arrived, else the template for the category ("Hold on. What can take it there? Tap it." / "Hold on. Something of theirs is free right now. Tap it." / "Hold on. Their last move reached one of yours. Tap it." / "Hold on. Two of theirs look at one square. Tap it."); the line never changes once shown; action bar [Take it back] (primary, ink) [Play it anyway] (quiet); "Show me" as a text link at the end of the line. RIGHT TAP: "Yes, d3. The pawn takes back: a knight for a pawn. Still want to?" WRONG TAP: "Not that one. Look at the pawns next to e4.", one retry, then the arrow d3 to e4 draws itself and the line reads "d3. Take it back?" SHOW ME: the attacker ghosts over and captures, "-2" floats up, a beat, everything slides back, no words. TAKE IT BACK: piece slides home, "Good. Your move.", nothing recorded against him. PLAY IT ANYWAY: commits; if punished, "There it goes. You saw it coming; that counts."; that piece is never held again this game; after the second play-anyway the hold stays quiet until the end. FREE CAPTURE TAKEN: "Free knight. You looked." (the only praise during play). GAME OVER: "Well played." or "That one got away."; action bar [Rewind] (primary) [New game]; if nothing was given away: "Nothing was given away for free this game." and [New game]. REWIND: the board rewinds move by move, fast then slowing, to the position before the biggest one-move-look loss (known from the in-play verdicts, no new engine pass), their last move replays slowly, line "Move 9. That pawn just stepped forward. Tap the piece of yours it is now attacking."; right: "Yes, the bishop. It had to move." and the ghost of what actually happened; action bar [Play from here]; the game resumes against the same opponent with the hold active; finishing with that piece kept earns "Answered: the bishop on b5." PROGRESS: holds this game as small marks under the board edge (filled for taken back, hollow for played anyway); a clean game: "You did not need the hold for 31 moves."; the next game's opening line names the trend from the stored holds. Reduced motion: every slide, pulse and rewind becomes an instant change with the same copy.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/src/{main,board,game,engine,coach,store,ui}.js, app/styles.css and app/pieces.svg (twelve inline symbols; licence checked beside stockfish.COPYING.txt), served by python3 -m http.server, published with files. In the slice: the identity in both themes at 400 px with the board as hero; tap-tap and drag input with legal dots and 180 ms slides (zero under reduced motion); play as White against the Worker at one fixed level; the silent gate for two categories (your move leaves a piece capturable for a net loss of two points or more with a capture or check refutation; a free capture of two points or more ignored), with the depth-12 pre-search and the drop check; the hold state with the templated question per category, tap-to-answer graded by chess.js, one retry then the arrow; "Show me" ghost capture with the "-2"; [Take it back] and [Play it anyway] with their lines and the two-play-anyway quiet rule; "Free knight. You looked."; the game-over lines; Rewind to the moment using the in-play verdicts, the templated tap question, and [Play from here]; holds per game as marks and the next game's opening line, kept in localStorage; Claude Call 1 only: quick tier, sample.json, fired by the drop that triggered the hold, input the FEN, the move in SAN, the mechanism facts from chess.js, the engine's refutation and cp before and after, which of the three looks it is, this game's holds and the last game's remembered line; output {question, answer_squares, yes, no} validated (real squares, a subset of the engine's answer set, no answer square named in the question) and used only if it arrives before the 1.5 s beat ends; window.__stubSample for tests; with sample null or not_granted the template carries the whole product and nothing looks missing. Acceptance, all from verified lesson positions: Italian after 3...Nf6, 4.Bxf7+ holds (answer e8), 4.Nxe5 holds (answer c6), 4.d3 silent; after 4.d3 Nxe4, 5.Nc3 holds (free capture, answer e4) and 5.dxe4 earns "Free knight. You looked."; Italian after 6...d6, 7.Nxe5 holds (d6 or c6), 7.Bxf7+ holds (f8 or e8), 7.h3 silent; Ruy after 3...a6, 4.O-O holds (b5), 4.Ba4 silent; four screenshots (desktop and 400 px, light and dark) with no horizontal overflow. Explicitly not in the slice: the post-game Claude note, the "But..." argue link, Claude-written rewind questions, the memory line written by Claude, level settings, playing Black, db plus user, PGN download, a Games sheet, any flip, any chip, any text input.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: Four of seven partners independently proposed the hold, which is the strongest signal this team has produced: it is the only interaction that acts at the exact moment under-1000 games are decided, the half-second before the piece lands, and no product in the world does it. It is a game, not a drill, which is what Sambudh asked for; the first screen is a board with one line, the primary action is always "make a move" or "tap a square", and he never reads a manual because the position itself tempts him into the first hold within fifteen seconds. The LLM's job is bounded and visibly worth its second: a question that points at the look he skipped without naming the answer and varies with him, where a template would become wallpaper by game five; the engine owns every chess fact and the page plays fully without Claude, so the craft bar is reachable in one page in a day. Rewind gives the game an ending that is a beginning, the delight the beginner asked for ("winning the game I lost, from the exact position where I lost it"), using work the engine already did during play. And the emotional design is the product: a blunder here is a question you answered, a take-back with no shame, a ghost that shows you the future and puts the pieces back, and a hold that you can watch become rare. The mission's own measure of done, three of five games with zero pieces hung, is exactly what the marks under the board count.

critiques.strengths: The call policy is right where it matters: Claude never decides whether to interrupt (the gate is the coach's thresholds in code), it only decides how to ask; a clean game makes zero calls; the sample.json contract returns the whole exchange in one shot ({question, highlight, expected_squares, follow_up_if_right/partial/wrong}) so the reply to the player's tap costs no second round; no tools in the beat; the templated fallback ('Hold on. What defends e5?') is named and window.__stubSample is in the slice. The scripted beginner tree for game one guarantees a verified moment by move five, which is also what makes a Playwright scenario deterministic.
critiques.weaknesses: 'The coach's question streams in within a second' cannot happen with sample.json: onText carries the raw JSON text, so there is nothing to stream; the question arrives whole in about 1-1.5 s on quick and the page must show the template meanwhile. The first call of the view lands the consent dialog on top of the hovering piece, the exact beat the concept is protecting. Nothing is specified on the way out: highlight must be a subset of the fact sheet's squares and the question must not contain expected_squares, or a wrong or spoiling reply reaches the board. Iteration two's typed reply with evaluate(fen) and legal_moves(fen) on the default tier turns a 2 s beat into a 30-90 s wait for facts the page already holds; a typed pushback can be answered on quick with the fact sheet and no tools.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Consent under a button: Claude is asked on a hold only after the first successful call of the view, and that first call comes only from a tap whose copy says it asks Claude on the viewer's account; until then the template question stands. Plus one validate(reply, facts) (squares subset of the fact sheet, no SAN token outside the listed moves, no signed number, none of blunder/mistake/inaccuracy, question must not contain the answer squares) that falls back to the template and bumps window.__coachRejects so the stub test can assert that a deliberately bad reply never reaches the board.

critiques.strengths: Claude is silent on a right answer (the engine already said it), which is the best cost rule in the whole set. The set-generation design gates on the tool log rather than on prose: 'the page refuses to include any puzzle whose refutation the tool log does not show as confirmed' is exactly how a generated drill stays honest. The long call has honest progress copy.
critiques.weaknesses: Building ten puzzles in one default-tier call with evaluate, line and legal_moves is twenty-plus tool rounds; the contract allows a handful per call and makes the last one the answer, so the call is cut off or must be split, and every round re-reads the whole PGN and trace, so 30-60 s is optimistic for that shape. The quick-tier question on a wrong try has no out-validator, and that is where a question can name the refutation square.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Invert the pipeline: the engine trace produces the candidate list (ply, FEN, cp loss, refutation already confirmed) with no Claude at all; one quick sample.json call, no tools, cache {gcTime: 86400000} keyed by the game id, writes the ten one-line setups from that list as a JSON array; the validator checks every SAN and square. Same product, one second instead of a minute, and nothing to gate because nothing was generated.

critiques.strengths: The rule-based three appear first and Claude's phrasing swaps in when it arrives; memory is counted by the page by category; 'the page records the confirmation and drops any moment Claude did not confirm'. Call (1) is well specified down to the output fields (question, expected squares, follow-up, acceptance criterion).
critiques.weaknesses: R3 asks Claude to compose a FEN. That is the most hallucination-prone request in the whole ideation: model-written FENs are routinely illegal or absurd (adjacent kings, pawns on the first rank, the wrong side to move, a 'tempting move' that is not legal), and the silent fallback to R2 hides a feature that will fail most of the time. Call (1) with four tools on the default tier is 30-90 s per game, and show(fen, highlight, arrows) as a tool lets Claude put any position on the board, including one that never happened in his game.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Selection, never generation: a seed bank of engine-verified positions tagged by category (the two lessons plus a few dozen authored with scripts/engine_check.py); for R3 Claude picks, on quick, the seed whose category matches and rewrites the question for it; the page never renders a FEN Claude typed. Restrict show() to plies of the game under review.

critiques.strengths: The 2.5 s swap rule is the right latency contract for a beat: the template appears instantly under the floating piece, Claude's question replaces it only if it arrives in time, and the hold never waits. The out-validator is stated (answer_squares real and a subset of the engine's set, the question must not contain them, else the template). The canned tutorial hold on the verified 3...Nf6 position means no call and no consent dialog before he knows what a hold is. Call 2's tools return small plain data and show_position is restricted to plies of this game, so Claude cannot show a position that did not happen.
critiques.weaknesses: Call 1 fires on every hold: in a bad game that is six or more calls, and the first real hold still brings the consent dialog mid-beat (the tutorial only delays it by one game). Call 2's prose ('two or three sentences') has no validator specified, and it is where a SAN token or a square outside the game is most likely to appear. The engine-only fallback 'Your three biggest swings' needs the same category rule as Call 1 or it lists positional swings the band should never see.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Consent under a button, a per-game cap on hold-question calls, and one validate(reply, facts) used by both calls with a rejection counter the stub test asserts. Keep the swap rule but make it 'before the player's first tap' rather than a fixed 2.5 s, so a slow first call never swaps the question under his thumb.

critiques.strengths: The hint prompt is tightly scoped ('from Black's point of view, name no move and no square') with a page-side scan for squares and move text that falls back to the engine's arrow. Tomorrow's five is selection from candidates(), an engine-produced list, not generation, and the page re-verifies each pick at 150 cp before it enters the set.
critiques.weaknesses: candidates() plus check() on the default tier is three or more rounds and 30-90 s for an editorial pick whose ten candidates fit in two kilobytes of prompt; inline them and the call is one quick round. 'The page only accepts text that does not contradict the engine's material count' is not checkable in prose: a page can validate tokens (squares, SAN, numbers), not meaning, and the promise should say so. Three prompt kinds for one drill is more prompt surface than the mechanic needs.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One quick JSON call with the candidates inline returning five {ply, caption}, the validator on every caption, and the consent dialog under the 'Make tomorrow's five' tap, which is already an explicit action.

critiques.strengths: The division is exact: rings, amber dots and the dashed reply arrow are engine work with no language, and Why? is restricted to the facts passed in with highlights refused outside them. 'Teach me this position' with ghost({move, say}) returning the engine's cp is a genuine thinking-partner loop: the tool result corrects Claude mid-answer, and the cap of four ghosts bounds the rounds.
critiques.weaknesses: As an LLM feature set it is three prompts on a playground that is mostly engine. The guided tour on the default tier is 30-90 s with every round re-reading the transcript, when quick with ghost() would be about five seconds and it is the engine's number in the tool reply, not the tier, that judges the line. Why? on every ghost is a paid tap for a curious player; the default five-minute cache helps only on exact repeats.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Run the tour on quick with ghost() and let the engine number in the tool reply do the correcting; cache Why? per FEN plus ghost move with gcTime one hour; show 'asks Claude' once on the first tap so the consent dialog has a visible reason.

critiques.strengths: The fact sheet, the square and SAN validator, a fresh AbortController per call that the next move handler aborts, the full error-code table and the phrasebook fallback are the right plumbing and should survive into whatever ships.
critiques.weaknesses: Self-critique: the telegraph fires from Mira's move, not from a tap. Six to twelve calls a game is affordable but it is the most expensive pattern on the table, and the consent dialog arrives unannounced in the middle of a game. The voice is flavour: a phrasebook carries four lines in five, so the LLM necessity is weak. The flipped-side threat probe adds engine time on every bot move and is undefined in check. Telegraphing every threat teaches dependence and the fade-out is not in the slice.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the telegraph a tap ('What is she up to?') and keep Claude for the one line only a model can write: the closing line that compares what she told him with what he missed.

critiques.strengths: Motif codes by rule, Claude phrases; a default-tier call with no tools and everything precomputed, cached 24 h keyed by the game id; free text graded against a rubric on quick; the SAN validator on every field; a template path for absent Claude with a tap-a-move answer graded by the engine.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing a reason after a lost game is a lot to ask of Sambudh; 10-30 s on default with only a sliding board to watch; the rubric is written by Claude and then used by Claude to grade, a closed loop that leans lenient; a 24 h cache replays stale cards whenever the prompt format changes during development unless the prompt carries a version tag.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A prompt version string in every prompt so a format change invalidates the cache, tap-a-move as the primary answer with typing optional, and the drill call on quick: the facts are precomputed, so there is nothing for the default tier to think about.

critiques.strengths: No text box: the question set is computed from the facts as chips; cache keyed by FEN plus chip for an hour so re-taps are free; the quiz answer key is the page's, never Claude's; arrows are drawn from the fact sheet before the call so the board answers at tap time.
critiques.weaknesses: 'What is it doing?' has no engine fact to validate beyond the attack map, so the answer is grounded but bland. Every first chip tap is a paid call and a curious player taps thirty times a game. Chips and the hold compete for the same single in-flight call. The quiz mode is a second prompt variant for little gain.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A visible chip budget per game (dots), template answers for repeat chips, and drop the quiz mode from the first version.

critiques.strengths: The cleanest call policy of the four Hold Ons: Claude is NOT called on ordinary moves and NOT for the hold sentence, which code templates from the facts; it is called only from two taps, 'Why?' and 'But...', so the consent dialog appears under a button with plain-words copy. 'But...' is the one place in the whole set where Claude is load-bearing: it reads the player's plan in his own words ('I'm attacking f2'), answers the plan with the facts, and ends in a question. The copy rules (never blunder, mistake, inaccuracy, never a number) come with a test that fails on those words. The game-end line is built only from stored fact lines.
critiques.weaknesses: highlight and play_ghost as tools on quick add a round each (a second per round) to a two-sentence answer; both can come back as JSON fields the page validates and draws in zero rounds. No out-validator is specified for the 'But...' reply (squares subset, no SAN outside the listed moves, no numbers). The 'one-line box' must be one line and one reply with no thread, or it becomes the chat the brief rejects.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Replace the tools with a JSON reply {say, squares, ghost}; the validator; and a prompt rule with a worked example: first clause acknowledges the plan, second states the fact that breaks it, then one question that names no move.

critiques.strengths: One call per game with a fixed input so the default cache replays it; Claude writes the question, chess.js grades the tap, answer_squares are validated and overridden; a fallback question so Rewind runs with no Claude; the pattern call returns an empty string under five moments instead of inventing one.
critiques.weaknesses: Tools highlight and play_ghost on quick again cost a round each for something a JSON field carries. The typed-answer grading on quick needs the same validator. No error branches are specified for the Rewind call (invalid_json should show Try again, rate_limited should keep the fallback question).
critiques.what_i_would_add: JSON fields instead of tools, and a fixed compact schema for stored moment lines so the pattern prompt is byte-identical across games and under a kilobyte, which is what makes it cacheable and cheap.

critiques.strengths: Claude is almost never called: seed positions ship with question, answer squares and feedback; the share link carries the question so a friend outside the viewer needs no Claude; the engine confirmation at load is a real gate against a stale seed.
critiques.weaknesses: 'One stable prompt per day, so it is cached' assumes a day-long cache; the default window is five minutes, so it needs cache {gcTime: 86400000} and a byte-identical prompt (no date in the body). The LLM is nearly absent, which is right for a daily and also why this is a layer, not the product Sambudh opens on day one.
critiques.what_i_would_add: gcTime 24 h with a deterministic prompt, and nothing else: this concept is correctly almost LLM-free and should stay that way.

critiques.strengths: 'What am I up to?' only on a tap, with the cost rule that three taps in a row get the engine's plain fact first; the stub test asserts the chip's text names only squares the page highlighted; rate_limited copy with no auto-retry.
critiques.weaknesses: 'Show me' inside the hold through Claude with show_line is a tool round to play a line the engine already produced: zero language needed. The point tool on quick adds a round per sentence; squares and arrows can come back in JSON. The end card on default with show_line and point is 30-90 s, not 10-30.
critiques.what_i_would_add: JSON {say, squares, arrows} for the chip with no tools; engine-only Show me; the end card on quick with the refutation line already in the prompt.

critiques.strengths: The swap is engine-only and Claude's post-swap line is one quick call with no tools and the memory counts in the prompt; the engine template stands in when sample is null.
critiques.weaknesses: That line has low necessity: 'e5 was defended by the knight on c6' from the template carries most of it. The 'what if I defend it' chip with try(moves) is the one LLM-shaped moment and is claimed at 10-30 s on default; with tools it is 30-90 s. The end-of-game line on default is unnecessary; quick suffices with the facts inline.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Run the what-if on quick with try() and let the engine's number judge the idea; a validator on the post-swap line; keep the swap itself free of Claude.

critiques.strengths: Captions generated at authoring time with engine_check.py, so the daily costs the viewer nothing unless they tap; the result line on quick; the engine as author and grader.
critiques.weaknesses: Why? on default with show_line and point is heavy for a two-sentence explanation of a line the page already holds; the memory line needs fourteen days of results in the prompt in a byte-identical shape to cache at all.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Why? on quick with the refutation line in the prompt and squares in JSON; the daily prompt cached with gcTime 24 h.

critiques.concept: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)
critiques.strengths: The most LLM-necessary interaction on the table: finding the false belief in the player's own sentence against a numbered fact list, which no template and no engine can do. Facts referenced by id, the validator against the fact list, no call at all when the sentence covers the facts and the move is clean, and a post-game call on default with no tools.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing before every move is friction, and a text field on the first frame is the chatbot shape the brief rejects even with the direction reversed; the first call lands the consent dialog in mid-game; quick-tier variance of one to four seconds would break the move rhythm if the move waited (it does not here, which is right).
critiques.what_i_would_add: Move the sentence to the hold: the player types only when he wants to argue ('But...'), the same prompt and the same validator, a tenth of the calls, and the consent dialog under a button. The silence and the 'Checked' mark survive as the hold's absence.

critiques.strengths: Honest about LLM necessity ('about 60 percent of looks could be served by a careful template') and ships the template as the no-capability path; token validation of every square in the sentence; cache false is unnecessary but harmless.
critiques.weaknesses: The LLM job is compressing a three-ply engine line into intent, the weakest necessity here; the ration and the refund are the pedagogy and they are engine rules. The first look brings the consent dialog, which is acceptable only because it is a tap.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A blind A/B in the stub harness: template versus Claude sentences for the same twenty verified looks, judged by Sambudh; drop Claude from this loop if the sentence is not clearly better.

critiques.strengths: Memory that changes live play with zero calls at the moment: the whisper is a stored sentence fired by an engine precondition. Five fixed labels validated against fact types; three instances before a habit whispers; the post-game call on default with no tools; counts and a templated sentence when Claude is absent.
critiques.weaknesses: It is a layer on a play loop that must exist first; a default-tier labelling call of 10-30 s with nothing on screen; sentences over-generalise from two examples; localStorage loses the habits between his laptop and his phone, which is exactly his case.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Run the labelling on quick (the input is a short list of flagged moves with fact types; naming needs no thinking), cache per game, a prompt version tag, and the habits in db plus user from iteration two.

critiques.strengths: The seams: coach.js resolves sample as window.__stubSample ?? claude.use('sample'), store.js hides db versus localStorage, and the scenario asserts zero sample calls before Why and the exact tool list after; Why? only on a tap; the game-end call on quick, cached 24 h keyed by the game id; the fallback sentence is engine-grounded so hiding Why on not_granted leaves a good product.
critiques.weaknesses: Tools highlight, arrow and evaluate on quick at a hold: two rounds is 'about two seconds' only if the worker is free, and evaluate at depth 12 inside a tool contends with the opponent's queued search. The prompt carries both cp numbers while instructing no numbers; the validator must enforce that. The hold question itself is template-only, which is fine, but then all of Claude's personalisation lives behind Why.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Drop evaluate from the hold's Why (the fact sheet already has the refutation), return squares and arrows in JSON, and add window.__stubErrors to app_check's stub so not_granted, rate_limited and invalid_json paths are driven in the same run.

critiques.strengths: The grounding lives in the page: show_line throws if a line presented as good scores more than 100 cp below best, so what the board shows cannot be wrong chess; try_line returns small plain data; the ledger of tried lines is the thinking indicator; a no-tools variant when limits() lacks tools.
critiques.weaknesses: Four rounds on quick is four to six seconds plus the consent dialog on the first chip; the quick tier may skip try_line and go straight to show_line, so the guard fires and the final text turns apologetic; every round re-reads the growing transcript.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Pre-compute the chip's engine answer (the line for 'what if this takes' at depth 12) and put it in the prompt, so the common case is one round with show_line only; keep try_line for the player's own idea.

critiques.strengths: The narrowest LLM job on the table: extraction only ({attacks, canTake, checks}) with the page deciding right and wrong from chess.js; 'I read: attacks f7' with a Fix link makes a misread visible; invalid_json shows Try again with no automatic retry; the three-tap fallback runs without Claude.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing on one move in four is friction for a thumb on a phone; the first 'Checked' raises the consent dialog mid-game; cache false is unnecessary because the sentence is in the input.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold it into the hold's 'But...': the extraction JSON becomes stage one of that prompt, so the squares he named light green or amber on the board before Claude's sentence arrives.

ranking: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)

merged_proposal.name: Hold On
merged_proposal.one_liner: A game against a soft engine where a move that would give a piece away is held in the air, you answer one question by tapping the board, and you can argue back in your own words: Claude reads your plan against facts the page computed first and answers it with a question, never a move.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction:
The held move you can argue with. One screen, 'Play': a tournament board with his white pieces at the bottom, one serif line above it, a 56 px action bar below that stays empty until a decision is needed. No eval bar, no move list, no rating, no chat box. The line at load: 'Your move. I'll only speak up if a piece is about to be lost.'

The hold (every partner proposed it; the coach's thresholds and the designer's beat are the version I take): when the engine gate finds that the move he just dropped loses material to a one-move reply, the piece does not land. It sits ghosted on the target square, the enemy piece that would take it glows, and the line reads a sentence the page templated from chess.js facts in one millisecond: 'Hold on. The king can take your bishop on f7, and nothing of yours protects it.' Under it, a question answered by tapping, never typing: 'What takes it? Tap the piece.' The action bar: Show me, Take it back, Play it anyway, But...

The new part is 'But...': the market skeptic's belief-reading moved to the one moment a beginner actually wants to talk, arguing for the move in his hand. He taps But..., a one-line field opens in the action bar ('Say what you were going for'; the OS keyboard's mic gives dictation for free), with the note 'Asks Claude on your account' the first time. He types 'it's check and I'm going for his king'. The line pulses 'Looking...' for about a second and a half. Claude, on the quick tier, with the fact sheet in the prompt and no tools, answers the plan: 'It is check, and he has to answer it. He answers by taking the bishop, because nothing of yours guards f7. After the king takes, what checks do you have left, and what do they win?' with f7, e8 and g5 lit from the squares it returned. One reply, no thread; the field closes; the four buttons remain. He looks (Ng5+ and the king walks away), taps Take it back, the bishop slides home, 'Good. Your move.' Silence resumes. This is not a chatbot next to a board: there is no open box, Claude speaks only when he presses a button, about nothing but the move in his hand, in two sentences that end in a question, and the board is the answer.

The first thirty seconds: 0 s, the board and the line. 0-5 s: 1.e4, Black's e5 slides in under half a second. 5-20 s: 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6; game one's Black follows a tiny book built from the verified lesson lines so a tempting move exists by move four, and Stockfish at Skill Level 1 takes over afterwards. Nothing is said. 20-24 s: he drops Bxf7+, check and a pawn. Hold. 24-28 s: Show me: the ghost king takes the bishop, a small '-2' floats up, a beat, everything slides back. 28-30 s: Take it back. (Verified in lesson 0001 at depth 20: 4.Bxf7+ cp_loss 371 with reply Kxf7; 4.Nxe5 cp_loss 335 with reply Nxe5; 4.d3 cp_loss 23.) He has read nothing, Claude has not been called, and no consent dialog has appeared.

What the engine does and why: Stockfish 18 lite in a Worker plus chess.js own every fact, instantly. The opponent (Skill Level 1, depth 6, a weighted pick among multipv 3 so it plays like a person at his level, but it always takes a hung piece worth two or more). The pre-search of the current position (depth 12, multipv 2) while he thinks. The verdict after the drop (depth 10 on the resulting position, about 0.3 s, while the piece visibly settles). The gate: cp loss of 200 or more AND the refutation is a capture or a check that wins material within two plies, or a mate in one allowed or missed, or a free capture of two points or more ignored; never a positional loss; suppressed when he is already five points down; at most one hold per two moves; after the second Play it anyway the coach is quiet until the end. The ghost refutation for Show me. The attackers and defenders behind every sentence. The grading of every tap. The per-move cp trace for the end card. The engine, not Claude, decides when the coach may speak.

What Claude does and why only Claude can: K1, after consent exists, the hold question: one quick sample.json call fired from the drop, returning {question, answer_squares, if_right, if_wrong}, swapped in for the template only if it arrives before his first tap; it chooses which of the three looks to ask about, varies with the position and his history line ('third time this week a knight went where a pawn attacks'), and never names the answer. K2, But...: reads the plan in his words, finds the belief that is false against the fact sheet, answers it in two sentences ending in a question, returns the squares to light; a template cannot read 'I'm going for his king'. K3, at game end, one quick call cached 24 h by game id: {one_thing of at most 18 words, next_game of at most 12 words} from the hold log and the last five games' category counts; the next game opens with that line ('Watch the pawns today.'). Claude never chooses or evaluates a move, never decides a hold, never types a FEN, never draws a square the page did not list.

Every chess claim is grounded twice. Before the call, facts(fen, move) computes the fact sheet (the landing square's attackers and defenders with values, his pieces left hanging after the move, the two-ply refutation, free captures missed, checks for both sides, the category code, the answer squares, the allowed squares, the listed moves) and the prompt contains nothing else, about 1.5 KB with one stable instruction block carrying a version tag. After the call, validate(reply, facts) requires squares to be a subset of the allowed set, no SAN token outside the listed moves, no signed decimal, none of blunder, mistake, inaccuracy or '??', a question that does not contain answer_squares, and word caps (20 for a question, 45 for a reply); a failure shows the template and increments window.__coachRejects, which the stub test asserts. Without Claude (sample null outside the viewer, declined, rate limited, any error) the hold, the question, the tap, Show me, Take it back, Play it anyway and the end card all run unchanged from templates; only But... is hidden, and nothing on the page looks missing.
merged_proposal.core_loop:
1. 'Your move.' While he thinks, the Worker searches the current position (depth 12, multipv 2) so the best move and its eval are known before he drops anything.
2. He drops a piece (tap-tap or drag). chess.js validates; the Worker runs depth 10 on the resulting position (about 0.3 s) while the piece visibly settles.
3. Gate silent: the piece lands, the bot replies in under a second. Silence is the reward. If he took a free piece: 'Free knight. You looked.' (template, no call).
4. Gate fires: the piece ghosts on its square, the attacker glows, the templated sentence and question appear at once from the chess.js facts. If claudeOk (a successful call already happened in this view), K1 fires with a fresh AbortController and its validated question swaps in only if it arrives before his first tap; otherwise no call is made.
5. He taps a square: chess.js grades it against answer_squares. Right: 'Yes. Pawn takes knight: a knight for a pawn.' Wrong: 'Not that one. Look at the pawns beside e5.', then the answer is drawn with an arrow. Or he taps Show me: the engine's refutation plays as ghost pieces with a '-2' float and rewinds.
6. Or he taps But...: one line typed; K2 on quick (1.5-2 s behind 'Looking...'); the validated reply appears with its squares lit and ends in a question; one reply only, the field closes. The first-ever call of the view happens here, under a button whose copy says 'Asks Claude on your account'; a success sets claudeOk; not_granted and its family set claudeOff and hide But... for the rest of the view; rate_limited hides it for a minute with 'Coach is resting.'; invalid_json turns the button into 'Try again' and the page never retries by itself.
7. He decides: Take it back (the piece slides home, 'Good. Your move.', nothing counted against him) or Play it anyway (commits; the bot punishes; one template line, 'There it goes. You saw it coming.'; counted on the end card, never nagged). Either tap aborts any pending K1 or K2 call.
8. The hold is logged as {fen, move, category, look, outcome, tapsToAnswer} through store.js (localStorage in the MVP, db plus user in iteration two).
9. Game over (mate, or the bot resigns a queen down so games actually end): the end card shows counts from the log ('Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4). Times you held on: 3.') and the worst moment as a small board. If claudeOk, K3 fires (quick, cache gcTime 24 h keyed by game id) and writes the one thing under the counts; otherwise a single button, 'One thing for next game', requests it. Template fallback: the category with the highest count, in words.
10. Play again: the next game opens with the stored next_game line (zero calls); the bot goes one notch harder only after a game with zero pieces given away.

Budget and latency: a typical game is 0-6 K1 calls (hard cap 6), 0-3 K2, 1 K3, each about 1.5 KB on quick; no default tier anywhere in the MVP; never more than one call in flight; the beat never waits on Claude; the consent dialog only ever appears under a button he pressed.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice:
One page, no build step, served by python3 -m http.server and published with files: app/index.html, app/styles.css (tokens on :root, dark via prefers-color-scheme guarded by :root:not([data-theme=light]) and again under :root[data-theme=dark], buff-and-green board, serif coach line, 16 px gutters at 400 px), app/pieces.svg, app/src/{main,board,game,engine,facts,templates,coach,validate,store,ui}.js, app/data/book.json (game-one Black replies from the verified lesson lines), app/vendor as is. engine.js: one Worker behind a serialized command queue, the pre-search and the verdict. facts.js: the fact sheet, the category code, answer and allowed squares, listed moves; used by templates.js, coach.js, validate.js and the tests, so there is one source of truth for every sentence. coach.js: sample = window.__stubSample ?? await window.claude?.use?.('sample'); three prompt builders (K1, K2, K3) sharing one instruction block with a version tag; one in-flight AbortController; the claudeOk and claudeOff flags; the error table (not_granted, sampling_disabled, not_declared, capability_disabled, capability_removed: off for the view, no message; rate_limited: But... hidden for 60 s, holds template-only; invalid_json: 'Try again' on the button; refused, empty_completion, upstream_error: template for this moment; cancelled: nothing). validate.js as specified in the interaction.

In the slice: play White against the bot at Skill Level 1; the hold for the capture category only (a piece left attacked-and-undefended or attacked by a pawn, net loss of two points or more, the refutation a capture, cp loss 200 or more at depth 10); the ghost Show me; tap-to-answer; Take it back; Play it anyway; But... (K2); K1 after consent; the end card with counts and K3; the localStorage log; light and dark at 400 px. Out of the slice: playing Black; a separate Why? button (But... with an empty line serves as Why); the default-tier 'Read my game' call with show_position(ply) and check(ply, move) tools restricted to this game's plies (iteration two, with a Stop button and progress from inside execute); db plus user; the Mira voice; the habit whisper; PGN download; a strength setting.

Acceptance, driven by Playwright through scripts/app_check.js with a scenario file, and with window.__stubErrors added to its stub: (a) Italian after 3...Nf6 (r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/RNBQK2R w KQkq - 4 4): 4.Bxf7+ holds, the pulse set is {e8, f7}, the template sentence names f7, window.__sampleCalls is empty; 4.Nxe5 holds with answer square c6; 4.d3 passes in silence. (b) Italian after 6...d6 (r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2NP1N2/PPP2PPP/R1BQ1RK1 w - - 0 7): 7.Nxe5 holds, tapping d6 is graded right, Show me plays Nxe5 dxe5 and rewinds to the same FEN; 7.Bxf7+ holds; 7.h3 is silent. (c) Ruy after 3...a6 (r1bqkbnr/1ppp1ppp/p1n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/RNBQK2R w KQkq - 0 4): 4.O-O holds with category ignored_attack; 4.Ba4 is silent. (d) Tap But..., type a line: __sampleCalls[0].opts.modelTier === 'quick' and tools is []; the stub JSON's say appears with its squares lit; a second stub reply with squares ['h8'] gives __coachRejects === 1 and the template stands; a third containing the word 'blunder' is rejected the same way. (e) After (d), the next hold makes a K1 call and the question swaps before any tap; a hold followed at once by Take it back shows a cancelled call and no stale swap. (f) __stubErrors = [{code: 'not_granted'}]: But... hidden, the hold unchanged. (g) --no-stub: But... absent, everything else identical. (h) Four screenshots with no horizontal overflow and zero console errors, plus a copy test that greps every string in the page for blunder, mistake, inaccuracy and '??'.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: Novelty: nobody holds a move in the air and lets you argue for it. Chess.com and Lichess mark the blunder afterwards, the chat-with-Stockfish apps make you ask, and this repo's own coach.py printed 'Your knight on g4 is undefended!' after the move was committed. The held piece is the new feeling; 'But...' is the new conversation, and it is the one place on the whole table where the LLM is load-bearing rather than decorative: reading a beginner's plan in his own words and finding the belief that is false. Beginner value: the gate fires only on what loses games under 1000 (the coach's band belief encoded as a rule), silence is the default, Take it back carries no shame, and the memory line names the habit in his words. Feasibility: one page, one Worker, one in-flight call, three quick prompts sharing one fact sheet and one validator, no default tier, no tools, no accounts; every acceptance position is already verified at depth 20 in lesson 0001; the stub harness already exists and needs one extra hook. Delight: the piece that will not land, the ghost king taking and sliding back, and the first time he types 'but it's check' and gets back a question instead of a verdict. From my discipline specifically: the cost is a few quick calls a game, each under two kilobytes; the consent dialog only ever appears under a button he pressed; the beat never waits on Claude; a wrong square can never reach the board; and with Claude absent the product is the same game minus one button, which is the test every LLM feature here has to pass before it ships. The iteration path is already laid: db plus user and Black in iteration two along with the once-per-game default-tier 'Read my game' with plies-restricted tools, the habit whisper from What You Keep Doing in iteration three, and the two-chair drill built from his own holds after that.

reviews.persona: The beginner: Sambudh's stand-in. Rated under 1000 once, studied nothing, opens 1.e4, lost most games to pieces taken for free without knowing why, and has closed every chess app that showed an evaluation bar. I don't know what "defends", "cp" or "R2" mean; I know "takes", "a knight for a pawn", and the feeling of a piece disappearing. I judge every concept by two moments: the second before I let go of a piece, and the second after I lose one.

critiques.strengths: "Your move. I'll stay quiet unless it matters." is the first line in this whole pile I would believe, and the silence on the other ninety percent of moves is the reward. I answer by tapping squares, never typing. "That's the one." when I find it myself. The scripted first game so something hangs by move five is sneaky and right: I get the hold in thirty seconds without knowing it was arranged. It stops interrupting after my second "play anyway", so it knows when to shut up. The end screen is small boards, not a list.
critiques.weaknesses: "What defends e5?" is still coach language; the first time I honestly don't know what "defends" means precisely and I'd tap at random. The gate goes quiet when I'm five points down ("we'll look at this one afterwards"): when I'm losing badly is exactly when I want the hand on my wrist, don't abandon me because I'm losing. "The Beginner bot resigns a queen down": I've never seen a bot resign and I'd think the page broke. The threshold is all centipawns, fine as long as I never see one.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ask the day-one question in day-one words: "Hold on. If the knight lands there, what takes it? Tap it." "Takes" I understand today; "defends" I'll understand by day three, so start with the taker and move to the defender later. And never go quiet because I'm losing; go quiet because I keep pressing "play anyway", which is a different thing.

critiques.strengths: Punish, then prevent. I would never think to look at my own move from the other side, and the second half (come back one move earlier and play something that doesn't allow it) is the half that would actually show up in my games. "A bishop for nothing." is the right sentence. Every position is verified, so I never get taught a wrong one.
critiques.weaknesses: It opens flipped with "You're Black. Punish it." and I'd spend the first ten seconds working out which way my pawns go. Ten positions last two bus rides. "Passes if within 50 cp of best": if I take the bishop with the wrong piece I fail a puzzle I solved and I won't know why. Underneath it is puzzles, and I don't do puzzles because I'm bad at them; that's the thing it has to overcome and it doesn't say how.
critiques.what_i_would_add: For the first three puzzles, a label on the board itself, not above it: "You are Black. Your pawns go this way" with an arrow, and a ring on my king for two seconds after every flip. Accept any capture that wins the piece, and if there was a cheaper way say "Yes. The pawn does it for less." instead of failing me.

critiques.strengths: Three, not thirty. "Four of your last six hung pieces were to a pawn. Pawns are the ones you don't see." is the one sentence in this whole document I'd still remember a week later. The rule-based three show instantly and Claude's nicer wording replaces them, so I'm never staring at a spinner. Day one isn't an empty shell.
critiques.weaknesses: It needs my games, and on day one it's someone else's. "R2", "R3", "harder next visit, no highlights" is teacher-speak, and it means opening the page is opening a test. The PGN paste box: I don't know what a PGN is or where Chess.com hides it. Thirty to sixty seconds of "Reading your game..." right after a loss: I've closed the tab by then.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Never open on the test. Open on Play, and put "your three" at the end of a game, after the result, as ONE board (the worst one) with "Two more" as a small link. Make the headline a count I understand: "Pieces given away last game: 2. Here they are."

critiques.strengths: The best first thirty seconds anywhere here: it opens mid-position and says "Your move. Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7." I'm invited to blunder on purpose, I learn what a hold is before anything is at stake, and the consent dialog doesn't appear until I already know why Claude is being asked. Amber, never red. "Relief, not shame." "Free knight. You looked." The template shows instantly and Claude's version only swaps in if it arrives within 2.5 s, so the floating piece never stalls on me. "A square you chose to play anyway is never held again that game." It looks like a chess board, not an AI app.
critiques.weaknesses: "That pawn on e4 has a friend. Tap what guards it." is cute and I wouldn't know what it means; "guards" has the same problem as "defends". The 30-90 s "One thing from this game" call is a long time to sit on a result screen after losing. The gate at 150 cp is looser than the coach's 200; from my chair, every hold on something that isn't a whole piece brings the day I switch it off closer.
critiques.what_i_would_add: In the tutorial, after I take it back, let me try the same tempting move once more and press "Play it anyway" so I feel the king take the bishop, then rewind. Two reps: one to take back, one to feel it. Forty-five seconds instead of thirty, and I've pressed both buttons before the real game starts.

critiques.strengths: "Now you are Black. Punish that, if you can." and then taking my own knight and reading "You just caught yourself." Laughing at my own blunder instead of flinching is new. Five dots instead of a score; a hollow dot when I had to be shown. The hint names no square.
critiques.weaknesses: The flip, every single position, on a phone. "You are White. Make a move." on a cold position with no story: which move? I'd grab whatever's grabbable because that's the trap, fine, but it feels like being set up. The MISSED loop ("There was something. Keep looking?") is where I get stuck and feel stupid. Positions from my own games need a play loop that doesn't exist here; on its own it's five puzzles with a twist.
critiques.what_i_would_add: After every flip, the first thing on screen for two seconds is "You are Black now. Your king is here." with a ring on the king, before any question. Without that I don't know who I am.

critiques.strengths: "Pick up any piece. See what happens before it happens." I understand it in five seconds. The dashed "They would play this" arrow half a second later is x-ray vision. Nothing is a number; everything is drawn.
critiques.weaknesses: It's training wheels that run the look for me: amber rings on pick-up for every square I could be taken on IS the blunder check, done by the page, every move. In a game that's cheating and I'd never learn to do it myself; after a game it's an analysis board with nicer colours. "You move both sides" by default: I'd lose track of whose turn it is. Chess.com's assisted mode already draws threat arrows, so to me this isn't that new.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make it a reward, not a mode: after a hold or after a loss, one button, "See it again, slowly", opens the ghost view on that one position only. A playground you earn by getting caught.

critiques.strengths: A named opponent who talks like a person: "That pawn hits your bishop. Move it or I take it." and then "Answered." when I do. I'd feel seen and I'd move the bishop. Nothing said in quiet positions. "Free knight, thank you." is funny and stings exactly right. The squares glow while she talks.
critiques.weaknesses: If Mira tells me every threat I never learn to look, and the fade-out is iteration two, by which time I'm hooked on her. Six to twelve Claude calls a game, and the consent dialog pops mid-game at her first sentence; I'd think she was asking permission to cheat. "Your rook has to give itself up": I don't know what that means. And she only talks about HER threats; she never stops MY hand, and I lose more games by hanging pieces than by missing threats.
critiques.what_i_would_add: From game one Mira only speaks when I tap her ("What are you up to?"), three taps a game. And right after she takes a piece I hung, a "Wait, what?" tap replays the capture as a ghost before it's final. Somewhere there has to be a hand on my wrist or she's a talking bot.

critiques.strengths: "This is where it turned." with the board sliding to the one move. "Before you take something, look at what takes it back." is a sentence I'd stick on the wall. Grading what I MEANT rather than the move name. "Nothing turned this game; well played." when nothing did.
critiques.weaknesses: A text field after a lost game, "Say, in a sentence, what you should have looked at." I just lost; I'm not writing an essay, and Skip feels like the F. Ten to thirty seconds of default-tier wait with a progress bar sliding along a move list I can't read. "Two more moments from this game" is the list creeping back in. The numbers stay in the prompt, good, but the move list is on screen.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the answer a tap by default ("Tap what should have stopped you.") and hide the sentence behind "Say it in words". Show the template one-thing card instantly and let Claude's nicer one replace it; never make me wait for the first card.

critiques.strengths: "Is it safe?" is literally the question in my head on every move, and it's a chip, not a chat box. The arrow from the attacker appears BEFORE the sentence finishes: the page saw what I felt. The quiz-back ("First: tap the piece that attacks your bishop.") makes me look before it tells me. Template answers when Claude isn't there, so nothing looks broken.
critiques.weaknesses: In a real game it's a free "is it safe?" on every piece: I'd tap it before every move and never run the look myself, and each first tap is a paid call. "What is it doing?" is going to be bland ("keeps your pieces off d4" means nothing to me). There's no game here; it's a side feature looking for a loop.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ration it in a game (three "Is it safe?" per game, refunded when the answer is yes, like the skeptic's looks) and make it unlimited after the game. And one more chip that only appears while I'm holding a piece mid-move: "What if I go here?", because that's the moment I'm actually asking.

critiques.strengths: My own, so I'll be honest about what's good in it: "Show me": his pawn slides over, takes, a small "-2" floats off my side, a beat, everything slides home, no words. "But...": arguing back in my own words and getting an answer about MY plan ("You are, and it's a good idea. But it's his move first"). The end card counts pieces given away, the only number I understand. "Play it anyway: counted, never nagged."
critiques.weaknesses: Four buttons on a hold (Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway / But...) is a lot of thumb on a phone; the designer's two-button bar is calmer. My hold sentence gives the answer straight away ("His knight on c6 takes yours back"); the coach is right that making me tap the taker first is what sticks. The pre-compute is hand-waved. And mine has no tutorial, so my first hold is also my first consent dialog.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The one thing from mine I'd fight to keep: the "-2" that floats off my side of the board during the ghost. Piece points are the single number I can feel, and watching it drift away without actually losing the piece is the whole lesson in one second.

critiques.strengths: "Play from here." Winning the game I lost from the exact position where I lost it, with the exact move I missed, is the thing I want most after a loss. The tape-rewind, his last move replaying so I see it arrive, a question instead of a verdict. "Nothing was given away for free this game. It was lost slowly, which is a different lesson." is honest.
critiques.weaknesses: Twenty to forty seconds of "Looking back over the game..." after a loss, while I'm sad. The engine's worst moment and the one I FELT was the problem can differ, and then I don't trust the rewind. "Answered" meaning "kept the piece" not "won": right, but I'd win the replay and still be told the game was lost, and that stings.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One big button on the end card: "Play it again from where it went wrong." If a hold fired that game, the position is already known from the hold log and nothing has to load; the scoring pass is only for games where I never got held.

critiques.strengths: One position, one question, one tap, forty seconds. "Copied. They'll see the same board and the same question." This is the only thing in the list I would actually send to a friend, because it's a question, not my score. "Day N" counts days played, not days in a row, so a missed day doesn't scold.
critiques.weaknesses: Six seed positions last a week. Day one is someone else's position and "Your own positions start after five games" is a promise, not a feature. It's a layer on a play loop; alone it's a nice daily puzzle. The question kinds will go samey fast if it's always "tap the attacked piece".
critiques.what_i_would_add: Let me share from a hold mid-game: "Send this one" on the hold card. The best moment to share isn't the daily, it's the moment I nearly blundered and caught it. "Can you see it?" to a friend is bragging that costs nothing.

critiques.strengths: The ring that shrinks as I stop needing it, until one day it's gone: that's the first progress bar I'd feel in my hands, with no number. "Looked." as a one-word chip when I drag a piece back. The opponent's voice only on tap. The bot hangs a minor piece now and then so I get to be the one who looks and takes. "You did not need the hold for 31 moves."
critiques.weaknesses: The hold is a beat on EVERY move, even when nothing is wrong. Ten moves in, that beat is lag and I'm tapping through it without looking, which kills the point. The their-chair pulse on every drop is the blunder check done for me, same crutch as Ghost Moves. The end card asks "What did my last move attack?" where "my" means the bot's; I'd be confused whose "my".
critiques.what_i_would_add: Hold only when something is actually hanging (the coach's gate), but keep the shrinking ring as the thing I watch across games: its size is how often the page had to catch me in the last five games. The ring shrinks because I needed it less, not because the wait got shorter.

critiques.strengths: Taking my own knight with my own finger, and the "-2" on the board edge. "Comfortable? Mine is the better chair, I think.": one joke a game and I'd tell people about it. "No chairs today. A real game." as a named event. Rewind and Play it anyway are both real, unscolded options.
critiques.weaknesses: The board rotates every time I hang something; in a bad game that's five rotations and I'm seasick even with the cap. The budget shrinking is framed as graduation, but the first time I hang a piece and no chair comes I'll feel dropped. "What would you take?" when two things are takeable, then "There was a bigger one": now I'm failing at punishing myself.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the chair the second option, never automatic: the hold fires, the piece hovers, and the buttons are "Show me" (ghost capture, no flip) and "Sit in their chair" (flip, take it myself). First-timers press Show me, the brave take the chair, nobody gets spun round by surprise.

critiques.strengths: Tapping looks instead of finding moves means the answer is never a move I can't find. The streak as grey grids, not a broken chain. "This is from your game last night." when it finally is.
critiques.weaknesses: Day one assumes I already know the three looks. "Any checks on the board, theirs or yours? Tap the piece that could give one, or None.": I don't yet know what "give a check" means from the other side, and None as a tap target is odd. The grid I'd share means nothing to a friend who doesn't play; Wordle's grid works because everyone plays Wordle. Thirty verified positions before day one is real work, and it looks like a puzzle app.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Looks unlock like levels: day one asks ONE look ("Their knight just moved. Tap what it's attacking."), the second arrives after I've got that right five times, the third after that. And the share is the position with "can you see it?", not a grid.

critiques.strengths: Honestly the newest idea in the pile: the coach reads what I BELIEVE and finds the gap ("You saw the threat to f2. Before you guard it: what does your h3 pawn attack right now?"). No app has ever argued with my reasoning instead of my move. Silence when I'm right. "That one was yours."
critiques.weaknesses: A text box under the board before every move. I will not type before every move on a phone, and the skeptic says so himself (80 percent skip). Worse, "Say your check": to me "check" means the king is attacked, so I'd type "no check" every time and be wrong about the question itself. The first frame has an input and a Move button: that's a form, not a game. Moves "listed faintly above the board" is notation I can't read on screen one.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep the belief-reading, lose the toll. The only time I type is when a hold fires and I disagree: "But...". THEN Claude reads my sentence against the facts and asks the question that exposes the gap. Same LLM job, a tenth of the typing, at the one moment I actually have something to say.

critiques.strengths: The refund ("Nothing for me there. I would probably just bring a piece out.") teaches me that most of my moves are fine, which nobody has ever told me. Three looks a game is a real decision I'd think about. "Thanks." from the opponent when I'm about to give up a bishop is a good small shock.
critiques.weaknesses: "Your knight check on g5 I answer with Kg8" is a three-ply line in words, and I lose the thread at "I answer with". The flip on every look. The author admits it's a hint machine in a costume and that the LLM barely earns its place. The post-game "which three would you spend" screen is where the learning lives, and it's cut from the slice.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Spend the ration on "Is it safe?" instead of on a flip-and-monologue: three per game, refunded when the piece is fine. And when a look finds something, show it as the ghost capture on MY side of the board, no flip, no sentence needed.

critiques.strengths: "Your habit. A pawn can reach something of yours." before I move, nothing highlighted: a whisper about ME, timed. "You stopped doing that." with the habit crossing itself out is the thing that would bring me back on day eight. Habits as sentences, not a radar chart.
critiques.weaknesses: Day one is three placement positions where I type "why": I'm being tested before I've played a game. Nothing personal happens for three games. Per-browser storage loses my habits the day I switch from laptop to phone, which is exactly what I'd do. A whisper that fires when my move was fine teaches me to ignore the whisper.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The whisper should be one word on the board edge, not a sentence: "Pawns." By the time I've read "Your habit. A pawn can reach something of yours." I've stopped looking at the board. One word, one habit, once a game.

critiques.strengths: "Nothing. Take it back" as the big button, because the right answer to "after they take back, what can you take?" is often nothing, and tapping around finding nothing is the lesson. Two squares pulse. Why? hidden when there's no Claude, with a fallback sentence good enough that nothing looks missing. Tap-tap as the main path, drag as a bonus. SVG pieces so it doesn't look like text on my phone. "0 pieces hung. Two holds, both taken back." is the right end card.
critiques.weaknesses: "Before this goes: after they take back with the king, what can you take?" is a two-step question: I have to hold the imagined position in my head, which is the exact thing I can't do yet. The held piece sits ON the square, dimmed; I'd think the move went through. The engine loading 2-4 s on a phone means the first bot move waits; fine only if the page says so.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Play the imagined step for me on the board as a ghost (their king takes, half-opacity) BEFORE asking "now what can you take?", so the two-step question becomes a one-step look. And keep the held piece visibly off the square, floating with a shadow, not on it dimmed.

critiques.strengths: The pieces move by themselves to answer me: ghost bishop takes, ghost king takes back, a caption per move, everything slides home "as if a friend had reached over the board". Chips, not typing. The page refuses to show a losing line as good.
critiques.weaknesses: Four quick rounds is five seconds of "Trying it..." on my turn and I'd tap again. The "tried Bxf7+ Kxf7" ledger is notation on screen. Three chips on every piece tap during a game is the hint button in disguise; I'd use it every move. It overlaps Point at It and Ghost Moves almost completely.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold it into the hold's "Show me" button, the one place I'm already waiting, and make the engine's own refutation the ghost line with no Claude round trip. Claude only writes the caption per ghost move if it arrives in time. Instant ghost, words optional.

critiques.strengths: My own words lighting up squares ("bishop hits f7" and f7 goes green) is a real moment: the first time my reasoning has ever been visible on the board. "I read: attacks f7" with a Fix link so I can see what it understood. The three-tap fallback without Claude.
critiques.weaknesses: The board REFUSES my move until I type ("the drop is refused with a gentle shake"). That's a locked door, one move in four, on a phone with the keyboard covering the board. A "Checked" button is a form. I'd type "nothing" to get through, they know it, and then the amber marks shame me for it. The first consent dialog arrives mid-game when the band appears.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Flip it: the board never locks. The band is an invitation after a hold ("Tell me what you saw") that lights squares green and amber, same magic, no door. And accepting taps on squares as the sentence should be the default, with typing as the option.

merged_proposal.name: Hold On
merged_proposal.one_liner: A game against a bot that plays like me, where a move that gives a piece away won't land: it hovers, I find the taker with my thumb, I can watch it happen as a ghost or argue back in my own words, and I take it back with no mark against me.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction: The half-placed move you can argue with. I drop my knight on e5. It doesn't land: it floats with a shadow, the board dims one shade, the d6 pawn glows amber (nothing on this page is ever red), and one serif line under the board says "Hold on. If the knight lands there, what takes it? Tap it." I tap d6: "That pawn. A knight for a pawn." Now four things can happen and all four are mine. Show me: his pawn slides over and takes, a small "-2" floats off my side of the board, a beat, everything slides home, no words. Take it back: the knight floats home, "Good. Your move.", nothing recorded against me. Play it anyway: counted, never nagged, and after the second one the coach goes quiet until the end. But...: the only text box in the product, and it only exists inside a hold. I type "I'm attacking his king" and the coach answers my plan, not a number: "You are, and the bishop on c4 is already pointing there. But it's his move first, and the d6 pawn takes the knight before you get there. Is there a square that still looks at f7 but no pawn can reach?", with d6, e5 and f7 lit. No product holds the move; none lets me answer with my thumb; none lets me push back in my own words and get an answer about MY idea that the engine checked before it was said. And on the other ninety percent of moves: silence. The silence is the reward, and it is the only reason I'll believe the coach when it speaks.
merged_proposal.core_loop: 1. "Your move." I move, tap-tap or drag; legal squares show as faint dots. 2. The engine judges silently (it searched my position to depth 12 while I was thinking; one depth-10 search on the result). Clean: the piece lands, the bot replies in under a second. If I took a free piece: "Free knight. You looked." 3. If my move leaves a piece capturable for a net loss of two or more to a one-move capture (cp loss of 200 or more, engine reply is a capture or a mate in one): HOLD. The template line shows instantly; Claude's question swaps in only if it arrives within 2.5 s. 4. I answer by tapping. Right: "That's the one." Wrong: "Not that one. Look at the pawns next to e5.", then the taker glows. When the honest answer is nothing, a button says "Nothing. Take it back". 5. Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway / But... 6. The bot replies (Skill 1-3; it always takes what I hang; it hangs a minor piece of its own every eight to twelve moves so I get to be the one who looks and takes). 7. Game over: one card, in pieces, not points: "Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4). Times I held your hand: 3." The worst played-anyway moment as a small board with one button: "Play it again from here." 8. "Again." The bot steps up a notch only when I gave nothing away. The two counts going down are what I come back for.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/vendor, a day's build. Opener (the designer's): the page opens on 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 with "Your move. Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7." Canned hold copy, no Claude call, no consent dialog; I tap e8, take it back, then play it anyway once to feel the king take the bishop and watch it rewind (two reps), then "That is all I do. Now a real game." Board: tap-tap and drag in one pointer path, legal dots, 150 ms slides, buff-and-green squares, inline SVG pieces, serif coach line, one action bar, 400 px, both themes via tokens, prefers-reduced-motion honoured.
