Bot: Stockfish worker at Skill 1-2, depth 6, multipv 3 with a weighted second or third choice so it sometimes hangs a minor piece and never its queen. Gate: ONE category only, from chess.js attackers and defenders plus the engine: my move leaves a piece capturable for a net loss of two or more points with a one-move capture refutation (cp loss of 200 or more at depth 10-12 AND the engine's reply is a capture); positional losses never hold. Hold UI: the piece floats with a shadow off the square, the attacker glows amber, the template question shows at once ("Hold on. If the knight lands there, what takes it? Tap it."), Claude's question arrives via sample.json on the quick tier and is validated (answer squares a subset of the engine's set, question names no answer square, else the template stands), tap-to-answer graded by chess.js, "Nothing. Take it back" when the answer is nothing. Show me plays the engine's own refutation as a ghost capture with the "-2" floating off my side, then reverts; no Claude needed. Take it back and Play it anyway. But... is a one-line box that makes one quick call with highlight(squares) and play_ghost(moves, two plies max) as tools, two sentences, ends with a question, hidden when sample is null. "Free knight. You looked." End card with the two counts in localStorage and "Play it again from here", which resumes against the bot from the hold's stored FEN (no scoring pass needed). window.__stubSample for Playwright. Acceptance test from the verified lesson positions: after 3...Nf6, Bxf7+ and Nxe5 hold and d3 passes; after 6...d6, Nxe5 and Bxf7+ hold and h3 passes; Ruy after 3...a6, O-O holds and Ba4 passes; a copy test fails on the words blunder, mistake, inaccuracy or "??" anywhere on the page. Not in the slice: board flip, daily, share link, db, memory line, typing before moves, eval bar, move list, ratings, any number that is not a piece count.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: Four of the six partners drew the same thing without talking to each other (coach, designer, me, architect), and the other two put the same hold inside their concepts (Both Ways' ring, Change Chairs' trigger). That's the team's consensus, which means every discipline can already see the moment and it can be built in a day. It's new in a way I can say in one breath, "the move won't land and you can argue with it", and a friend looking over my shoulder would get it without a word. The LLM is used only where language is: phrasing the question in my words and answering my "But..." (the skeptic's one real insight, reading my belief, moved to the single moment I'd actually type); the engine does everything else, so the coach can never be wrong about chess and can never stall the beat. It meets me in exactly the two moments I named: the second before I let go, and the second after I lose a piece ("Play it again from here"). The number it counts is one I can feel going down. It's silent most of the time, which is the only way I'll trust it when it speaks. And the next iterations are already on the table from the others: "Send this one" from a hold (Can You See It), the ring that shrinks across games (Both Ways), "You stopped doing that" with db plus user (What You Keep Doing), and "Sit in their chair" as the brave option next to Show me (Change Chairs).

critiques.strengths: The strictest gate in the set (200 cp AND a capture-or-check refutation AND not already five points down) is exactly the tuning a designer wants, because an interrupt that fires on positional losses would be a nag by game three. The scripted beginner tree for game one is a tutorial level in disguise: something hangs by move five whichever natural moves he plays. The bot resigns a queen down, so games actually end. Answering by tapping squares is a verb, not a reading task, and 'That's the one.' is good juice. 'After the second play-anyway the coach goes quiet' is the right anti-nag rule.
critiques.weaknesses: 'On the other ninety percent of moves nothing happens at all' is a game with no reward schedule. The player who finds the free knight gets the same silence as the player who walked past it; silence is the right response to a neutral move, not to a good one. The opponent is Stockfish at Skill Level 1, which plays alien moves and after move six rarely leaves anything free, so the predator half of the lesson ('what can I take?') never gets prey. The end screen is small boards and two sentences; nothing is felt going down from game to game. No social hook at all.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A reward beat for the predator look: when he captures a piece the bot left free, it pops off with a small '+3' and one line, 'Free knight. You looked.' And a gift rate in the bot (a verified-free minor piece roughly one move in eight, falling as his catch rate rises) so that look has something to find. The end card then counts the two numbers he understands: pieces given away (against last game) and pieces caught.

critiques.strengths: Punish-then-prevent is a two-act puzzle with a real reversal, and the flip is a physical verb a beginner remembers. One position in six with nothing to punish keeps the look honest instead of becoming 'find the capture'. The engine as the only judge of 'prevent' (cp loss under 100, nothing left hanging, top three shown afterwards) stops the second act feeling arbitrary.
critiques.weaknesses: As a game it is a puzzle app with a flip: no opponent, no stakes, no win state, and ten built-in positions is two sessions. The second act has no juice: any safe move passes, so the reward is 'Saved. Next.' every time. 'Make ten from my game' is a 30 to 60 s wait for the only version that is personal, and it needs games that do not exist on day one.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make it the daily, not the product, and seed it from the player's own holds in the play loop. Score a set as a row of small chairs turned to face away rather than '8 of 10', so a finished set reads as chairs he no longer needs.

critiques.strengths: The mastery loop (R1 with the squares lit, R2 without, R3 the same mistake in a position he has never seen) is spaced repetition that is felt as 'that moment closed'. 'Pawns: none this week.' is progression a player hears rather than reads off a bar. The rule-based three appearing instantly with Claude's phrasing swapping in later is the right latency design.
critiques.weaknesses: It is homework after the game, on a second screen, with a 30 to 90 s default-tier call at the exact moment a player wants 'Again'. R3 silently reverting to R2 when generation fails looks like the feature is missing. It needs games first, so on day one it is a demo with three borrowed positions.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Deliver the review inside play: the next game opens with the moment's one line, and the first hold of that game asks the stored question. Let one of the three be 'Play from here' so the player re-enters the lost game at the moment instead of answering about it.

critiques.strengths: The canned first hold ('Your move. Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7.') is a tutorial level in twenty seconds with no consent dialog and no Claude, on a verified position. 'Free knight. You looked.' is the only Hold On variant that rewards the predator look. 'A square you chose to play anyway is never held again that game' kills nagging with one rule. The 2.5 s swap rule protects the beat, amber instead of red protects the feeling, and Easier / Like me / Harder is a dial the player understands.
critiques.weaknesses: The opponent is a risk-list item ('must be tuned against Sambudh's real games') rather than a mechanic, so the hardest game-design problem is deferred. Nothing is felt across games except a games sheet with PGN downloads. No social hook. 'One thing from this game' is a 30 to 90 s wait at the end of a session, which is where most players close the page.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The gift rate and the resign rule in the bot so games are winnable and instructive; the hold's pulse visibly smaller across games as the hold rate falls; and 'Send this one' on the end screen carrying the game's moment as a question for a friend.

critiques.strengths: 'Make a move, the board turns, punish yourself' is lesson 0001 phase 3 made physical, and 'You just caught yourself.' is the first time a beginner laughs at a blunder. Five dots with a hollow one for 'needed to be shown' is a kind score. The hint from Black's side that names no square is well restrained.
critiques.weaknesses: A drill of twelve positions with no opponent: the player never experiences his move being punished by someone else, which is the fear the habit is built to answer. A hollow dot is a cost with nothing at stake. Without own games it goes stale in a week and reads as puzzles with a rotation.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold the chair into the play loop as the consequence of 'Play it anyway', so the swap happens inside a game with stakes and the drill version becomes the daily.

critiques.strengths: See-before-commit is pure direct manipulation, and the dashed 'They would play this' arrow arriving half a second after the ghost is x-ray delight. Never red, no eval bar, no engine lines in text: restraint a designer respects.
critiques.weaknesses: A sandbox with no goal, no pressure, no progression and no end: a toy. Consequence rings on every pickup make the look automatic and therefore never learned; in a real game it is a crutch, outside one it is an analysis board with nicer colours. Nothing to come back for tomorrow.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ration the ghost inside a real game: one ghost per game, spent on demand, refunded when the ghost shows nothing was wrong. Seeing the future becomes a resource the player learns to stop needing.

critiques.strengths: Mira is a character, and characters carry retention in a way a 'coach' never does. 'Answered.' is a reward for defending, which almost no concept here gives. Adapting Skill Level on hung-piece count rather than on results is the right dial. The five-in-a-row fade-out is felt progression: the voice goes quiet because you no longer need it.
critiques.weaknesses: A push-telegraph is the player being told the look six to twelve times a game; dependence is the whole risk and the fade-out is not in the MVP. The bubble lands about 1.5 s after Mira's move, which interrupts the rhythm of a fast game. Mira never leaves anything free, so the player is prey only and never gets to be the one who looks and takes.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Mira hangs pieces on purpose at a tuned rate, verified free by the engine, so she is a rival of his level and not a wall; and after game one her voice becomes pull-based (tap her name) with a small ration of free pushes, so hearing the threat costs something.

critiques.strengths: One question about the move that lost the game, not a list, is the right size for this band. The re-ask three games later without the glow and the about-you line after five games are a real memory. 'Nothing turned this game; well played.' is an honest empty state.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing a reason on a phone after a loss, with Skip, is friction at the lowest-energy moment of the session. A 10 to 30 s default-tier wait while the board slides is where the player taps away. The first frame is a review of a demo game he did not play, which is a report about someone else.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Tap-a-move as the primary answer and typing only as the 'But...' path when he disagrees; and the re-ask delivered inside the next game as the first hold's question, so the memory is felt during play.

critiques.strengths: Chips instead of a chat box, the arrow drawn from the facts before the sentence arrives, the quiz-back answered by a tap: all of it keeps the board as the interface. The attack ring on a threatened piece is a quiet, useful tell.
critiques.weaknesses: Not a loop: nothing changes from asking, no stakes, no win. Every first chip tap is a paid call and a curious player taps thirty times a game. 'What is it doing?' is bland because it has no engine fact behind it. It competes with the hold for the same bubble and the same quick-call slot.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the chips a per-game resource inside the play loop: three questions a game, refunded when the answer was 'safe', so asking has a cost and the player learns which pieces are worth asking about.

critiques.strengths: 'Show me' with his pawn sliding over, taking, a small '-2' floating up, a beat, and everything sliding back is the best piece of juice in the whole set. 'But...' is motivated typing: he is arguing, not doing homework, and the coach ends with a question. The end card 'Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4)' is a number he understands going down. The bot goes a notch harder only when he hung zero pieces, which ties difficulty to the lesson rather than to wins. The copy rule enforced by a test that fails on 'blunder' is a designer's rule.
critiques.weaknesses: Four buttons on the hold card at 400 px is one too many for a beat. The bot's weakening (Skill Level plus random second choices) is the right instinct but random hangs are not verified free, so some gifts will be traps. No social hook. The mid-game '?' chip is a second system next to the hold.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The chair as the 'Play it anyway' path, so the consequence is his own hand; and the hold's pulse shrinking across games so improvement is seen on the board, not only on the end card.

critiques.strengths: 'Play from here' is a checkpoint: review becomes play, and winning the game you lost from the exact move you missed is the strongest felt reward in any post-game concept. 'Answered' meaning you kept the piece, not that you won, is honest. The tape-rewind animation and the honest state when nothing was given away are both right.
critiques.weaknesses: It needs a finished game, then scores forty positions at depth 14 before the question appears, on a second screen the player has to choose. 'Which moment' can disagree with what he felt was the problem.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Offer the rewind at the moment of loss during the game: a one-move-back, one-chance replay with the question, so the checkpoint is inside the game and the second screen is only for the full post-mortem.

critiques.strengths: The best social hook in the set: a position and a question travel in the link, the friend taps before seeing your answer, no Claude needed in any browser, and only then the invitation to play. 'Day N counts days played, not days in a row' is the right streak. Seed positions verified at load so a shared link can never teach a wrong line.
critiques.weaknesses: Six seeds is a week. A daily is a layer on a play loop, not a loop a player opens on day one. The only play in it is the 'What do you play?' follow-up.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The day's position comes from yesterday's hold, and the share carries the sender's time ('Sambudh saw it in 9 s'), so the link is a challenge between two people rather than a puzzle with a comparison.

critiques.strengths: The hold shows their chair (the enemy piece that would take pulses under his move), the ring shrinks as he stops needing it, the bot gives gifts at a tuned rate and always punishes, and 'Looked.' is a one-word reward for a good move. The clean-games marks on the board edge are progression felt, not displayed.
critiques.weaknesses: Two mechanics (the hold plus a transparent opponent) is one too many for an MVP, and I said so in my own risks. 'What am I up to?' is pull-based and a beginner will not tap it. A beat on every move, even clean ones, reads as lag. 'They take back, free' on the ring is a label where the pulse already says it.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Cut the chip to iteration two and keep the hold-plus-pulse; make the beat zero-length on clean moves so the only time the game pauses is when something is at stake.

critiques.strengths: Punishment becomes the player's own move: consequence with agency, the 'oh' of the road-crossing analogy, and it is funny. The chair budget is the only progression in the set that is felt as graduation ('No chairs today. A real game.'). One joke per game is the right amount of personality.
critiques.weaknesses: A swap every third move in a bad game stops the game being a game. The rotation on a phone is the riskiest animation here. It shares the bot and the plumbing with Both Ways, and shipping both half-made was the risk I named.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The hold before the chair: hover and question first, and the chair only when he chooses 'Play it anyway', so the swap is the consequence of a decision rather than an interruption.

critiques.strengths: The verb is the look, not the move, which is the lesson. The three-square grid shared like a word game, a missed day as a grey grid rather than a broken chain, and the engine as both author and grader so nothing is a judgment call.
critiques.weaknesses: It has the shape of a puzzle app, and the world is full of those. Thirty verified positions before day one is real authoring. Without games from the play loop it is a layer with no personal position in it.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The day's position from the player's own game and a time-to-beat inside the grid so the share is a challenge.

critiques.concept: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)
critiques.strengths: The only concept where the player talks first and the coach listens; finding the false belief in his own sentence is the most novel LLM job in the set. Silence as reward with a 'Checked' mark and 'Five moves, nothing hung' is a real schedule. A planted free piece every six to ten moves is the gift rule by another name.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing before every move on a phone is homework inside the game; the skeptic's own 80 percent skip estimate is the verdict. The first frame has an input box under the board, so the board is no longer the hero. Even optional, an empty box is a small guilt on every move.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep the planted-piece bot and move the typing to the hold's 'But...' where it is motivated: he types because the board just stopped him and he disagrees.

critiques.strengths: The ration and the refund are a genuine resource economy: three looks, and a clean look costs nothing, so the player learns when something is at stake, which is the skill. 'Nothing for me there.' teaches that most moves are safe, which beginners do not know. The ghost plies on the flipped board make a three-ply line legible.
critiques.weaknesses: A hint button in a costume: the player learns to spend looks, not to look. The post-game 'which three would you spend next time' is where the learning is and it is cut from the slice. The skeptic admits the LLM necessity is the weakest here.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Tie the ration to the hold: a look spent before the drop pre-empts the hold on that move, so the player who looks first is never held, and the day he spends none and is never held is the graduation.

critiques.strengths: 'You stopped doing that.' with the old move numbers still showing is the best progression line in the whole set: a progress bar that reads like a person noticing. The whisper before the moment with nothing highlighted is scaffolding at the right time. Five fixed labels validated against engine facts keeps the memory honest.
critiques.weaknesses: A layer on a typing loop, with a three-game cold start and nothing to feel until then. A whisper that fires when the precondition is met but the move was fine teaches ignoring. It is memory for a game nobody is yet playing.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Let the whisper replace the hold for that habit: whisper first, and hold only if he still hangs it. Stepping down from a hold to a whisper to silence is scaffolding he feels being removed, which is what progression is.

critiques.strengths: 'Nothing. Take it back' accepts that finding nothing is the correct answer to a look, which the other variants miss. Colours swap on play again. The hold as a data attribute with the pulse set as a tested fact is the right way to make a beat reliable. Why? inside the hold with highlight, arrow and evaluate tools is the most grounded 'ask' in the set.
critiques.weaknesses: The question is wordy for a beat ('Before this goes: after they take back with the king, what can you take?'). Two tool rounds inside a hold is a two-second stall exactly where the hand is on the wrist. The game-end note is cut, so nothing is felt across games. Fixed Skill Level 2 with no gifts means the player is prey only.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The gift rate and resign rule in the bot, and an end card with the two counts, so the engineering serves a loop that changes from game to game.

critiques.strengths: Ghost playback with one caption per move is the best 'answer by moving the pieces' in the set, and the 100 cp guard means the board can never show wrong chess as good. The real pieces dimming to 35 percent while the line plays is the right stagecraft.
critiques.weaknesses: Four to six seconds per answer during play; a chips-and-ghosts feature without a loop of its own; a crutch in a real game. Nothing is at stake in asking.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One Show Me per game as a spendable resource, refunded when the line shown was clean, so it is a decision rather than a reflex.

critiques.strengths: Your own words lighting squares green is a genuine moment: the first time his reasoning has ever been visible on the board. The three-tap fallback without Claude is actually the better design.
critiques.weaknesses: The board refuses the drop until you write: a locked door inside a game, on a phone, one move in four. Typing 'nothing, nothing' to unlock is the player routing around the design, and the amber marks then scold. This is the worst game feel in the set.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ship the three-tap version as the hold's answer mode and drop the typing lock entirely; keep typing for 'But...' only.

ranking: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)

merged_proposal.name: Hold On
merged_proposal.one_liner: A game against a rival of your own level who leaves pieces for you and always takes yours, where a move that hangs something refuses to land, you answer one question by tapping the board, and if you play it anyway you sit in their chair and take it with your own hand.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction: The held move, with their chair inside it. When the engine sees that the move he just dropped loses material to a one-move reply, the piece does not land: it hovers on the target square at 60 percent, the enemy piece that would take it pulses, the board dims one shade, and one serif line under the board asks a question he can answer with a thumb: 'Hold on. That knight is about to land on e5. Tap what defends that square.' He taps d6 and the line says 'Yes, the d6 pawn. A knight for a pawn. Take it back?' with two buttons, Take it back (primary) and Play it anyway (quiet), and a small 'Show me' that plays the capture as a ghost: the pawn slides over, takes, a small '-2' floats up, a beat, everything slides back. Take it back is free and unrecorded; the piece slides home and a one-word chip reads 'Looked.' Play it anyway is the new part: the board turns around (a fade with the caption 'You are Black now' under prefers-reduced-motion), the line reads 'Sit here. What would you take?', and he makes the capture himself: his own knight comes off with a soft thud, the board turns back, and the game goes on with him down material. No red mark, no label, no eval bar: a blunder is a question he answered and a chair he sat in. The second new thing is the opponent: a rival that always punishes a hung piece (which human beginners do not, so they never learn) and at a tuned rate leaves a verified-free minor piece for him, so the look works in both directions. When he takes one, the piece pops off with '+3' and one line: 'Free knight. You looked.' Nothing in the world holds a move, lets you punish it from the other side, and rewards the look as well as catching the miss. Claude's role is small and only where language earns it: it chooses which of the three looks he skipped and asks it in his words without naming the answer (quick tier, JSON, the engine's template shown instantly and swapped only if Claude's arrives within 2.5 s, every square validated against the engine's answer set), it answers 'But...' when he argues with the hold ('but I'm attacking f2': 'You are, and the bishop already points there. But it is their move first, and the d3 pawn takes the knight before you get there. Is there a square that still looks at f2 that no pawn can reach?'), and at game end it writes two sentences with memory of his last games. Stockfish and chess.js do everything else: legality, the gate, the facts, the ghost line, the opponent, the resignation rule, and the verification that every gift is really free.
merged_proposal.core_loop: Every 20 seconds: pick up a piece (legal squares dot), drop it. About 85 percent of the time it lands and the rival answers inside a second with a 180 ms slide; nothing is said, because silence is right for a neutral move. When their last move attacked something of his and his move answered it: the one-word chip 'Looked.' When he captures a piece the rival left free: pop, '+3', 'Free knight. You looked.' When his move hangs something: the hold beat (hover, pulse, question, tap, Show me / Take it back / Play it anyway, and the chair on play-anyway). The gate is the coach's rule encoded: cp loss of 200 or more at depth 12, with the refutation a capture or check, or a free capture of two points or more skipped, or a mate in one allowed or missed; never a positional loss; suppressed when already five points down; after the second play-anyway in a game the coach goes quiet until the close. The opponent (Stockfish depth 10 to 12, MultiPV 8, a weighted sampler): always plays the top move when it captures two points or more or mates, never hangs its queen or walks into mate, otherwise samples within 60 cp of best, and at a gift rate (one move in eight at first) deliberately plays a MultiPV move that leaves a minor piece free, confirmed by a depth-12 check that the capture wins 200 cp or more with no in-between tactic. Game one follows the coach's scripted beginner tree out of 1.e4 e5 (built from the verified lesson positions) so a gift or a hold arrives by move five whichever natural moves he plays. The rival resigns nine points down with no mate threat, so games end in 25 to 35 moves. Every session (10 to 15 minutes): one game; then one end card, not a review: 'Pieces given away: 1 (last game 4). Caught: 2. Holds: 2, both taken back.', the moment that mattered as a small board with its question, and two buttons, 'Again' and 'Send this one'. Claude's two sentences stream under the card ('Both holds today were a knight landing where a pawn could reach it. Next game, before the knight lands: look for the pawns.') and the next game opens with that one line. Difficulty moves on the lesson, not on wins: after a game with zero pieces given away the gift rate drops a step and the sampler tightens a step; after a game with three or more hung it loosens. Every week: the hold's pulse ring is drawn visibly smaller as his hold rate falls, clean games chain as marks on the board edge, the rival's gifts dry up ('The rival stopped giving things away'), and in iteration two the chair budget shrinks toward the named event 'No chairs today. A real game.' The social hook is a moment, not a score: 'Send this one' puts the end card's position, its question and its answer squares in the URL hash; a friend opens it in any browser with no Claude, sees 'Sambudh saw it in 9 s. Can you see it?', taps, watches the ghost, and only then reads 'Play a game that holds your hand before you give a piece away.' On day one it works with the six verified lesson positions; after that every share is from his own game.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/src modules and the vendored engine, no build step, phone-first at 400 px in both themes. First thirty seconds: the page opens on the verified Italian after 3...Nf6 with the line 'Your move. Try the tempting one: bishop takes f7.'; he drags Bxf7+, it hovers, e8 pulses, the canned line 'Hold on. Check and a pawn, and then? Tap the piece that takes your bishop back.'; he taps e8, 'The king takes. A bishop for a pawn. Take it back?'; he taps Take it back, the bishop slides home, 'Looked.', then 'That is all I do. Now a real game.' and the board resets, the rival playing the scripted beginner tree so by move five something is free or something is held. In the slice: tap-tap and drag input with an inline SVG piece set; the Worker engine warmed at load; the rival with the sampler, the always-punish rule, the verified gift rate at a fixed one-in-eight, the game-one tree and the resign rule; the gate for the two material shapes (your move hangs a piece to a one-move capture; a free capture of two points or more skipped) plus mate in one; the hold with hover, their-chair pulse, template question shown instantly, Claude's question on quick tier via sample.json swapped in within 2.5 s and validated against the engine's answer squares (window.__stubSample for Playwright, template-only when sample is null); tap-to-answer graded by chess.js with one retry then the arrow; Show me ghost capture with the floating '-2'; Take it back with 'Looked.'; Play it anyway turning the board (fade under reduced motion) for the capture by his own hand, turning back, and the game continuing; the quiet-after-second-play-anyway rule; 'Free knight. You looked.' with '+3' on a gift taken; the end card with the three counts and the moment as a small board; 'Send this one' writing the URL hash and the page reading it on load into a friend mode with no Claude; counts and the pulse size in localStorage. A copy test fails the build on 'blunder', 'mistake', 'inaccuracy' or '??' anywhere in the page's strings. Cut from day one, in order of what goes first if time runs out: the chair (fallback: the rival takes and says one phrasebook line), 'But...', the end-of-game Claude sentences (fallback: the counts alone), the adaptive gift rate (fallback: fixed), playing Black, the daily, db plus user, and the chair budget. The MVP is proven if Sambudh drags a piece back inside a hold at least once per game, takes at least one gift per game, finishes a game, and his second game ends with fewer pieces given away than his first.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: It is a game first: a rival tuned so a beginner can win while losing exactly the way he needs to lose, with a reward for looking ('Looked.', 'Free knight. You looked.') and not only a catch for missing. The blunder becomes a question answered by touching the square and a chair he sits in to punish it himself, so consequence stays in the game (the thing Lichess and Chess.com never give a beginner: a dignified take-back, and a punishment he performs rather than receives). Progression is felt in the hands before it is shown anywhere: the ring shrinks, the gifts dry up, the end card's one number goes down, and later the chairs run out. It never waits on Claude during the beat (template first, swap within 2.5 s, engine-grounded squares only) and it plays fully with no Claude at all, so a friend's link in any browser is the same game. Claude does only what a template cannot: pick the look he skipped and ask it in his words, answer his argument, and remember what he keeps doing. And the thing he sends is a moment with a question ('Can you see it?'), not a rating, which is why it travels. It beats 'chat next to a board' because nothing is ever typed unless he chooses to argue, and it beats every post-game review because the learning happens in the half-second before the piece lands, which is the only place a player under 1000 ever loses a game.

reviews.persona: Market skeptic and competitive analyst. Evidence note: WebSearch was available and used (about 15 queries); WebFetch was DNS-blocked from this container for chess.com, support.chess.com, lichess.org, help.chessbase.com, hiarcs.com, arxiv.org, alphaxiv.org, chessiverse.com and ai.engineer, so every product claim below rests on search snippets of the vendors' own pages, announcements and help articles, not hands-on use; Lichess Learn and Practice are described partly from prior knowledge.

critiques.strengths: The strictest gate on the team: cp loss of 200 or more AND a capture or check refutation AND not already five points down, quiet after the second "play anyway", zero Claude calls in a clean game. That is the under-1000 band belief encoded, and it is the only thing that separates this from a desktop coach set to warn at two pawns. The scripted beginner tree so something hangs by move five is the best cold-start trick offered. The acceptance test is written from verified lesson positions, which no incumbent's marketing can say.
critiques.weaknesses: The pitch's central claim, "a hand on your wrist is not in the world", is false. Chessmaster 9000 (2002) shipped a Blunder Alert that "immediately notifies players of better moves when they move their pieces into danger"; Fritz's coach since Fritz 11 (2009) "appears when you make a mistake" with a pawn-unit threshold and take-back; HIARCS has a "coach warning dialog" offering "take back your move or discover the refutation"; Lucas Chess's tutor flags the move as it is made with a settable threshold and takebacks; Chess.com's Play Coach gives "pointers at critical moments, like when a piece is attacked" plus Undo. All of them fire after the drop and before the reply, which is the same beat as the hover. What is not in the world is a hand that asks instead of tells and never names the move; the concept has it (tap d6, "That's the one") but leads with the interrupt. Stockfish at Skill Level 1 is not a beginner: engines weakened by randomness "blunder obviously" in a non-human way, which is why Chessiverse and Noctie train bots on human games at 400-800.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Lead every line of copy and every demo with the refusal ("I will never tell you the move. I will ask."), because a Lichess forum thread will post the Fritz 11 coach screenshot within an hour of launch otherwise. And no threshold slider, ever: Fritz has one, and the moment this page has one it is Fritz on a web page.

critiques.strengths: Punish-then-prevent is the one drill shape I could not find in any product. Lichess and Chess.com puzzles never flip the seat; Aimchess's Blunder Preventer is "given two possible moves, spot the blunder"; a Chess.com forum thread asks for a flipped Tactics Trainer and gets a workaround; a coach's article recommends solving with the board turned around by hand. Demand with no supply. The engine as sole judge of "prevent", with the top three shown afterwards, is right. Generating sets from his own game on the slow tier, once, on a result screen, with the page gating every puzzle on the tool log, is the correct use of a 30-60 s call.
critiques.weaknesses: Ten built-in positions is two sessions; without games it is a demo, and the team has not agreed which play loop feeds it. The 30-60 s generation is the wait the market has moved away from: Chessiro reviews in the browser with Stockfish 18 and Take Take Take reports sub-3 s post-game on Gemini Flash. "Prevent" acceptance (cp loss under 100, nothing hanging) will accept passive moves a coach would frown at; fine at 800, but the copy must say "safe", not "good".
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make every set a link with no account, because Chess.com cannot (Play Coach is one free game a month, puzzles are rated and gated) and because a club coach sending it to five students is the only acquisition channel a one-page artifact has. And put the one-in-six "nothing to punish" position in the first ten; the forum crowd will test for it on day one.

critiques.strengths: The honest version of game review for this band: three moments, all hung pieces, re-asked harder, and the R3 "same mistake in a new position" is the one step beyond Noctie's spaced-repetition puzzles and Chessable's MoveTrainer, which Matuschak notes can reinforce recall of moves but not a concept. The engine-gated generation with silent fallback to R2 is the right failure mode. The memory line ("four of your last six hung pieces were to a pawn") is the one sentence no app says.
critiques.weaknesses: This square is crowded: Lichess "Learn from your mistakes" (walks you through your own mistakes, hides the best move until asked), Chessiro's Replay Mistakes and recurring-weakness prompts, Noctie's puzzles-from-your-games with SRS, D4Chess.Club's "recurring error patterns ... Socratic-style walkthroughs", Chess.com Game Review v2's Coach recap. The delta (hung pieces only, tap to answer, generated R3) is invisible in a screenshot. Needs games, so ships third. A 30-90 s tools call per game is slower than every incumbent. The memory line arrives after six games.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Treat it as the retention layer of the play loop, never a product, and make the PGN paste the on-ramp for Chess.com and Lichess players who already have games: that is the only piece of this product aimed at anyone who is not Sambudh, and it is the only acquisition path for players with a history.

critiques.strengths: The best first thirty seconds on the team: opens mid-position on a verified trap, the first hold is canned so the consent dialog never lands before the player knows what a hold is, and "template instantly, Claude swaps in only if it arrives within 2.5 s" is the only honest answer to quick-tier latency variance. "Nothing on this page is ever red" and no eval bar are real differentiators against Game Review v2, which still leads with labels and a report card. The output validation (answer squares must be a subset of the engine's set, the question must not contain them) is the right contract.
critiques.weaknesses: Same prior art as every hold (Chessmaster, Fritz, HIARCS, Lucas Chess, Play Coach's Undo), and the pitch again leads with "the board intercepts your move" rather than "the board asks". Call 2 ("One thing from this game", 30-90 s with tools) is Game Review v2's Coach recap on a slower clock; rightly cut from the slice. Opponent calibration is a "weighted top-N picker", while Chessiverse's whole business is bots trained on human games at 400-800 because handicapped engines blunder unlike people; this is the hardest engineering and the slice treats it as a setting.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The share moment. A held piece with a question and no answer is the most screenshot-able frame in chess software; let him send that exact position and question as a link. It costs nothing, it is the only growth loop a one-page artifact has, and no subscription product can match it.

critiques.strengths: The flip as a solo drill is the Steps Method's change-chairs made physical, and I found no product that does it; the forum demand for flipped puzzle training is real. Three outcomes with "Show me" leaving a hollow dot is a scoreless social cost that works. Twelve engine-verified positions baked in is honest supply.
critiques.weaknesses: Without a game loop it reads as a puzzle app with a twist, and the twist does not show in a store screenshot. The opener "You are White, make a move" is weaker than the coach's "Punish it": an 800 makes a random safe move and gets "nothing to punish" three times running; the tempting move must be planted. Claude's hint and "Why did that work?" are garnish; the drill is engine-only, which also means it does not need this platform.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Feed it from the player's own last game first, which makes it a layer on a play loop, not a product; and show one number only, chairs you did not need this week, because Chess.com and Lichess give ratings and this must give the opposite.

critiques.strengths: Pre-commit consequence display is genuinely absent: ChessUp users asked for "see move quality while holding the piece" and staff answered "not implemented"; Chess.com's Assisted mode draws threat arrows on the current position, never on a hypothetical. The dashed "They would play this" arrow is good UI. "Teach me this position" with a ghost() tool that returns the engine's verdict is the one thinking-partner moment the brief asked for.
critiques.weaknesses: It is an analysis board with restraint, and restraint does not survive users asking for the eval bar. For Sambudh it is a crutch: the thesis is that the look must move into his head, and a tool that draws the look for him every move trains the opposite. The LLM is optional (rings, dots and arrows are chess.js) and "Why?" is DecodeChess-lite. A YouTuber would call it Lichess analysis with training wheels.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make it cost something: one ghost per game inside the play loop, spent like a timeout, with the page recording whether he used it before or after the blunder. As a free playground it is the hint machine I warned about in my own concept.

critiques.strengths: The best-specified LLM contract on the team: fact sheet in, JSON out, a SAN regex validator, and a counter for discarded replies so stub tests measure the violation rate. That is the ACT-Eval lesson (about 22 percent wrong sub-claims for the best model without tools, over 40 percent for small open models) turned into engineering. Abort on the next move is right. "Answered." is a good tick.
critiques.weaknesses: Chess.com Play Coach already "gives you pointers at critical moments of the game, like when a piece is attacked" and ships red threat arrows; Open Hand's delta is the first-person voice and the fade-out streak, and the fade is explicitly not in the MVP, so the MVP is Play Coach's pointers in a nicer voice on a free page. Telegraphing every threat trains dependence; the cure is deferred. Six to twelve calls a game is the highest spend on the team for the thinnest novelty.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ship the fade-out in the slice and make the quiet game the headline: "Mira stopped talking on move 14" is the only sentence from this concept a forum would repeat, and it costs nothing. And never let the bubble look like a hint button; Play Coach's hint is a paid feature and this must not read as a free copy.

critiques.strengths: Grading the typed reason rather than the move is not shipped anywhere I found (D4Chess does Socratic walkthroughs, Chessiro follow-up chat; neither grades your stated reasoning). Once per game on a result screen is the right place for the product's only text field. Motif codes by rule, never by Claude, and "no drill when every swing is under 150 cp" are honest.
critiques.weaknesses: Game Review v2 opens with a Coach recap; Chessiro gives a free, unlimited, in-browser Stockfish 18 review with arrows; "the one thing" card is a shorter Game Review, and shorter is only visible after you have used both. The about-you line is D4Chess.Club's pitch word for word ("finds your mistake patterns, not just your blunders"). Default-tier 10-30 s on a 3 KB prompt while the market is at sub-3 s post-game. The concept admits Skip may become the primary path, at which point it is Lichess "learn from your mistakes" with prose.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Grade the reason by tap first and text second ("tap what you should have looked at" is the same rubric with no keyboard), and show the card inside the next game rather than on the result screen, because the result screen is where Chess.com already wins.

critiques.strengths: Chips instead of a chat box is the right instinct, and computing the chips from the facts so a chip exists only when its question is live is clever. The quiz-mode tap-back keyed by the page is new. Caching by FEN and chip is the right cost control.
critiques.weaknesses: This is "Ask Coach any question" with three buttons; DecodeChess has explained "piece functionality" for years; Chessiro's chat draws arrows. The concept's own risk list says the fourth question is a text box, "exactly the chatbot this concept refuses", so it is a chatbot with the box hidden. It competes with the opponent's bubble for the same slot. "What is it doing?" is bland by design, and every chip tap spends the viewer's Claude usage on a question Lichess answers free with an arrow.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Ship it only inside a hold or chair, as the second tap after a wrong answer, where "Is it safe?" has a stake. As a free-roaming feature it is the commodity.

critiques.strengths: The "-2" floating up during "Show me" is the best piece of feedback copy on the team and comes from the only partner who has actually lost those pieces. "But..." is the one place free text belongs: after the hold, optional, about the player's intention, with Claude required to end in a question. The end card counts "pieces given away" and "times you held on", numbers an 800 understands, instead of a rating. Templated hold line with Claude only behind Why and But is the cheapest honest shape.
critiques.weaknesses: Same prior art as every hold, and this version's templated sentence ("His knight on c6 takes yours back") is the closest of all to what Fritz and Lucas Chess already print, so Why and But carry the whole novelty and both are hidden until tapped. The pre-compute (multipv over all legal moves at depth 10 during think time) is a bigger single-thread engine design than the writer thinks. The bot's "sprinkle of second and third choices" is the opponent problem again.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Put "But..." in the MVP and lead with it: "a coach you can argue with, who answers your plan and never names the move" is the sentence a YouTuber would say on camera, and it is the only thing here no 2009 desktop program did.

critiques.strengths: Rewinding to the moment, asking before telling, then "Play from here" against the same bot is the right beginner review, and "answered means you kept the piece, not that you won" is a precise, kind rule. The honest state "nothing was given away; it was lost slowly, which is a different lesson" beats any Game Review label.
critiques.weaknesses: Lichess has shipped both halves for years: "Learn from your mistakes" (your mistakes, best move hidden until asked) and Practice mode ("play against the computer from any position, instant feedback after each move"); Chess.com Game Review has Retry. The tap-to-answer question is the delta, and it is small. Scoring 40 positions at depth 14 on a phone is 20-40 s against a market at seconds. It needs a game to exist first.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep the mid-game "?" chip and cut the post-game screen: a rewind thirty seconds after the loss, inside the same game, is something Lichess cannot do because its analysis is a separate page, and it costs one quick call.

critiques.strengths: Share a moment with no account, question carried in the URL hash, no Claude on the receiving end: the only distribution mechanic on the team and the only one that reaches the friend who has never opened a chess app. "Day N counts days played, not days in a row" is the right anti-Wordle rule. Seed positions verified at load by the engine so a bad one is skipped.
critiques.weaknesses: Lichess daily puzzle, Chess.com daily puzzle, Noctie daily puzzles and weekly scenarios; the twist (a question about looking, not the best move) is real and invisible in a screenshot. Six seeds is one week. Positions from his own games arrive only after a play loop exists. As a first product it is a puzzle app with a nicer sentence.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Move the share button onto the hold or chair moment instead of the daily: the thing he wants to send is "look what it caught me doing", and the recipient should land on the same held piece with the same question and only then be offered the game.

critiques.strengths: The ring that shrinks as you stop needing it is the best progress metaphor on the team: felt in the hands, no number, cannot be gamed. The bot spec (always punish, never hang the queen, deliberately hang a minor piece at a rate that falls with the catch rate, tuned by headless self-play) is the most concrete opponent design offered and the one most worth building once for every concept. "Looked." as a one-word chip is good.
critiques.weaknesses: Two mechanics in one MVP (hold plus telegraph chip), the sin the same partner warns against in Change Chairs' risks. The "What am I up to?" chip is Play Coach's "pointers when a piece is attacked" in the first person; the hold is the Fritz beat. The weekly "ring is half the size" line needs weeks of use. The self-play tuning is a day the slice does not budget.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Cut the chip, keep the ring and its shrink, and make the ring's size the thing he shares ("my hold is half the size it was"): a progress artefact no rating system produces, and honest because the engine counted it.

critiques.strengths: The one interaction that fuses the interrupt (which has prior art) with the flip (which has none): when you hang a piece the bot does not reply, the board turns, and you take your own piece with your own thumb. No shipping product does this, the forum demand for flipped training exists, it is the most filmable twenty seconds on the team, and it is understood without a word of instruction. The budget that shrinks toward a named "No chairs today" game is graduation, not a safety net, and it turns intervention count into the progress bar. Claude's role (one line tying this chair to the look that was skipped, with memory) is small, necessary and cheap; it never decides and never evaluates.
critiques.weaknesses: The rotation on a 400 px phone is make-or-break and untested with Sambudh. A swap every third move in a bad game is a lot of stopping; the 200 cp trigger and the one-swap-per-two-moves cap must be enforced by tests, not taste. The one post-swap line will read as templated until memory exists, so db plus user must follow fast. The joke wears by game three. The what-if tools call is correctly excluded.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Lead with the chair in every sentence of copy, never the hold; keep "Play it anyway" a real counted option; and make the first zero-chair game a shareable card ("No chairs today. 31 moves."), the first chess progress artefact that reads as a story rather than a number.

critiques.strengths: Asking for the three looks as three taps instead of a move is a true change of verb, and the engine can author and grade it deterministically with the reason drawn on a miss. The grid share is Wordle's loop with a chess object and no account.
critiques.weaknesses: It has the exact shape of a daily puzzle app, which both incumbents and a dozen indies run; the delta lives in the verb and is missed by anyone scrolling. Thirty verified positions is real authoring before day one. Own-game positions need the play loop. Claude's job is one sentence a day that a template could do for months. There is no notification channel in an artifact to collect on a daily cadence.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Fold the three taps into the end of every game as the review of the moment that mattered, instead of a separate daily; the end of a game is a moment he is already in, and the daily is a retention bet with no way to ring the bell.

critiques.concept: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)
critiques.strengths: The reversal (the player speaks first, the coach listens and finds the false belief) is shipped nowhere I could find, and it is the one job here that is pure language understanding. Facts-by-id output with token validation is the right contract. Silence plus a "Checked" mark is the right reward.
critiques.weaknesses: Typing before moves on a phone is friction most players will skip, and I wrote the pivot rule myself: a skip rate above 80 percent makes it Play Coach with better questions. Its first screen has a text input under the board, which breaks "the board is the hero". Quick-tier grading leniency on free text is unmeasured, and the research on LLM-graded reasoning says calibrate against humans first. It competes with Change Chairs for the same moment and loses on delight.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Demote it to the "But..." tap inside a chair or hold: say your reasoning only after the engine has already found something, optionally. That keeps the one genuinely new LLM job and removes the friction from every quiet move.

critiques.strengths: The ration and the refund are the clever part, and the flip plus the opponent's first-person sentence is filmable. The engine decides refunds, never Claude. The template path covers the no-capability case honestly.
critiques.weaknesses: I said it in the concept and I stand by it: it is a hint machine in a costume, and without the ration it is Chess.com Assisted mode (threat arrows, engine on). The LLM necessity is the weakest on the team; templates serve most looks. Change Chairs does the flip at a moment with stakes (your own hanging piece) instead of on demand, which is strictly better pedagogy with strictly fewer calls.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Kill it as a standalone and keep one piece: the refund line "Nothing for me there" as the chair's answer when a swap fires on a borderline position, so the player learns that most of his moves are fine.

critiques.strengths: Carrying a habit into the next live game and whispering before the precondition is met is the one memory timing no incumbent has: Aimchess, Chessiro, Noctie and D4Chess.Club all remember after the fact. Five fixed labels with an engine-fact validator is the right guard. "You stopped doing that" is a progress line that reads like a person.
critiques.weaknesses: Cold start by design; needs db plus user and a play loop that exists; the placement borrowed from the lesson engine is a test dressed as play. A whisper that fires on a met precondition when the move was fine teaches him to ignore it, and that tuning needs real games. It is a layer, and shipping it first would be a memory feature for a game nobody is playing.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Make the whisper the chair's opening line from game four on ("Your habit. A pawn can reach something of yours.") so it ships inside the one interaction rather than as a feature, and never whisper a habit before three instances.

critiques.strengths: The only concept with a buildable architecture: a piece layer positioned by transform so moves, takebacks and flips animate for free, pointer events in one path, a serialized engine queue, store.js that is db plus user inside the viewer and localStorage outside, window.__app for the headless checker, and the rule "no nameable mechanism, no hold". "Why?" inside the hold with highlight, arrow and evaluate tools at two rounds is a sensible place for tools.
critiques.weaknesses: Prior art as every hold. "Why?" with tools adds two seconds inside the beat and the first consent dialog lands there; the designer's 2.5 s swap rule handles the moment better. The game-end note is cut, so the slice's only LLM moment is a hidden button. Skill Level 2 at depth 6 is still an engine-shaped opponent.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Build this architecture once and put Change Chairs on it: the transform-driven piece layer is exactly what makes the board rotation and the take-your-own-piece capture cheap, and the two-slot engine queue is what makes the swap trigger instant.

critiques.strengths: The best of the ask cluster because the LLM tests the player's idea with try_line before the board shows one line, and the page refuses to show a losing line as good. That is the "thinking partner grounded by the engine" the brief asked for; Chess.com's "Show Line" only animates the engine's own continuation, never yours.
critiques.weaknesses: Four quick rounds is four to six seconds of "Trying..." on his own turn with the first consent dialog in the middle; Chessiro and Chess.com Coach draw arrows on the review page in under three seconds. Chips on his own turn are a hint button with extra steps; as a playground it duplicates Ghost Moves and as a game feature it is a crutch. Ghosts over a real layer dimmed to 35 percent on a 400 px board is busy.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Only inside the chair, after "Play it anyway": "Show me what happens" is then a question with a stake, one tap, no chips, and the answer is the engine's refutation played with Claude's captions, which is where ghost playback earns its latency.

critiques.strengths: Lighting f7 green because the page understood "bishop hits f7" is a lovely moment, and the extraction contract (Claude maps words to squares, chess.js judges) is the cleanest division of labour on the team. The three-tap fallback when sample is null is right.
critiques.weaknesses: Locking the board until he types, on one move in four, on a phone, is friction cubed; no incumbent does this because nobody would play. "I read: attacks f7" plus a Fix link is a second screen of UI on top of the board. A player can type "nothing" to unlock. It is my own concept with a lock added, and the lock is the wrong direction.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Keep the extraction and the green squares, drop the lock, and run it as the optional "But..." after a chair, where the green and amber marks become the coach's answer to his argument.

ranking: Say It Before You Move (market skeptic)

merged_proposal.name: Sit Here
merged_proposal.one_liner: Play a bot that hangs pieces like an 800; when you hang one, the game stops, the board turns, and you take your own piece with your own thumb before you decide whether to play the move.
merged_proposal.the_new_interaction: The chair swap at the moment of the blunder. Every blunder warning that has ever shipped does the same three things: tells you the move was bad, shows or offers the better move, and lets you take it back. Chessmaster 9000's Blunder Alert (2002) "immediately notifies players of better moves when they move their pieces into danger"; Fritz's coach since Fritz 11 "appears when you make a mistake" with a pawn-unit threshold; HIARCS's "coach warning dialog" offers "take back your move or discover the refutation"; Lucas Chess's tutor flags the move with a threshold and takebacks; Chess.com Play Coach gives "pointers at critical moments, like when a piece is attacked" and an Undo. Here nobody tells you anything. When your dropped move leaves a piece for free, the bot does not reply. The board turns (400 ms rotation; a fade under prefers-reduced-motion), the side badge reads "You are Black now", and one serif line says: "Sit here. What would you take?" You find and play the capture yourself. Your own knight comes off the board with a soft thud and the count on the board edge drops to -2. The board turns back: "Still want to play it?" with [Take it back] (primary) and [Play it anyway] (quiet, counted, never nagged). Only now does Claude speak, one line, grounded by the engine's fact sheet and your record: "The e5 pawn was guarded by the knight beside it. You asked what you could take; the question you skipped was from this chair." On the other ninety percent of moves nothing happens: no eval bar, no labels, no move list, no rating. The move is never named, the number is never shown, and the punishment is executed by the player's own hand, which no product does because every incumbent's coach is a dialog, not a seat. The first thirty seconds: 0-3 s, a tournament buff-and-green board, white at the bottom, one line: "Your move. If you hang something, I'll let you sit in my chair before I take it." and a small badge "Black: Beginner". 3-18 s, 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, each reply in under half a second, silence. 18-23 s, he plays 4.Nxe5 because the pawn looks free (lesson 0001 phase 3, verified at depth 20: 4.Nxe5?? Nxe5, cp loss 335). The bot does not reply; the board turns; "Sit here. What would you take?" 23-28 s, he taps the c6 knight, taps e5; the white knight comes off; the edge reads -2. The board turns back: "Still want to play 4.Nxe5?" He taps Take it back; the knight slides home; the count returns to 0. 28-30 s, one line arrives: "That pawn was guarded by the knight beside it. Before you let go: what can they take?" Then "Your move." He plays 4.d3 and nothing is said. He has understood the whole product and nobody showed him a move. The two things that make it new are the seat (he punishes himself) and the silence (it never names the move, never shows a number, and says nothing on quiet moves); the two things that make it LLM-native are the one line with memory after the swap and, in iteration two, the "But..." tap where he argues his plan and the coach answers the plan with a question.
merged_proposal.core_loop: Every move: (1) tap-tap or drag; chess.js validates. (2) The engine gate, instant: chess.js counts attackers and defenders on every piece of his after the move; the pre-move position was searched at depth 12 while he thought, so only the post-move eval at depth 10-12 is needed (0.3-0.6 s, hidden under the piece settling). (3) Clean: the move commits, the bot replies in under a second (Skill Level 1-3, depth 6, multipv 8 with a weighted picker: always takes free material worth two or more and always mates, never hangs its queen or walks into mate-in-one, otherwise samples within 60 cp of best, and at a tuned rate starting near one move in ten hangs a minor piece so he gets to be the one who looks and takes; the rate falls as his catch rate rises). (4) Swap fires only when cp loss is 200 or more AND the refutation is an immediate capture or check or a mate-in-one is allowed; never on a positional loss, never when he is already five points down, at most one swap per two moves, and after the second "Play it anyway" in a game no more swaps until the close. (5) Rotate; "Sit here. What would you take?"; he captures; chess.js checks it is the punishing capture (take the wrong thing and the smaller gain shows while the bigger one pulses: "There was a bigger one."); count on the edge; rotate back; Take it back or Play it anyway. (6) One quick-tier sample.json call, 1-2 s, no tools, fired by the turn-back: input is the position before the move, the move, the capture he made, attackers and defenders on the landing square, the category code (hung-to-pawn, hung-undefended, grabbed-defended, ignored-last-move, walked-into-mate), the three-looks vocabulary, and the last five games' chair categories from the store; output {say, squares}; the page validates that every square is in the fact sheet and that say contains no SAN token outside the listed moves and never names a move, else the template ("e5 was defended by the knight on c6.") shows; not_granted or null sample means templates everywhere and no message; rate_limited means templates for the next three chairs. Zero calls on quiet moves. Every session: one game of 25-40 moves that ends because the bot resigns a queen down; the chairs used are drawn as small chairs along the board edge, not a number; one quick call writes the close ("Three chairs tonight, all guarded pawns. You never hung a piece to a one-move threat; that look is working."); [Again]. Across games (iteration two, with db plus user): games one to three have unlimited chairs; then the budget is the average used minus one, down toward zero; the first zero-chair game is announced before it starts, "No chairs today. A real game.", and is a shareable card when finished; after it, one chair a game can still be asked for and is counted; clean games chain into a row of chairs turned away. From game four, the whisper: when the facts show his recorded habit's precondition (a pawn can reach a piece of his), one quiet line before he touches anything, once per game, nothing highlighted.
merged_proposal.mvp_slice: One page, app/index.html plus app/src/{main,board,game,engine,coach,store,ui}.js, app/styles.css, app/pieces.svg (inline symbols; Unicode glyphs as fallback), on the frontend architect's structure: transform-positioned piece layer (which makes the rotation and the take-your-own-piece capture cheap), pointer events in one path, a serialized Stockfish worker queue with the pre-move search, store.js on localStorage behind the db interface. White against the bot at one fixed level, unlimited chairs. The swap in full for ONE category: a piece of his left capturable for a net loss of two points or more by a one-move capture (including capture by a pawn), plus mate-in-one allowed. Rotate (fade under reduced motion), capture by hand with the chess.js check and the "There was a bigger one" pulse, count on the edge, rotate back, Take it back and Play it anyway. The one post-swap line through sample.json on the quick tier with the square and SAN validator and the template fallback; window.__stubSample for Playwright, including one canned reply that names an off-list square to prove the validator discards it. The close: chairs along the edge, "Pieces given away: 1" and "Times you sat in my chair: 3", [Again]. Light and dark tokens, 400 px with 16 px gutters, no eval bar, no move list, no rating, no settings, no chat box, no red anywhere. Acceptance, all from verified lesson positions: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, 4.Nxe5 fires the chair and Nxe5 by hand reads -2; 4.Bxf7+ fires and Kxf7 reads -2; 4.d3 passes in silence. After 6...d6 (FEN r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/4p3/2B1P3/2NP1N2/PPP2PPP/R1BQ1RK1 w - - 0 7), 7.Nxe5 fires (dxe5), 7.Bxf7+ fires (Rxf7), 7.h3 passes. In the Ruy after 3...a6, 4.O-O fires (axb5) and 4.Ba4 passes. Screenshots at desktop and 400 px in both schemes with no horizontal overflow. Explicitly not in the slice: the budget and "No chairs today" (iteration two, with db plus user), the "But..." pushback with the beginner's tools highlight and play_ghost (iteration two, the product's only free-text field), the share link of a chair moment (iteration two), playing Black (iteration two), the habit whisper (iteration three), the what-if tools call (never in a live move). If the rotation fails in Sambudh's hands, the fallback is the designer's Hold On with the question on the same architecture: nothing built is wasted.
merged_proposal.why_this_wins: Novelty, checked against the market: the interrupt alone is twenty-four years old (Chessmaster 9000 Blunder Alert, https://legacy.prod.metacritic.com/game/pc/chessmaster-9000; Fritz 11 coach, https://en.chessbase.com/post/the-coach-in-fritz11 and https://help.chessbase.com/Fritz/19/Eng/000056.htm; HIARCS coach warning dialog, https://www.hiarcs.com/hce-manual/pc/Playgamemode.html; Lucas Chess tutor, https://lichess.org/@/mullerrj/blog/learning-from-mistakes-when-they-happen-with-lucas-chess/he1cgG3P; Chess.com Play Coach pointers and Undo, https://support.chess.com/en/articles/10877257-how-do-i-play-against-the-coach), so any concept that leads with the hold will get the Fritz screenshot posted under it. No product I could find turns the board and makes the player execute the punishment of his own move; the nearest things are a coach's article recommending flipped-board tactics by hand and a Chess.com forum request for a flipped Tactics Trainer that was answered with a workaround (https://chess.com/forum/view/suggestions/tactics-trainer-flip-board). That is demand without supply, and it is the twenty seconds a YouTuber films and a Lichess thread calls new. Beginner value: the chess master's band belief is that under 1000 nothing but the hung piece matters; the gate encodes exactly that and nothing else, and the lesson is in the hands (you took your own knight) rather than in a label, which is the mechanism Game Review v2 (https://www.chess.com/news/view/chesscom-launches-game-review-v2), Lichess Learn from your mistakes (https://lichess.org/blog/WFvLpiQAACMA8e9D/learn-from-your-mistakes) and Chessiro (https://chessiro.com/blog/inside-chessiro-game-review) cannot offer because their coaching happens on a separate screen after the game. Honest LLM use: the ACT-Eval benchmark (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04240) measures about a fifth of commentary sub-claims wrong for the best model without tools, so prose-first coaches are a liability at this band; here Claude is handed a fact sheet, limited to one line, validated on the way out, and silent on ninety percent of moves, and its one necessary job (connecting this chair to what the player keeps doing, in his words) is the one thing a template cannot vary and the engine cannot know. Feasibility: one page, one board, one bot, one gate, one call shape, on an architecture a partner has already specified, with acceptance tests from positions verified at depth 20 in this repo; the engine runs locally the way Chessiro's does, and the Claude calls spend the viewer's own usage, so the page has no server and no subscription against Play Coach's one free game a month, Noctie at roughly 14-16 a month (https://apps.appfollow.io/ios/noctie-chess-trainer/6444289077?country=us) and Chessiverse at 9.99 (https://chessiverse.com/compare/best-chess-bot-for-beginners). The known hard part is the opponent: Chessiverse and Noctie train bots on human games because a handicapped engine blunders unlike a person, and Maia's lowest model is 1100 (https://lichess.org/blog/X9PUixUAANCqFRSh/introducing-maia-a-human-like-neural-network-chess-engine); the weighted picker with a planted minor-piece hang is a workable substitute at 800 and must be tuned with headless self-play before Sambudh plays. Delight: the board turning and his own knight coming off under his own thumb is a physical "oh" that no evaluation bar produces, and the progress artefact is a row of chairs he no longer needs, not a number. What is deliberately refused: a chat box, an eval bar, a move list, a hint button, a threshold slider and a rating, because each one is the exact feature that turns this back into the commodity that Chessiro, ChessGPT (https://apps.apple.com/app/id6481724799), DecodeChess (https://decodechess.com/faq/) and Chess.com already ship.

reviews.persona: Frontend architect: plain ES modules, one published page, vendored chess.js and Stockfish 18 lite in a Web Worker, a pointer-event board that is the whole interface, state behind a store seam (db+user in the viewer, localStorage elsewhere), and every flow drivable in headless Chromium through scripts/app_check.js with window.__stubSample.

critiques.strengths: The gate is a pure function of (evalBefore, evalAfter, refutation, chess.js facts) and so is unit-testable with no browser at all. Zero sample calls in a clean game sits well with per-call consent. The templated question from chess.js means the hold renders with Claude absent. The beat budget is already engineering (depth 12 MultiPV 2 pre-search while he thinks, depth 10 after the drop, ~0.3 s). The scripted beginner tree for game one makes the first thirty seconds deterministic, which makes it screenshot-able and assertable. The acceptance test is written against the verified lesson FENs, which is exactly what scripts/app_check.js scenarios need.
critiques.weaknesses: 'The piece does not land, it hovers' needs the verdict before the 150 ms slide ends, but the verdict arrives ~300 ms after the pre-search is stopped; without an explicit pending state the hover is a lie on a slow phone. The worker is single-threaded: the pre-search must be `stop`ped before the verdict `go`, and the stale `bestmove` from the stop arrives asynchronously, so the queue needs search ids or it will attribute the wrong bestmove. Answering by tapping squares turns the board into a second input mode (tap = answer, not select); that flag and its affordance are unmentioned. The end screen's small boards need board.js to be a factory with a static mode. Flip for Black is deferred, correctly, but the piece layer must be flip-ready on day one or it is a rewrite.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A `pending` drop state in the piece layer (landed at full opacity, input locked, no chip) that the verdict either commits or converts to `held` within ~300 ms, so the hold honestly 'catches' a landed piece; plus the engine queue's stop-then-go handshake with search ids so a late bestmove from the pre-search is discarded, never played.

critiques.strengths: Data-driven: ten pre-verified positions in a JSON file, no live opponent, one depth-12 check per answer. Pass/fail rules are pure functions. A flipped start is a mapping change, not a feature. It is the best Playwright fixture of the set: load position, play move, assert class.
critiques.weaknesses: A 'turn around' animation implemented as a CSS rotate turns the pieces and coordinates upside down unless each piece counter-rotates; a translate-based remap is cleaner but then it is not a rotation. Generating sets from a PGN needs page tools backed by the worker while the worker may be busy, so the two-slot queue is a prerequisite. The PGN paste box is a textarea on a phone. The authoring pipeline (engine_check.py) lives outside the page, which is fine, but the page must not recompute the truth at load.
critiques.what_i_would_add: Implement the flip as the piece layer's coordinate mapping: each piece translates to its mirrored cell over 400 ms under one `--flip` variable, coordinates re-label without rotating, and prefers-reduced-motion sets the duration to 0.

critiques.strengths: The trace is a batch job the worker can run while the end card is already on screen; the rule-based three appear before Claude; the per-move progress line maps directly onto queue events.
critiques.weaknesses: It needs games, so it is a second page's dependency. Forty positions at depth 14 is ~50 s headless (the brief measured 1.3 s per depth-14 search) and 2-3x that on a phone, and it blocks the opponent search, so it can only run after a game ends. R3's generated FEN needs chess.js validation plus evaluate and line, fine, but the default-tier call with tools plus progress-from-execute is the most UI work for the least first-day value. The PGN box is a text input.
critiques.what_i_would_add: An interruptible trace job in engine.js: one `go` per position, yielding between them, cancelable by any user pointerdown, emitting `progress` events the UI maps to 'checking move 9...', with a priority rule that a live move's search pre-empts it.

critiques.strengths: The most renderable spec on the table: tokens for both themes, a 44 px header, one serif line clamped to three lines, the board at full width minus gutters, a 56 px action bar that is empty until a decision is needed. The canned opening hold on the verified 3...Nf6 position sequences the consent dialog after the player already knows what a hold is, which is the single smartest UX decision in the pile. The 2.5 s swap rule is a concrete, testable timing contract. Pieces as inline SVG is correct for headless Chromium and Android.
critiques.weaknesses: 'Floats over the destination with a soft shadow' has the same pending-state problem: the verdict is ~300 ms after landing. The weighted multipv-3 pick for the opponent means parsing every info line and a second move-choice path; fine, but it is tuning work. cburnett is CC BY-SA 3.0, a licence question next to a GPL engine; I would hand-draw twelve silhouettes instead. Swapping in Claude's question while the player is already reading the template is jarring unless the swap is gated on 'no tap yet'. Nothing says pieces are focusable, and keyboard focus is a design rule.
critiques.what_i_would_add: The swap as a state machine: question state is {template, claude-pending, claude}; Claude's text replaces the template only while the hold is still open and no answer tap has happened; Take it back / Play it anyway abort the call's controller so a late reply is cancelled, not rendered.

critiques.strengths: No opponent engine; baked positions; a three-outcome state machine (CAUGHT / SAFE / MISSED) that is trivially testable; the five dots are one render; the turn caption is one attribute.
critiques.weaknesses: The 400 ms rotation on every position is the same flip concern. Grading the Black reply 'within 50 cp of best' needs a multipv or a `searchmoves` search per answer, which is fine but a second search shape. Playing both colours means the input lock must be per-position, not per-colour, and the board must accept pickups for whichever side the state allows.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A `data-side` attribute on the board root that drives which colour the pointer may pick up and what the coordinates say, so the chair swap, the playground's both-sides mode and the puzzle's punishing chair are one mechanism.

critiques.strengths: Entirely chess.js plus one depth-12 search per ghost; the ghost layer is the piece layer at 50% opacity; consequence rings are static data; the position in the URL hash makes sharing free and testable with no backend.
critiques.weaknesses: Tap-to-ghost then tap-to-commit is a different input grammar from tap-tap-to-move; two grammars in one page is a bug farm unless the ghost IS the universal pending state. A curious player placing ten ghosts in ten seconds floods the single worker; each new ghost must `stop` the previous search. Long-press conflicts with drag on touch, as noted.
critiques.what_i_would_add: One `pending` move object shared across modes: the playground's preview and the game's hold are the same UI state with two policies, and the engine queue coalesces searches so the latest ghost wins and the prior search is stopped.

critiques.strengths: The fact-sheet module is specified precisely and it is the one module every concept needs. The SAN regex validator is implementable and measurable in tests. A fresh AbortController per call, aborted by the next move handler, is exactly the contract sample.d.ts asks for. The error-code table is complete. The null-move probe (FEN with side to move swapped, skipped in check) is a clean chess.js plus engine trick.
critiques.weaknesses: The heaviest engine and sample budget of any concept: per bot move, opponent (depth 8) + facts (depth 12 MultiPV 3) + probe (depth 12) + a call, 1.5-2 s on desktop and 3-5 s on a phone, and the bubble often lands after the player has moved on. A bubble 'by the board' at 400 px has nowhere to go but over the board edge, and it competes with Point at It's chips for the same slot.
critiques.what_i_would_add: An engine schedule per move pair in engine.js: opponent first, facts next, the probe only when the facts show a candidate moment, every search cancelable by the player's next pointerdown so the worker is never mid-search when a drop needs a verdict.

critiques.strengths: The default-tier call sits on the result screen with no tools and everything precomputed, which is the right place for a 10-30 s wait; the engine grades the tap-a-move fallback; the review runs when the worker is otherwise idle.
critiques.weaknesses: A text field for reasoning on a phone pushes the board off screen when the keyboard opens. The review (depth 12 on 60 plies) blocks the engine for 20-60 s. 'The board slides to move 12' requires a history cursor, a new component. The 24 h cache keyed by game id means the prompt bytes must be stable across versions or stale cards replay. A progress bar along a move list contradicts 'no move list'.
critiques.what_i_would_add: A replay model in game.js: a history cursor with goto(ply) that drives the same piece layer, so result-screen boards, re-asked drills and any 'show me' share one renderer instead of a second board.

critiques.strengths: Chips come from the fact sheet with no call; arrows are drawn from facts before the call so the UI is instant; the cache key (FEN + chip) uses the platform cache correctly; the quiz answer set is keyed locally; template answers when sample is absent.
